paragraphs: This paper treats neural network learning as statistical inference over possible weights. Conventional training chooses a single weight vector, which can fit the training examples too closely and generalize poorly. The Bayesian approach instead combines predictions from many weight settings according to how probable they are after observing the training data.

The computational proposal is to obtain those weight settings by simulating a stochastic dynamical system. The system is constructed so that its stationary distribution is the posterior distribution over weights. Once sampled in this way, networks contribute to the prediction through their outputs, turning an average over uncertain models into a practical sampling objective.

The approach addresses overfitting through posterior averaging without requiring a validation set. The supplied text also illustrates the probabilistic interpretation with observed outputs modeled as network outputs plus Gaussian noise. The key contribution is the connection between Bayesian prediction and stochastic dynamics: a process that moves through weight space provides the networks whose predictions are averaged.
summary.tldr: Stochastic dynamics can sample neural network weights from their posterior distribution for Bayesian prediction by averaging.

title: Bayesian Learning via Stochastic Dynamics

abstract: We compare the generalization performance of three distinct rep(cid:173) resentation schemes for facial emotions using a single classification strategy (neural network). The face images presented to the clas(cid:173) sifiers are represented as: full face projections of the dataset onto their eigenvectors (eigenfaces); a similar projection constrained to eye and mouth areas (eigenfeatures); and finally a projection of the eye and mouth areas onto the eigenvectors obtained from 32x32 random image patches from the dataset. The latter system achieves 86% generalization on novel face images (individuals the networks were not trained on) drawn from a database in which human sub(cid:173) jects consistently identify a single emotion for the face .

paragraphs: The paper examines how the representation of a face image affects emotion classification on previously unseen people. It compares three representations while keeping the classification strategy fixed as a neural network. This setup focuses attention on how image information is presented to the classifier rather than on choosing different classifier families.

The first representation projects whole faces onto eigenvectors derived from the dataset, producing eigenfaces. The second restricts a similar projection to eye and mouth regions, producing eigenfeatures. The third also uses those regions but projects them onto eigenvectors derived from random 32-by-32 image patches drawn from the dataset.

The third representation achieves 86% generalization on new face images from individuals absent from network training. The database contains faces for which human observers consistently identify one emotion, which defines the setting of the reported result. The finding demonstrates the effectiveness of combining selected facial regions with a basis learned from random image patches when transferring emotion classification to unfamiliar individuals.
summary.tldr: Eye and mouth representations built from random-patch eigenvectors achieve 86% generalization to unseen individuals in the stated emotion dataset.

title: Representing Face Images for Emotion Classification

abstract: When triangulating a belief network we aim to obtain a junction tree of minimum state space. According to (Rose, 1970), searching for the optimal triangulation can be cast as a search over all the permutations of the graph's vertices. Our approach is to embed the discrete set of permutations in a convex continuous domain D. By suitably extending the cost function over D and solving the continous nonlinear optimization task we hope to obtain a good triangulation with respect to the aformentioned cost. This paper presents two ways of embedding the triangulation problem into continuous domain and shows that they perform well compared to the best known heuristic.

By suitably extending the cost function over D and solving the continous nonlinear optimization task we hope to obtain a good triangulation with respect to the aformentioned cost. paragraphs: The paper addresses triangulation of belief networks with the goal of obtaining a junction tree with a small state space. The optimization can be expressed as a search over all orderings of the graph’s vertices. This turns the desired graph transformation into a discrete problem involving a large collection of possible permutations.

The authors propose embedding those permutations in a convex continuous domain. They then extend the cost function to that domain and solve a continuous nonlinear optimization problem. The intended benefit is to use continuous optimization to find a good triangulation under the original state-space objective, providing another route through the discrete search problem.

The paper presents two ways to construct this embedding and reports that both perform well compared with the best known heuristic. The result supports continuous embedding as a practical approach to triangulation. The stated aim is a good solution rather than a guarantee of the optimal one, and the key contribution is translating a permutation-based graph problem into a form accessible to continuous optimization.
summary.tldr: Two continuous embeddings turn belief-network triangulation into nonlinear optimization and perform well against the best known heuristic.

title: Triangulation by Continuous Embedding

abstract: Neural one-unit learning rules for the problem of Independent Com(cid:173) ponent Analysis (ICA) and blind source separation are introduced. In these new algorithms, every ICA neuron develops into a sepa(cid:173) rator that finds one of the independent components. The learning rules use very simple constrained Hebbianjanti-Hebbian learning in which decorrelating feedback may be added. To speed up the convergence of these stochastic gradient descent rules, a novel com(cid:173) putationally efficient fixed-point algorithm is introduced.

In these new algorithms, every ICA neuron develops into a sepa(cid:173) rator that finds one of the independent components. The learning rules use very simple constrained Hebbianjanti-Hebbian learning in which decorrelating feedback may be added. To speed up the convergence of these stochastic gradient descent rules, a novel com(cid:173) putationally efficient fixed-point algorithm is introduced.

paragraphs: This paper introduces learning rules for independent component analysis and blind source separation. The organizing idea is to give each individual neuron the job of finding one independent component. A neuron learns to act as a separator, turning mixed observations into an output corresponding to one of their underlying independent sources.

The proposed rules use simple constrained Hebbian or anti-Hebbian learning, with the option of adding decorrelating feedback. These mechanisms define how the separator adapts while imposing structure on the learning process. The one-unit formulation focuses the learning task on extracting a single component, making that unit the central building block of the approach.

The authors also introduce a computationally efficient fixed-point algorithm to accelerate convergence of the stochastic gradient rules. This adds a second contribution alongside the learning formulation: a faster way to reach the separator sought by the updates. The abstract presents the fixed-point method as a response to convergence speed, linking the design of the learning rule with the practicality of carrying out the resulting computation.
summary.tldr: One-unit ICA rules learn individual source separators, with a fixed-point algorithm introduced to accelerate convergence.

title: One-unit Learning Rules for Independent Component Analysis

abstract: Many machine learning algorithms for clustering or dimensionality re- duction take as input a cloud of points in Euclidean space, and construct a graph with the input data points as vertices. This graph is then parti- tioned (clustering) or used to redeﬁne metric information (dimensional- ity reduction). There has been much recent work on new methods for graph-based clustering and dimensionality reduction, but not much on constructing the graph itself. Graphs typically used include the fully- connected graph, a local ﬁxed-grid graph (for image segmentation) or a nearest-neighbor graph. We suggest that the graph should adapt locally to the structure of the data. This can be achieved by a graph ensemble that combines multiple minimum spanning trees, each ﬁt to a perturbed version of the data set. We show that such a graph ensemble usually pro- duces a better representation of the data manifold than standard methods; and that it provides robustness to a subsequent clustering or dimension- ality reduction algorithm based on the graph.

paragraphs: Graph-based clustering and dimensionality reduction depend on a graph built from the input points. Its edges determine the relationships available to the later algorithm, whether that algorithm partitions the graph or uses it to define distances. This paper concentrates on constructing that graph, a stage the authors argue has received less attention than downstream methods.

The proposed construction combines several minimum spanning trees, each fitted to a perturbed version of the dataset. The resulting graph ensemble is intended to adapt locally to the data's structure. Multiple perturbed constructions contribute to the final representation, making the neighborhood relationships depend on a collection of related views of the same points.

The authors report that these ensembles usually represent the underlying manifold better than standard graph constructions and make subsequent clustering or dimensionality reduction more robust. The qualifier matters: the claim is a usual improvement, not an assertion that every ensemble is superior. The contribution shows that changing the input graph itself can improve the foundation on which several different learning algorithms operate.
summary.tldr: Combining minimum spanning trees from perturbed datasets produces adaptive proximity graphs that usually improve manifold representation and downstream robustness.

title: Proximity Graphs for Clustering and Manifold Learning

abstract: Lasso regression tends to assign zero weights to most irrelevant or redundant features, and hence is a promising technique for feature selection. Its limitation, however, is that it only offers solutions to linear models. Kernel machines with feature scaling techniques have been studied for feature selection with non-linear models. However, such approaches require to solve hard non-convex optimization problems. This paper proposes a new approach named the Feature Vector Machine (FVM). It reformulates the standard Lasso regression into a form isomorphic to SVM, and this form can be easily extended for feature selection with non-linear models by introducing kernels defined on feature vectors. FVM generates sparse solutions in the nonlinear feature space and it is much more tractable compared to feature scaling kernel machines. Our experiments with FVM on simulated data show encouraging results in identifying the small number of dominating features that are non-linearly correlated to the response, a task the standard Lasso fails to complete.

paragraphs: Lasso regression can select features by assigning zero weight to many irrelevant or redundant inputs. The paper addresses its restriction to linear models. Extending feature selection to nonlinear relationships is challenging because kernel methods that scale features can require difficult, nonconvex optimization.

The proposed Feature Vector Machine starts by rewriting standard Lasso in a form structurally equivalent to a support vector machine. This reformulation permits a nonlinear extension through kernels defined on feature vectors. The resulting method produces sparse solutions in the nonlinear feature space and is described as substantially more tractable than kernel machines based on feature scaling.

Experiments on simulated data give encouraging results for identifying a small number of dominant features whose relationships with the response are nonlinear. Standard Lasso fails to complete that task in the reported experiments. The significance is the route from a familiar linear selection method to a nonlinear one: changing the formulation makes kernels available while preserving a sparse representation.
summary.tldr: The Feature Vector Machine reformulates Lasso to enable tractable kernel-based selection of features with nonlinear relationships to the response.

title: From Lasso regression to Feature vector machine

abstract: It has been established that a neuron reproduces highly precise spike response to identical fluctuating input currents. We wish to accurately predict the firing times of a given neuron for any input current. For this purpose we adopt a model that mimics the dynamics of the membrane potential, and then take a cue from its dynamics for predicting the spike occurrence for a novel input current. It is found that the prediction is significantly improved by observing the state space of the membrane potential and its time derivative(s) in advance of a possible spike, in comparison to simply thresholding an instantaneous value of the estimated potential.

It is found that the prediction is significantly improved by observing the state space of the membrane potential and its time derivative(s) in advance of a possible spike, in comparison to simply thresholding an instantaneous value of the estimated potential.

paragraphs: A neuron can respond to repeated identical fluctuating input currents with highly precise spike timing. This motivates the paper's goal of predicting when a given neuron will fire under a new input current. The authors approach the problem by modeling the membrane potential, the changing electrical state that precedes a spike.

The model mimics the dynamics of that potential and uses its behavior to predict spike occurrence. The key comparison is between thresholding a single instantaneous estimated potential and examining a richer state description before a possible spike. That richer description includes the potential together with its time derivative or derivatives, capturing how the voltage is changing.

The authors find that using this dynamical state significantly improves prediction relative to the instantaneous-threshold approach. The result suggests that information about the trajectory toward a spike adds predictive value beyond voltage level alone. It supports a more dynamic spike-prediction rule, while the stated ambition of handling any input current remains the motivating goal.
summary.tldr: Considering membrane voltage and its changes improves spike-time prediction over thresholding the estimated voltage alone.

title: Predicting spike times from subthreshold dynamics of a neuron

abstract: Motivated by stochastic systems in which observed evidence and conditional de- pendencies between states of the network change over time, and certain quantities of interest (marginal distributions, likelihood estimates etc.) must be updated, we study the problem of adaptive inference in tree-structured Bayesian networks. We describe an algorithm for adaptive inference that handles a broad range of changes to the network and is able to maintain marginal distributions, MAP estimates, and data likelihoods in all expected logarithmic time. We give an implementation of our algorithm and provide experiments that show that the algorithm can yield up to two orders of magnitude speedups on answering queries and responding to dy- namic changes over the sum-product algorithm.
originalAbstract: Motivated by stochastic systems in which observed evidence and conditional de- pendencies between states of the network change over time, and certain quantities of interest (marginal distributions, likelihood estimates etc.) must be updated, we study the problem of adaptive inference in tree-structured Bayesian networks. We describe an algorithm for adaptive inference that handles a broad range of changes to the network and is able to maintain marginal distributions, MAP estimates, and data likelihoods in all expected logarithmic time. We give an implementation of our algorithm and provide experiments that show that the algorithm can yield up to two orders of magnitude speedups on answering queries and responding to dy- namic changes over the sum-product algorithm.

paragraphs: In a changing probabilistic system, new evidence can arrive and the dependencies between variables can change. Quantities computed from the network must then be updated to reflect its current state. This paper studies how to perform those updates efficiently for tree-structured Bayesian networks, where the network's connections have a tree organization.

The proposed adaptive inference algorithm handles a broad range of network changes. It maintains marginal distributions, which describe uncertainty about individual variables; MAP estimates, which identify most probable assignments; and data likelihoods, which measure how the model accounts for observed evidence. The authors state expected logarithmic-time performance for maintaining these quantities, making update efficiency a central contribution.

An implementation and experiments compare the method with the sum-product algorithm. The reported gains reach two orders of magnitude for answering queries and responding to dynamic changes. These results show that exploiting the adaptive setting can substantially accelerate inference in the evaluated tree networks, with the stated computational guarantee expressed in expected time.
summary.tldr: An adaptive algorithm maintains inference quantities in changing tree-structured Bayesian networks in expected logarithmic time, with large reported experimental speedups.

title: Efficient Bayesian Inference for Dynamically Changing Graphs

abstract: Multiple object class learning and detection is a challenging problem due to the large number of object classes and their high visual variability. Specialized detectors usually excel in performance, while joint representations optimize sharing and reduce inference time --- but are complex to train. Conveniently, sequential learning of categories cuts down training time by transferring existing knowledge to novel classes, but cannot fully exploit the richness of shareability and might depend on ordering in learning. In hierarchical frameworks these issues have been little explored. In this paper, we show how different types of multi-class learning can be done within one generative hierarchical framework and provide a rigorous experimental analysis of various object class learning strategies as the number of classes grows. Specifically, we propose, evaluate and compare three important types of multi-class learning: 1.) independent training of individual categories, 2.) joint training of classes, 3.) sequential learning of classes. We explore and compare their computational behavior (space and time) and detection performance as a function of the number of learned classes on several recognition data sets.

paragraphs: Learning to detect many object categories raises a tradeoff between specialized detectors and representations shared across classes. Specialized detectors tend to perform well, while sharing can reduce inference time but complicate training. Learning categories sequentially offers another option: transfer existing knowledge to new classes to shorten training, with possible dependence on learning order and incomplete use of shared structure.

The paper implements three strategies within one generative hierarchical framework: training categories independently, training them jointly, and learning them sequentially. A common framework makes it possible to examine these learning choices together. The study focuses particularly on what happens as the number of learned object classes increases.

The authors evaluate detection performance alongside computational requirements, covering both space and time on several recognition datasets. The contribution is a systematic experimental comparison of the three strategies in a hierarchical setting. It makes the relevant decision broader than detection accuracy alone: a strategy must also be assessed by how its training, inference, and storage behavior develop as more categories are introduced.
summary.tldr: The paper compares independent, joint, and sequential object-category learning within one hierarchical framework as the number of classes grows.

title: Evaluating multi-class learning strategies in a generative hierarchical framework for object detection

abstract: Graph matching and MAP inference are essential problems in computer vision and machine learning. We introduce a novel algorithm that can accommodate both problems and solve them efficiently. Recent graph matching algorithms are based on a general quadratic programming formulation, that takes in consideration both unary and second-order terms reflecting the similarities in local appearance as well as in the pairwise geometric relationships between the matched features. In this case the problem is NP-hard and a lot of effort has been spent in finding efficiently approximate solutions by relaxing the constraints of the original problem. Most algorithms find optimal continuous solutions of the modified problem, ignoring during the optimization the original discrete constraints. The continuous solution is quickly binarized at the end, but very little attention is put into this final discretization step. In this paper we argue that the stage in which a discrete solution is found is crucial for good performance. We propose an efficient algorithm, with climbing and convergence properties, that optimizes in the discrete domain the quadratic score, and it gives excellent results either by itself or by starting from the solution returned by any graph matching algorithm. In practice it outperforms state-or-the art algorithms and it also significantly improves their performance if used in combination. When applied to MAP inference, the algorithm is a parallel extension of Iterated Conditional Modes (ICM) with climbing and convergence properties that make it a compelling alternative to the sequential ICM. In our experiments on MAP inference our algorithm proved its effectiveness by outperforming ICM and Max-Product Belief Propagation.

paragraphs: Graph matching often optimizes a continuous relaxation and only afterward rounds it to a discrete assignment. That final step can discard much of the apparent improvement in the relaxed objective. This paper makes discrete solution construction a central part of an algorithm for matching and MAP inference.

The integer projected fixed-point method optimizes a quadratic score incorporating individual-feature similarity and pairwise geometry. It has ascent and convergence properties and can run independently or refine the output of another matching algorithm. In MAP inference, it forms a parallel extension of Iterated Conditional Modes.

Experiments outperform existing graph-matching methods and improve them further when used as a refinement stage. MAP tests also surpass ICM and Max-Product Belief Propagation. The contribution emphasizes that progress must survive the discrete constraints of the original task; a high-quality relaxed solution is only useful if the algorithm can turn it into a good feasible prediction.
summary.tldr: Integer projected fixed-point optimization improves graph matching and MAP inference by treating discrete assignments as part of optimization.

title: An Integer Projected Fixed Point Method for Graph Matching and MAP Inference

abstract: Optimal coding provides a guiding principle for understanding the representation of sensory variables in neural populations. Here we consider the influence of a prior probability distribution over sensory variables on the optimal allocation of cells and spikes in a neural population. We model the spikes of each cell as samples from an independent Poisson process with rate governed by an associated tuning curve. For this response model, we approximate the Fisher information in terms of the density and amplitude of the tuning curves, under the assumption that tuning width varies inversely with cell density. We consider a family of objective functions based on the expected value, over the sensory prior, of a functional of the Fisher information. This family includes lower bounds on mutual information and perceptual discriminability as special cases. In all cases, we find a closed form expression for the optimum, in which the density and gain of the cells in the population are power law functions of the stimulus prior. This also implies a power law relationship between the prior and perceptual discriminability. We show preliminary evidence that the theory successfully predicts the relationship between empirically measured stimulus priors, physiologically measured neural response properties (cell density, tuning widths, and firing rates), and psychophysically measured discrimination thresholds.

paragraphs: This paper asks how the frequency of sensory stimuli should shape an efficiently organized neural population. Its focus is the allocation of cells and spikes: which stimuli receive more representational resources, and how strongly cells respond. The prior distribution over stimuli enters as a description of the sensory conditions the population is expected to encounter.

The model treats each cell's spikes as an independent Poisson process controlled by a tuning curve. It assumes that tuning width varies inversely with cell density and uses this relationship to approximate Fisher information. The authors optimize a family of objectives averaged over the sensory prior, including lower bounds associated with mutual information and perceptual discriminability.

For every objective considered, the optimum has a closed-form expression in which cell density and gain follow power laws of the stimulus prior. The theory also predicts a power-law relationship with discriminability. Preliminary empirical evidence supports links among stimulus frequencies, neural response properties, and discrimination thresholds. These observations support the model provisionally, alongside its explicit response and tuning assumptions.
summary.tldr: Under a specified neural response model, optimal cell density and gain encode stimulus priors through power laws, with preliminary empirical support.

title: Implicit encoding of prior probabilities in optimal neural populations

abstract: Although the standard formulations of prediction problems involve fully-observed and noiseless data drawn in an i.i.d. manner, many applications involve noisy and/or missing data, possibly involving dependencies. We study these issues in the context of high-dimensional sparse linear regression, and propose novel estimators for the cases of noisy, missing, and/or dependent data. Many standard approaches to noisy or missing data, such as those using the EM algorithm, lead to optimization problems that are inherently non-convex, and it is difficult to establish theoretical guarantees on practical algorithms. While our approach also involves optimizing non-convex programs, we are able to both analyze the statistical error associated with any global optimum, and prove that a simple projected gradient descent algorithm will converge in polynomial time to a small neighborhood of the set of global minimizers. On the statistical side, we provide non-asymptotic bounds that hold with high probability for the cases of noisy, missing, and/or dependent data. On the computational side, we prove that under the same types of conditions required for statistical consistency, the projected gradient descent algorithm will converge at geometric rates to a near-global minimizer. We illustrate these theoretical predictions with simulations, showing agreement with the predicted scalings.

We study these issues in the context of high-dimensional sparse linear regression, and propose novel estimators for the cases of noisy, missing, and/or dependent data. Many standard approaches to noisy or missing data, such as those using the EM algorithm, lead to optimization problems that are inherently non-convex, and it is difficult to establish theoretical guarantees on practical algorithms. While our approach also involves optimizing non-convex programs, we are able to both analyze the statistical error associated with any global optimum, and prove that a simple projected gradient descent algorithm will converge in polynomial time to a small neighborhood of the set of global minimizers. On the statistical side, we provide non-asymptotic bounds that hold with high probability for the cases of noisy, missing, and/or dependent data. On the computational side, we prove that under the same types of conditions required for statistical consistency, the projected gradient descent algorithm will converge at geometric rates to a near-global minimizer. We illustrate these theoretical predictions with simulations, showing agreement with the predicted scalings.

paragraphs: The paper develops estimators for high-dimensional sparse linear regression when data are noisy, missing, or dependent. These settings depart from the familiar assumption of complete, noiseless, independently sampled observations. Addressing them often leads to nonconvex optimization, making it difficult to establish both the quality of an estimator and the behavior of a practical algorithm.

The authors analyze those statistical and computational questions together. They bound the statistical error associated with any global optimum and prove that projected gradient descent reaches a small neighborhood of the global minimizers in polynomial time. This separates the accuracy of the optimization target from the ability of an implementable procedure to approach it.

The statistical bounds hold with high probability at finite sample sizes. Under the same types of conditions required for statistical consistency, the optimization algorithm converges geometrically to a near-global minimizer. Simulations agree with the predicted scaling behavior. The resulting message is conditional but substantive: nonconvexity in these regression problems can coexist with useful accuracy guarantees and efficient convergence.
summary.tldr: Nonconvex estimators for sparse regression with imperfect data admit statistical guarantees and polynomial-time convergence to near-global solutions under stated conditions.

title: High-dimensional regression with noisy and missing data: Provable guarantees with non-convexity

abstract: We study differentially private mechanisms for answering \emph{smooth} queries on databases consisting of data points in $\mathbb{R}^d$. A $K$-smooth query is specified by a function whose partial derivatives up to order $K$ are all bounded. We develop an $\epsilon$-differentially private mechanism which for the class of $K$-smooth queries has accuracy $O (\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)^{\frac{K}{2d+K}}/\epsilon)$. The mechanism first outputs a summary of the database. To obtain an answer of a query, the user runs a public evaluation algorithm which contains no information of the database. Outputting the summary runs in time $O(n^{1+\frac{d}{2d+K}})$, and the evaluation algorithm for answering a query runs in time $\tilde O (n^{\frac{d+2+\frac{2d}{K}}{2d+K}} )$. Our mechanism is based on $L_{\infty}$-approximation of (transformed) smooth functions by low degree even trigonometric polynomials with small and efficiently computable coefficients.

paragraphs: This paper studies private answers to smooth queries on databases of points in d-dimensional space. A query is K-smooth when all its partial derivatives through order K are bounded. This restriction supplies mathematical structure that the mechanism can exploit when balancing the accuracy of answers with differential privacy.

The mechanism first releases a summary of the database. Users then answer queries through a public evaluation algorithm, with database information supplied by the released summary. The construction relies on approximating transformed smooth functions using low-degree even trigonometric polynomials whose coefficients are small and efficiently computable.

The authors establish epsilon-differential privacy with accuracy O(n^(-K/(2d+K))/epsilon), where n is the database size. The expression shows how the stated guarantee depends jointly on smoothness, dimension, data size, and privacy strength. They also give explicit runtime bounds for producing the summary and evaluating each query. Separating these stages makes the summary a reusable basis for answering queries in the supported smooth class.
summary.tldr: A differentially private database summary supports efficient smooth-query evaluation with accuracy guarantees that depend on smoothness, dimension, and database size.

title: Efficient Algorithm for Privately Releasing Smooth Queries

abstract: We study Nyström type subsampling approaches to large scale kernel methods, and prove learning bounds in the statistical learning setting, where random sampling and high probability estimates are considered. In particular, we prove that these approaches can achieve optimal learning bounds, provided the subsampling level is suitably chosen. These results suggest a simple incremental variant of Nyström kernel ridge regression, where the subsampling level controls at the same time regularization and computations. Extensive experimental analysis shows that the considered approach achieves state of the art performances on benchmark large scale datasets.

In particular, we prove that these approaches can achieve optimal learning bounds, provided the subsampling level is suitably chosen. These results suggest a simple incremental variant of Nyström kernel ridge regression, where the subsampling level controls at the same time regularization and computations. Extensive experimental analysis shows that the considered approach achieves state of the art performances on benchmark large scale datasets.

paragraphs: Large-scale kernel methods can use Nyström subsampling to reduce the amount of computation required. This paper investigates what that reduction means for learning performance. Its analysis treats the data as randomly sampled and develops guarantees that hold with high probability, connecting the computational approximation to statistical learning behavior.

The main theoretical result is that Nyström approaches can attain optimal learning bounds when the subsampling level is chosen appropriately. That condition is central: the result depends on a suitable amount of subsampling. The analysis also suggests that the size of the approximation can serve as a regularization control, influencing how the method learns as well as how much work it performs.

The authors use this insight to motivate a simple incremental version of Nyström kernel ridge regression. In this approach, the subsampling level jointly controls computation and regularization. Extensive experiments report state-of-the-art performance on large benchmark datasets. The broader contribution is to show that a computational approximation can also provide a statistically meaningful way to regulate learning.
summary.tldr: Suitably chosen Nyström subsampling can achieve optimal learning bounds while using approximation size to control both computation and regularization.

title: Less is More: Nyström Computational Regularization

abstract: Many recent Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) samplers leverage continuous dynamics to define a transition kernel that efficiently explores a target distribution. In tandem, a focus has been on devising scalable variants that subsample the data and use stochastic gradients in place of full-data gradients in the dynamic simulations. However, such stochastic gradient MCMC samplers have lagged behind their full-data counterparts in terms of the complexity of dynamics considered since proving convergence in the presence of the stochastic gradient noise is non-trivial. Even with simple dynamics, significant physical intuition is often required to modify the dynamical system to account for the stochastic gradient noise. In this paper, we provide a general recipe for constructing MCMC samplers--including stochastic gradient versions--based on continuous Markov processes specified via two matrices. We constructively prove that the framework is complete. That is, any continuous Markov process that provides samples from the target distribution can be written in our framework. We show how previous continuous-dynamic samplers can be trivially reinvented in our framework, avoiding the complicated sampler-specific proofs. We likewise use our recipe to straightforwardly propose a new state-adaptive sampler: stochastic gradient Riemann Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (SGRHMC). Our experiments on simulated data and a streaming Wikipedia analysis demonstrate that the proposed SGRHMC sampler inherits the benefits of Riemann HMC, with the scalability of stochastic gradient methods.

paragraphs: Many sampling algorithms explore a probability distribution by simulating continuous dynamics. Using gradients computed from only part of the data can make these methods more scalable, but it introduces additional noise. Accounting for that noise has often required specialized arguments, making more elaborate stochastic-gradient samplers difficult to design and justify.

The paper introduces a general construction in which two matrices specify a continuous Markov process for sampling. Its completeness result says that any continuous Markov process that samples the target distribution can be expressed within this framework. This gives existing continuous-dynamics methods a shared mathematical description and reduces the need for separate sampler-specific proofs.

The authors also use the construction to develop stochastic gradient Riemann Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, a new sampler whose dynamics adapt to the current state. Experiments with simulated data and streaming Wikipedia analysis indicate that it combines benefits of Riemann Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with stochastic-gradient scalability. The contribution therefore includes both a unifying construction and a concrete demonstration of how it supports new sampler designs.
summary.tldr: A complete two-matrix framework unifies continuous-time sampling methods and supports the design of scalable stochastic-gradient samplers.

title: A Complete Recipe for Stochastic Gradient MCMC

abstract: Many popular network models rely on the assumption of (vertex) exchangeability, in which the distribution of the graph is invariant to relabelings of the vertices. However, the Aldous-Hoover theorem guarantees that these graphs are dense or empty with probability one, whereas many real-world graphs are sparse. We present an alternative notion of exchangeability for random graphs, which we call edge exchangeability, in which the distribution of a graph sequence is invariant to the order of the edges. We demonstrate that edge-exchangeable models, unlike models that are traditionally vertex exchangeable, can exhibit sparsity. To do so, we outline a general framework for graph generative models; by contrast to the pioneering work of Caron and Fox (2015), models within our framework are stationary across steps of the graph sequence. In particular, our model grows the graph by instantiating more latent atoms of a single random measure as the dataset size increases, rather than adding new atoms to the measure.
originalAbstract: Many popular network models rely on the assumption of (vertex) exchangeability, in which the distribution of the graph is invariant to relabelings of the vertices. However, the Aldous-Hoover theorem guarantees that these graphs are dense or empty with probability one, whereas many real-world graphs are sparse. We present an alternative notion of exchangeability for random graphs, which we call edge exchangeability, in which the distribution of a graph sequence is invariant to the order of the edges. We demonstrate that edge-exchangeable models, unlike models that are traditionally vertex exchangeable, can exhibit sparsity. To do so, we outline a general framework for graph generative models; by contrast to the pioneering work of Caron and Fox (2015), models within our framework are stationary across steps of the graph sequence. In particular, our model grows the graph by instantiating more latent atoms of a single random measure as the dataset size increases, rather than adding new atoms to the measure.

paragraphs: The paper examines a mismatch between a common symmetry assumption in network models and the sparsity of many real networks. Under traditional vertex exchangeability, relabeling vertices does not change the graph distribution. The abstract invokes the Aldous-Hoover result that such graphs are dense or empty with probability one, creating a difficulty for modeling sparse structures.

The authors instead introduce edge exchangeability: the distribution of a graph sequence is unchanged when the order of its edges changes. They demonstrate that models with this symmetry can exhibit sparsity. The result shows that exchangeability itself need not rule out sparse graphs; the objects over which symmetry is imposed matter.

Their generative framework is stationary across steps of the graph sequence. As the dataset grows, the graph expands by instantiating additional latent atoms from a single random measure, rather than adding atoms to that measure. This provides a specific mechanism for graph growth while maintaining the framework's underlying probabilistic structure across successive observations.
summary.tldr: Replacing vertex exchangeability with edge exchangeability allows random graph models that can be sparse and stationary across graph-sequence steps.

title: Edge-exchangeable graphs and sparsity

abstract: With a goal of understanding what drives generalization in deep networks, we consider several recently suggested explanations, including norm-based control, sharpness and robustness. We study how these measures can ensure generalization, highlighting the importance of scale normalization, and making a connection between sharpness and PAC-Bayes theory. We then investigate how well the measures explain different observed phenomena.
originalAbstract: With a goal of understanding what drives generalization in deep networks, we consider several recently suggested explanations, including norm-based control, sharpness and robustness. We study how these measures can ensure generalization, highlighting the importance of scale normalization, and making a connection between sharpness and PAC-Bayes theory. We then investigate how well the measures explain different observed phenomena.

paragraphs: The paper investigates why deep networks can perform well beyond their training examples. It examines several proposed explanations: controlling parameter norms, measuring sharpness, and studying robustness. The aim is to understand both how these quantities can support generalization guarantees and how well they account for behavior observed in deep learning.

A central point is the importance of scale normalization. When a proposed measure is used to explain generalization, the scale on which it is evaluated affects how it should be interpreted. The paper highlights this issue while studying the candidate measures, making normalization part of the analysis rather than treating the measures as immediately comparable quantities.

The authors also connect sharpness with PAC-Bayes theory, placing this proposed explanation in a framework for reasoning about generalization. They then investigate whether the measures explain different observed phenomena. The contribution is an examination of the relationship between theoretical guarantees and explanatory usefulness: a measure’s ability to support a bound and its ability to explain observed behavior are both subjects of the study.
summary.tldr: The paper examines norm, sharpness, and robustness explanations of deep-network generalization, emphasizing scale normalization and a connection to PAC-Bayes theory.

title: Exploring Generalization in Deep Learning

abstract: Generative adversarial nets (GANs) are a promising technique for modeling a distribution from samples. It is however well known that GAN training suffers from instability due to the nature of its saddle point formulation. In this paper, we explore ways to tackle the instability problem by dualizing the discriminator. We start from linear discriminators in which case conjugate duality provides a mechanism to reformulate the saddle point objective into a maximization problem, such that both the generator and the discriminator of this ‘dualing GAN’ act in concert. We then demonstrate how to extend this intuition to non-linear formulations. For GANs with linear discriminators our approach is able to remove the instability in training, while for GANs with nonlinear discriminators our approach provides an alternative to the commonly used GAN training algorithm.
originalAbstract: Generative adversarial nets (GANs) are a promising technique for modeling a distribution from samples. It is however well known that GAN training suffers from instability due to the nature of its saddle point formulation. In this paper, we explore ways to tackle the instability problem by dualizing the discriminator. We start from linear discriminators in which case conjugate duality provides a mechanism to reformulate the saddle point objective into a maximization problem, such that both the generator and the discriminator of this ‘dualing GAN’ act in concert. We then demonstrate how to extend this intuition to non-linear formulations. For GANs with linear discriminators our approach is able to remove the instability in training, while for GANs with nonlinear discriminators our approach provides an alternative to the commonly used GAN training algorithm.

paragraphs: Generative adversarial networks learn a distribution from examples through a generator and a discriminator. Their training objective has a saddle point structure, with the two components pursuing opposing directions of optimization. The paper targets the training instability associated with that structure by changing the mathematical formulation of the discriminator’s part of the problem.

The authors begin with linear discriminators, where conjugate duality allows the saddle point objective to be rewritten as a maximization problem. In this formulation, the generator and the transformed discriminator work toward the same optimization direction. This is the central idea behind the proposed dualing GAN: reorganize the interaction that produces the training difficulty.

For GANs with linear discriminators, the approach is reported to remove training instability. The paper also extends the underlying intuition to nonlinear formulations, producing an alternative to the usual training algorithm. The distinction matters: the abstract makes the stronger stability claim for the linear case, while presenting the nonlinear extension as another training approach without asserting the same guarantee.
summary.tldr: Dualizing the discriminator removes reported training instability for linear-discriminator GANs and motivates an alternative training method for nonlinear GANs.

title: Dualing GANs

abstract: Self-paced learning and hard example mining re-weight training instances to improve learning accuracy. This paper presents two improved alternatives based on lightweight estimates of sample uncertainty in stochastic gradient descent (SGD): the variance in predicted probability of the correct class across iterations of mini-batch SGD, and the proximity of the correct class probability to the decision threshold. Extensive experimental results on six datasets show that our methods reliably improve accuracy in various network architectures, including additional gains on top of other popular training techniques, such as residual learning, momentum, ADAM, batch normalization, dropout, and distillation.
originalAbstract: Self-paced learning and hard example mining re-weight training instances to improve learning accuracy. This paper presents two improved alternatives based on lightweight estimates of sample uncertainty in stochastic gradient descent (SGD): the variance in predicted probability of the correct class across iterations of mini-batch SGD, and the proximity of the correct class probability to the decision threshold. Extensive experimental results on six datasets show that our methods reliably improve accuracy in various network architectures, including additional gains on top of other popular training techniques, such as residual learning, momentum, ADAM, batch normalization, dropout, and distillation.

paragraphs: Training examples need not contribute equally to neural-network learning. Existing approaches adjust their influence through self-paced learning or hard-example mining. This paper proposes two alternatives that use lightweight estimates of uncertainty to decide which examples deserve emphasis during stochastic gradient descent.

The first estimate tracks how much the predicted probability of an example's correct class changes across training iterations. A probability that fluctuates substantially indicates uncertainty in the model's treatment of that example. The second estimate examines how close the correct-class probability is to the decision threshold. These approaches use different signals: variability over training and proximity to a decision boundary.

Experiments on six datasets report reliable accuracy improvements across several network architectures. The methods also provide additional gains alongside residual learning, momentum, ADAM, batch normalization, dropout, and distillation. The findings support uncertainty-based weighting as a useful addition to those training techniques in the evaluated settings, with the emphasis placed on choosing informative training contributions rather than changing the network architecture.
summary.tldr: Weighting training examples using prediction variability or closeness to a decision threshold improves neural-network accuracy in the reported experiments.

title: Active Bias: Training More Accurate Neural Networks by Emphasizing High Variance Samples

abstract: Adversarial machines, where a learner competes against an adversary, have regained much recent interest in machine learning. They are naturally in the form of saddle-point optimization, often with separable structure but sometimes also with unmanageably large dimension. In this work we show that adversarial prediction under multivariate losses can be solved much faster than they used to be. We first reduce the problem size exponentially by using appropriate sufficient statistics, and then we adapt the new stochastic variance-reduced algorithm of Balamurugan & Bach (2016) to allow any Bregman divergence. We prove that the same linear rate of convergence is retained and we show that for adversarial prediction using KL-divergence we can further achieve a speedup of #example times compared with the Euclidean alternative. We verify the theoretical findings through extensive experiments on two example applications: adversarial prediction and LPboosting.

We verify the theoretical findings through extensive experiments on two example applications: adversarial prediction and LPboosting.

paragraphs: The paper studies optimization problems in which a learner competes with an adversary. These naturally lead to saddle-point formulations, where the two sides optimize in opposing directions. For adversarial prediction with multivariate losses, the resulting problem can be extremely large, making both its representation and its optimization expensive.

The authors first use suitable sufficient statistics to reduce the problem size exponentially. They then adapt an existing stochastic variance-reduced algorithm so that it can use any Bregman divergence. This broadens the geometry available to the optimizer: progress need not be measured using only the usual Euclidean notion of distance.

The analysis retains the algorithm's linear convergence rate. For adversarial prediction, choosing KL divergence can additionally provide a speedup by a factor equal to the number of examples compared with the Euclidean alternative. Experiments on adversarial prediction and LPboosting support the theoretical findings. The two contributions address complementary bottlenecks: sufficient statistics shrink the problem, while the choice of divergence can make solving the reduced problem faster.
summary.tldr: Sufficient statistics and Bregman-based variance reduction accelerate adversarial prediction while preserving a linear convergence guarantee.

title: Bregman Divergence for Stochastic Variance Reduction: Saddle-Point and Adversarial Prediction

abstract: We propose an alternative framework to existing setups for controlling false alarms when multiple A/B tests are run over time. This setup arises in many practical applications, e.g. when pharmaceutical companies test new treatment options against control pills for different diseases, or when internet companies test their default webpages versus various alternatives over time. Our framework proposes to replace a sequence of A/B tests by a sequence of best-arm MAB instances, which can be continuously monitored by the data scientist. When interleaving the MAB tests with an online false discovery rate (FDR) algorithm, we can obtain the best of both worlds: low sample complexity and any time online FDR control. Our main contributions are: (i) to propose reasonable definitions of a null hypothesis for MAB instances; (ii) to demonstrate how one can derive an always-valid sequential p-value that allows continuous monitoring of each MAB test; and (iii) to show that using rejection thresholds of online-FDR algorithms as the confidence levels for the MAB algorithms results in both sample-optimality, high power and low FDR at any point in time. We run extensive simulations to verify our claims, and also report results on real data collected from the New Yorker Cartoon Caption contest.

paragraphs: Running experiments repeatedly creates two connected challenges: deciding which alternative performs best and controlling false discoveries across the growing collection of tests. This paper combines those decisions in a framework that replaces successive A/B tests with successive multi-armed bandit problems, each aimed at identifying the best option.

The framework lets researchers monitor each experiment continuously. The authors define null hypotheses for these bandit problems and construct sequential p-values that remain valid during monitoring. They then connect individual experiments to an online false discovery rate procedure, using its rejection thresholds to set the confidence levels of the bandit algorithms.

This connection makes sampling efficiency and error control part of the same design. The paper reports sample optimality, high statistical power, and low false discovery rates at any point in time within its framework. Extensive simulations and an application to New Yorker Cartoon Caption contest data support the claims. The contribution concerns both how efficiently experiments gather evidence and how their conclusions remain controlled across an ongoing sequence.
summary.tldr: The framework combines continuously monitored bandit experiments with online false discovery control to support efficient testing over time.

title: A framework for Multi-A(rmed)/B(andit) Testing with Online FDR Control

abstract: In this paper we consider parallelization for applications whose objective can be expressed as maximizing a non-monotone submodular function under a cardinality constraint. Our main result is an algorithm whose approximation is arbitrarily close to 1/2e in O(log^2 n) adaptive rounds, where n is the size of the ground set. This is an exponential speedup in parallel running time over any previously studied algorithm for constrained non-monotone submodular maximization. Beyond its provable guarantees, the algorithm performs well in practice. Specifically, experiments on traffic monitoring and personalized data summarization applications show that the algorithm finds solutions whose values are competitive with state-of-the-art algorithms while running in exponentially fewer parallel iterations.

Our main result is an algorithm whose approximation is arbitrarily close to 1/2e in O(log^2 n) adaptive rounds, where n is the size of the ground set. This is an exponential speedup in parallel running time over any previously studied algorithm for constrained non-monotone submodular maximization. Beyond its provable guarantees, the algorithm performs well in practice. Specifically, experiments on traffic monitoring and personalized data summarization applications show that the algorithm finds solutions whose values are competitive with state-of-the-art algorithms while running in exponentially fewer parallel iterations.

paragraphs: This paper studies selecting a limited number of items to maximize a non-monotone submodular objective. Submodularity captures diminishing returns, while non-monotonicity allows an additional item to reduce the objective. The cardinality constraint limits the selection size. The central question is how to solve this class of problems with much less sequential dependence.

The authors give an algorithm with an approximation guarantee arbitrarily close to 1/(2e), using O(log² n) adaptive rounds for a ground set of n items. Adaptive rounds count stages that depend on results from earlier stages. Reducing their number allows more work to proceed in parallel, yielding an exponential improvement in parallel running time over previously studied algorithms for this constrained problem.

Experiments examine traffic monitoring and personalized data summarization. The algorithm produces objective values competitive with state-of-the-art methods while using exponentially fewer parallel iterations. The theoretical and empirical contributions emphasize the same tradeoff: obtaining useful solution quality while sharply reducing the sequential stages that limit parallel execution.
summary.tldr: A non-monotone submodular maximization algorithm achieves a near-1/(2e) approximation in O(log² n) adaptive rounds.

title: Non-monotone Submodular Maximization in Exponentially Fewer Iterations

abstract: This paper studies the problem of deriving fast and accurate classification algorithms with uncertainty quantification. Gaussian process classification provides a principled approach, but the corresponding computational burden is hardly sustainable in large-scale problems and devising efficient alternatives is a challenge. In this work, we investigate if and how Gaussian process regression directly applied to classification labels can be used to tackle this question. While in this case training is remarkably faster, predictions need to be calibrated for classification and uncertainty estimation. To this aim, we propose a novel regression approach where the labels are obtained through the interpretation of classification labels as the coefficients of a degenerate Dirichlet distribution. Extensive experimental results show that the proposed approach provides essentially the same accuracy and uncertainty quantification as Gaussian process classification while requiring only a fraction of computational resources.

Gaussian process classification provides a principled approach, but the corresponding computational burden is hardly sustainable in large-scale problems and devising efficient alternatives is a challenge. In this work, we investigate if and how Gaussian process regression directly applied to classification labels can be used to tackle this question. While in this case training is remarkably faster, predictions need to be calibrated for classification and uncertainty estimation. To this aim, we propose a novel regression approach where the labels are obtained through the interpretation of classification labels as the coefficients of a degenerate Dirichlet distribution. paragraphs: Classification systems often need both accurate decisions and useful estimates of uncertainty. Gaussian process classification offers a principled way to obtain these, but its computational requirements can be difficult to sustain at large scale. This paper investigates whether the faster machinery of Gaussian process regression can provide a practical route to the same goal.

Directly treating classification labels as regression targets makes training faster, but the resulting predictions need calibration for classification and uncertainty estimation. The authors address this through a new construction of the regression labels. They interpret classification labels as coefficients of a degenerate Dirichlet distribution and use that interpretation to formulate the regression approach.

The experiments report essentially the same predictive accuracy and uncertainty quantification as Gaussian process classification while using only a fraction of its computational resources. The significance is that target construction can help connect an efficient regression procedure to a probabilistic classification task. The reported similarity is empirical and qualified as approximate, rather than an exact equivalence between the two models.
summary.tldr: Dirichlet-derived regression targets make Gaussian process classification substantially cheaper while empirically preserving similar accuracy and uncertainty quality.

title: Dirichlet-based Gaussian Processes for Large-scale Calibrated Classification

abstract: We analyze the Kozachenko–Leonenko (KL) fixed k-nearest neighbor estimator for the differential entropy. We obtain the first uniform upper bound on its performance for any fixed k over H\"{o}lder balls on a torus without assuming any conditions on how close the density could be from zero. Accompanying a recent minimax lower bound over the H\"{o}lder ball, we show that the KL estimator for any fixed k is achieving the minimax rates up to logarithmic factors without cognizance of the smoothness parameter s of the H\"{o}lder ball for $s \in (0,2]$ and arbitrary dimension d, rendering it the first estimator that provably satisfies this property.
originalAbstract: We analyze the Kozachenko–Leonenko (KL) fixed k-nearest neighbor estimator for the differential entropy. We obtain the first uniform upper bound on its performance for any fixed k over H\"{o}lder balls on a torus without assuming any conditions on how close the density could be from zero. Accompanying a recent minimax lower bound over the H\"{o}lder ball, we show that the KL estimator for any fixed k is achieving the minimax rates up to logarithmic factors without cognizance of the smoothness parameter s of the H\"{o}lder ball for $s \in (0,2]$ and arbitrary dimension d, rendering it the first estimator that provably satisfies this property.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes the Kozachenko–Leonenko estimator of differential entropy, which uses distances to a fixed number of nearest neighbors. The central question is how its estimation error compares with the best achievable performance across a class of underlying probability densities, and whether it needs prior knowledge of their smoothness.

The authors establish a uniform upper bound over Hölder classes on a torus for any fixed neighbor count. The bound does not require restrictions preventing the density from approaching zero. Comparing this result with an existing minimax lower bound shows that the estimator achieves the optimal rate up to logarithmic factors for smoothness values greater than zero and at most two, in arbitrary dimension.

The estimator achieves this without knowing the smoothness parameter. That is the adaptive aspect of the result: the stated guarantee does not require selecting the estimator using that unknown property. The authors identify it as the first estimator proved to have this combination of guarantees. The contribution gives a widely defined nearest-neighbor procedure a precise near-optimality justification within the specified distribution classes.
summary.tldr: The fixed-neighbor KL entropy estimator achieves minimax rates up to logarithmic factors without knowing smoothness over the specified Hölder classes.

title: The Nearest Neighbor Information Estimator is Adaptively Near Minimax Rate-Optimal

abstract: We analyze the global convergence of gradient descent for deep linear residual networks by proposing a new initialization: zero-asymmetric (ZAS) initialization. It is motivated by avoiding stable manifolds of saddle points. We prove that under the ZAS initialization, for an arbitrary target matrix, gradient descent converges to an $\varepsilon$-optimal point in $O\left( L^3 \log(1/\varepsilon) \right)$ iterations, which scales polynomially with the network depth $L$. Our result and the $\exp(\Omega(L))$ convergence time for the standard initialization (Xavier or near-identity) \cite{shamir2018exponential} together demonstrate the importance of the residual structure and the initialization in the optimization for deep linear neural networks, especially when $L$ is large.
originalAbstract: We analyze the global convergence of gradient descent for deep linear residual networks by proposing a new initialization: zero-asymmetric (ZAS) initialization. It is motivated by avoiding stable manifolds of saddle points. We prove that under the ZAS initialization, for an arbitrary target matrix, gradient descent converges to an $\varepsilon$-optimal point in $O\left( L^3 \log(1/\varepsilon) \right)$ iterations, which scales polynomially with the network depth $L$. Our result and the $\exp(\Omega(L))$ convergence time for the standard initialization (Xavier or near-identity) \cite{shamir2018exponential} together demonstrate the importance of the residual structure and the initialization in the optimization for deep linear neural networks, especially when $L$ is large.

paragraphs: This paper studies how gradient descent trains deep linear residual networks, focusing on the interaction between depth and initialization. The authors introduce zero-asymmetric initialization, abbreviated ZAS. Its motivation is to avoid stable manifolds of saddle points: configurations associated with saddle points that can obstruct progress toward a good solution.

For an arbitrary target matrix, the authors prove that gradient descent under ZAS reaches an epsilon-optimal point in O(L³ log(1/epsilon)) iterations, where L is network depth. The bound grows polynomially with depth and logarithmically with the inverse of the requested accuracy. It therefore gives an explicit relationship between network size, optimization precision, and the number of iterations.

The paper contrasts this guarantee with an existing exponential-in-depth convergence-time result for standard Xavier or near-identity initialization. Together, these results demonstrate why residual structure and initialization matter for optimizing deep linear networks, especially at large depths. The guarantee concerns this particular linear residual setting and the proposed initialization, which are central to the result’s meaning.
summary.tldr: Zero-asymmetric initialization gives gradient descent a polynomial-in-depth convergence guarantee for deep linear residual networks.

title: Global Convergence of Gradient Descent for Deep Linear Residual Networks

abstract: Interest point detection and local feature description are fundamental steps in many computer vision applications. Classical approaches are based on a detect-then-describe paradigm where separate handcrafted methods are used to first identify repeatable keypoints and then represent them with a local descriptor. Neural networks trained with metric learning losses have recently caught up with these techniques, focusing on learning repeatable saliency maps for keypoint detection or learning descriptors at the detected keypoint locations. In this work, we argue that repeatable regions are not necessarily discriminative and can therefore lead to select suboptimal keypoints. Furthermore, we claim that descriptors should be learned only in regions for which matching can be performed with high confidence. We thus propose to jointly learn keypoint detection and description together with a predictor of the local descriptor discriminativeness. This allows to avoid ambiguous areas, thus leading to reliable keypoint detection and description. Our detection-and-description approach simultaneously outputs sparse, repeatable and reliable keypoints that outperforms state-of-the-art detectors and descriptors on the HPatches dataset and on the recent Aachen Day-Night localization benchmark.

paragraphs: Image matching requires finding useful points and describing their local appearance so they can be recognized elsewhere. A point may be detected repeatedly yet still be difficult to distinguish from other points. R2D2 focuses on this distinction between repeatability and reliability: selecting a location consistently does not guarantee that its descriptor supports a confident match.

The method jointly learns point detection, local descriptors, and a prediction of each descriptor’s discriminativeness. That additional prediction helps avoid ambiguous image regions. The authors also argue that descriptor learning should focus on regions where matching can be performed confidently. Detection and description are therefore coordinated around both the ability to rediscover a point and the ability to identify it unambiguously.

The system outputs a sparse collection of keypoints designed to be both repeatable and reliable. It outperforms leading detectors and descriptors on HPatches and the Aachen Day-Night localization benchmark. These results support assessing the quality of a potential match during keypoint selection, rather than treating repeatable detection as sufficient evidence that a point will be useful.
summary.tldr: R2D2 jointly learns keypoints, descriptors, and descriptor reliability to select image locations that are both repeatable and confidently matchable.

title: R2D2: Reliable and Repeatable Detector and Descriptor

abstract: Neural network-based generative language models like ELMo and BERT can work effectively as general purpose sentence encoders in text classification without further fine-tuning. Is it possible to adapt them in a similar way for use as general-purpose decoders? For this to be possible, it would need to be the case that for any target sentence of interest, there is some continuous representation that can be passed to the language model to cause it to reproduce that sentence. We set aside the difficult problem of designing an encoder that can produce such representations and, instead, ask directly whether such representations exist at all. To do this, we introduce a pair of effective, complementary methods for feeding representations into pretrained unconditional language models and a corresponding set of methods to map sentences into and out of this representation space, the reparametrized sentence space. We then investigate the conditions under which a language model can be made to generate a sentence through the identification of a point in such a space and find that it is possible to recover arbitrary sentences nearly perfectly with language models and representations of moderate size.

This paper asks whether they can also serve as general-purpose decoders. That possibility requires a continuous representation that causes the model to reproduce any particular target sentence of interest.

The authors deliberately separate this question from the harder task of building an encoder that reliably produces those representations. They introduce two complementary ways to feed representations into pretrained unconditional language models, together with methods for mapping sentences into and out of the resulting reparametrized sentence space. They then investigate when a point in that space can generate a desired sentence.

The study finds that arbitrary sentences can be recovered nearly perfectly using models and representations of moderate size. This supports the feasibility of using such models as decoders through continuous representations. The result concerns finding representations that enable recovery; designing a general encoder to produce them remains outside the problem the paper chooses to solve.
summary.tldr: The study finds continuous representations that let pretrained unconditional language models recover arbitrary sentences nearly perfectly.

title: Can Unconditional Language Models Recover Arbitrary Sentences?

abstract: While Nash equilibrium in extensive-form games is well understood, very little is known about the properties of extensive-form correlated equilibrium (EFCE), both from a behavioral and from a computational point of view. In this setting, the strategic behavior of players is complemented by an external device that privately recommends moves to agents as the game progresses; players are free to deviate at any time, but will then not receive future recommendations. Our contributions are threefold. First, we show that an EFCE can be formulated as the solution to a bilinear saddle-point problem. To showcase how this novel formulation can inspire new algorithms to compute EFCEs, we propose a simple subgradient descent method which exploits this formulation and structural properties of EFCEs. Our method has better scalability than the prior approach based on linear programming. Second, we propose two benchmark games, which we hope will serve as the basis for future evaluation of EFCE solvers. These games were chosen so as to cover two natural application domains for EFCE: conflict resolution via a mediator, and bargaining and negotiation. Third, we document the qualitative behavior of EFCE in our proposed games. We show that the social-welfare-maximizing equilibria in these games are highly nontrivial and exhibit surprisingly subtle sequential behavior that so far has not received attention in the literature.

paragraphs: The paper examines correlated equilibrium in games that unfold through a sequence of decisions. An external device privately recommends moves as play progresses. Players may reject a recommendation, but doing so ends their access to future recommendations. This setup makes the timing and continuation of advice part of the strategic situation.

The authors show that an extensive-form correlated equilibrium can be represented as the solution of a bilinear saddle-point problem. They use this representation, together with structural properties of these equilibria, to develop a simple subgradient descent method. The method offers better scalability than the prior linear-programming approach, providing a computational use for the new formulation.

The paper also introduces two benchmark games covering mediation for conflict resolution and bargaining or negotiation. Studying these games reveals that equilibria maximizing social welfare can involve subtle sequential behavior. These examples therefore serve two purposes: they provide problems for evaluating future solvers and show why understanding correlated recommendations requires attention to how decisions unfold over time.
summary.tldr: A saddle-point formulation enables a more scalable correlated-equilibrium solver and reveals subtle recommendation strategies in sequential games.

title: Correlation in Extensive-Form Games: Saddle-Point Formulation and Benchmarks

abstract: We provide single-model estimates of aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty for deep neural networks. To estimate aleatoric uncertainty, we propose Simultaneous Quantile Regression (SQR), a loss function to learn all the conditional quantiles of a given target variable. These quantiles can be used to compute well-calibrated prediction intervals. To estimate epistemic uncertainty, we propose Orthonormal Certificates (OCs), a collection of diverse non-constant functions that map all training samples to zero. These certificates map out-of-distribution examples to non-zero values, signaling epistemic uncertainty. Our uncertainty estimators are computationally attractive, as they do not require ensembling or retraining deep models, and achieve state-of-the-art performance.
