To estimate aleatoric uncertainty, we propose Simultaneous Quantile Regression (SQR), a loss function to learn all the conditional quantiles of a given target variable. These quantiles can be used to compute well-calibrated prediction intervals. To estimate epistemic uncertainty, we propose Orthonormal Certificates (OCs), a collection of diverse non-constant functions that map all training samples to zero. These certificates map out-of-distribution examples to non-zero values, signaling epistemic uncertainty. Our uncertainty estimators are computationally attractive, as they do not require ensembling or retraining deep models, and achieve state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: A neural network’s prediction can be uncertain because the target itself varies or because the input falls outside familiar data. This paper offers single-model estimates for these two forms, called aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. The approach avoids needing an ensemble of deep models or retraining those models.

For aleatoric uncertainty, Simultaneous Quantile Regression learns all conditional quantiles of a target variable through a proposed loss function. Quantiles describe different positions in the target’s conditional distribution and can be used to form well-calibrated prediction intervals. This provides information about the range of plausible outcomes rather than just a single predicted value.

For epistemic uncertainty, Orthonormal Certificates are diverse, nonconstant functions that return zero on all training samples. They return nonzero values on out-of-distribution examples, providing an uncertainty signal. The authors report state-of-the-art performance and emphasize computational attractiveness. The two components address different uncertainty sources within the paper’s single-model approach.
summary.tldr: Quantile regression and orthonormal certificates estimate two forms of uncertainty without ensembling or retraining deep models.

title: Single-Model Uncertainties for Deep Learning

abstract: This work tackles the problem of robust zero-shot planning in non-stationary stochastic environments. We study Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) evolving over time and consider Model-Based Reinforcement Learning algorithms in this setting. We make two hypotheses: 1) the environment evolves continuously with a bounded evolution rate; 2) a current model is known at each decision epoch but not its evolution. Our contribution can be presented in four points. 1) we define a specific class of MDPs that we call Non-Stationary MDPs (NSMDPs). We introduce the notion of regular evolution by making an hypothesis of Lipschitz-Continuity on the transition and reward functions w.r.t. time; 2) we consider a planning agent using the current model of the environment but unaware of its future evolution. This leads us to consider a worst-case method where the environment is seen as an adversarial agent; 3) following this approach, we propose the Risk-Averse Tree-Search (RATS) algorithm, a zero-shot Model-Based method similar to Minimax search; 4) we illustrate the benefits brought by RATS empirically and compare its performance with reference Model-Based algorithms.

paragraphs: Planning becomes difficult when an environment changes while decisions are being made. This paper studies a setting where the agent knows the current environment model at each decision point but does not know how it will evolve. It assumes continuous change at a bounded rate, giving the planner some structure despite that uncertainty.

The authors formalize this setting as non-stationary Markov decision processes. Transition and reward functions satisfy a Lipschitz continuity condition with respect to time, which limits how rapidly they can change. Planning then treats the environment's possible evolution as adversarial, asking how to act under an unfavorable future consistent with the assumed regularity.

The resulting Risk-Averse Tree-Search algorithm, or RATS, is a zero-shot model-based planning method resembling Minimax search. Its worst-case perspective addresses uncertainty about future change rather than requiring that evolution to be known. Experiments illustrate its benefits and compare performance with reference model-based algorithms, grounding the proposed planning strategy in empirical evaluation.
summary.tldr: RATS plans against worst-case environmental change when the current model is known and transition and reward functions evolve at bounded rates.

title: Non-Stationary Markov Decision Processes, a Worst-Case Approach using Model-Based Reinforcement Learning

abstract: A broad class of convex optimization problems can be formulated as a semidefinite program (SDP), minimization of a convex function over the positive-semidefinite cone subject to some affine constraints. The majority of classical SDP solvers are designed for the deterministic setting where problem data is readily available. In this setting, generalized conditional gradient methods (aka Frank-Wolfe-type methods) provide scalable solutions by leveraging the so-called linear minimization oracle instead of the projection onto the semidefinite cone. Most problems in machine learning and modern engineering applications, however, contain some degree of stochasticity. In this work, we propose the first conditional-gradient-type method for solving stochastic optimization problems under affine constraints. Our method guarantees O(k^{-1/3}) convergence rate in expectation on the objective residual and O(k^{-5/12}) on the feasibility gap.

paragraphs: Many convex optimization problems can be expressed as semidefinite programs, combining a positive-semidefinite constraint with affine constraints. Classical solvers commonly assume that problem data are directly available. Machine learning and engineering applications often include stochasticity, creating a need for methods that can operate with uncertain or sampled information.

Frank-Wolfe-type methods offer a scalable approach by using a linear minimization oracle instead of projecting onto the semidefinite cone. This paper introduces a conditional-gradient method for stochastic optimization with affine constraints. Its contribution extends this style of optimization to a setting where both random information and explicit constraints must be handled.

The authors prove an expected objective residual rate of O(k^(-1/3)) and a feasibility gap rate of O(k^(-5/12)), where k counts iterations. The objective residual tracks progress toward the optimal objective value, while the feasibility gap tracks constraint violation. Reporting both matters because a useful constrained solution must make progress on the objective and satisfy the constraints. The guarantees quantify how the method improves on these two requirements as computation proceeds.
summary.tldr: A stochastic Frank-Wolfe-type method handles affine constraints with convergence guarantees for objective error and constraint violation.

title: Stochastic Frank-Wolfe for Composite Convex Minimization

abstract: Efforts to understand the generalization mystery in deep learning have led to the belief that gradient-based optimization induces a form of implicit regularization, a bias towards models of low "complexity." We study the implicit regularization of gradient descent over deep linear neural networks for matrix completion and sensing, a model referred to as deep matrix factorization. Our first finding, supported by theory and experiments, is that adding depth to a matrix factorization enhances an implicit tendency towards low-rank solutions, oftentimes leading to more accurate recovery. Secondly, we present theoretical and empirical arguments questioning a nascent view by which implicit regularization in matrix factorization can be captured using simple mathematical norms. Our results point to the possibility that the language of standard regularizers may not be rich enough to fully encompass the implicit regularization brought forth by gradient-based optimization.

paragraphs: Gradient descent can favor particular solutions even when the training objective contains no explicit preference for them. This behavior is called implicit regularization. The paper investigates it in deep matrix factorization, where a sequence of linear transformations represents a matrix, focusing on matrix completion and sensing problems.

The first finding is that increasing depth strengthens a tendency toward low-rank solutions. A low-rank matrix has a more compact underlying structure, so favoring such solutions can help recover the matrix from incomplete information. Theory and experiments support this depth-dependent tendency, and the authors report that it often produces more accurate recovery.

The second finding concerns how to describe that preference mathematically. The authors present theoretical and empirical arguments against the view that simple matrix norms fully capture implicit regularization in this setting. Their results suggest that standard regularizers may be too limited to describe all the effects of gradient-based optimization. The conclusion is a qualified challenge to a common explanatory framework, alongside evidence that depth changes the kinds of solutions optimization favors.
summary.tldr: Deeper matrix factorizations strengthen gradient descent’s bias toward low rank, while simple norms may not fully explain that bias.

title: Implicit Regularization in Deep Matrix Factorization

abstract: We consider the problem of differentially private selection. Given a finite set of candidate items, and a quality score for each item, our goal is to design a differentially private mechanism that returns an item with a score that is as high as possible. The most commonly used mechanism for this task is the exponential mechanism. In this work, we propose a new mechanism for this task based on a careful analysis of the privacy constraints. The expected score of our mechanism is always at least as large as the exponential mechanism, and can offer improvements up to a factor of two. Our mechanism is simple to implement and runs in linear time.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to choose a high-quality item while satisfying differential privacy. The input consists of a finite collection of candidates and a quality score for each. The objective is to return an item with as large a score as possible while respecting the privacy requirement governing the selection mechanism.

The authors propose Permute-and-Flip as an alternative to the commonly used exponential mechanism. Its design comes from a careful analysis of the privacy constraints. The key result compares expected scores: the new mechanism's expectation is always at least as large as that of the exponential mechanism. This guarantee concerns average selection quality under the mechanism's randomness.

The improvement can reach a factor of two, although that maximum gain is not asserted for every input. The method is also simple to implement and runs in time linear in the number of candidates. These properties pair a strong expected-quality comparison with a computationally straightforward mechanism for private selection.
summary.tldr: Permute-and-Flip performs private selection in linear time with expected score at least as high as the exponential mechanism.

title: Permute-and-Flip: A new mechanism for differentially private selection

abstract: Causal discovery is at the core of human cognition. It enables us to reason about the environment and make counterfactual predictions about unseen scenarios that can vastly differ from our previous experiences. We consider the task of causal discovery from videos in an end-to-end fashion without supervision on the ground-truth graph structure. In particular, our goal is to discover the structural dependencies among environmental and object variables: inferring the type and strength of interactions that have a causal effect on the behavior of the dynamical system. Our model consists of (a) a perception module that extracts a semantically meaningful and temporally consistent keypoint representation from images, (b) an inference module for determining the graph distribution induced by the detected keypoints, and (c) a dynamics module that can predict the future by conditioning on the inferred graph. We assume access to different configurations and environmental conditions, i.e., data from unknown interventions on the underlying system; thus, we can hope to discover the correct underlying causal graph without explicit interventions. We evaluate our method in a planar multi-body interaction environment and scenarios involving fabrics of different shapes like shirts and pants. Experiments demonstrate that our model can correctly identify the interactions from a short sequence of images and make long-term future predictions. The causal structure assumed by the model also allows it to make counterfactual predictions and extrapolate to systems of unseen interaction graphs or graphs of various sizes.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to infer physical interactions directly from video without being given the correct interaction graph during training. The goal is to identify which environmental and object variables influence a system's behavior, including the types and strengths of their interactions. Such a representation can support predictions about configurations beyond those previously observed.

The model connects three components. A perception module extracts meaningful keypoints that remain consistent over time. An inference module estimates a distribution over interaction graphs from those keypoints. A dynamics module predicts future behavior using the inferred graph. The approach assumes access to different configurations and environmental conditions, interpreted as unknown interventions on the system; this variation provides the basis for attempting causal discovery.

Experiments cover planar systems with multiple interacting bodies and fabrics shaped like shirts and pants. The model identifies interactions from short image sequences and produces long-term predictions. Its assumed causal structure also supports counterfactual predictions and extrapolation to previously unseen interaction graphs or different graph sizes.
summary.tldr: A video model learns physical interaction graphs and uses them for future and counterfactual predictions, assuming observations across varying system conditions.

title: Causal Discovery in Physical Systems from Videos

abstract: Most of the work on interpretable machine learning has focused on designing either inherently interpretable models, which typically trade-off accuracy for interpretability, or post-hoc explanation systems, whose explanation quality can be unpredictable. Our method, ExpO, is a hybridization of these approaches that regularizes a model for explanation quality at training time. Importantly, these regularizers are differentiable, model agnostic, and require no domain knowledge to define. We demonstrate that post-hoc explanations for ExpO-regularized models have better explanation quality, as measured by the common fidelity and stability metrics. We verify that improving these metrics leads to significantly more useful explanations with a user study on a realistic task.

Importantly, these regularizers are differentiable, model agnostic, and require no domain knowledge to define. We demonstrate that post-hoc explanations for ExpO-regularized models have better explanation quality, as measured by the common fidelity and stability metrics. We verify that improving these metrics leads to significantly more useful explanations with a user study on a realistic task.

paragraphs: Explanations of a trained black-box model can vary in quality, while choosing an inherently interpretable model can involve an accuracy trade-off. ExpO combines elements of these approaches by making explanation quality part of training. It regularizes the predictive model so that explanations produced afterward are better supported by the behavior the model has learned.

The proposed regularizers are differentiable, do not depend on a particular model family, and require no domain knowledge to define. These properties make explanation quality an optimization target rather than only a criterion checked after training. The approach retains a distinction between the predictive model and its post-hoc explanation system while deliberately shaping the former to improve the latter.

The authors show improvements in fidelity and stability, two common measures of explanation quality. They also conduct a user study on a realistic task, finding that improvements in those measures lead to significantly more useful explanations. This human evaluation connects the technical criteria to practical usefulness, supporting training-time regularization as a way to improve subsequent interpretation.
summary.tldr: ExpO trains black-box models with explanation-quality regularizers, improving explanation fidelity, stability, and usefulness in a user study.

title: Regularizing Black-box Models for Improved Interpretability

abstract: Haplotype assembly and viral quasispecies reconstruction are challenging tasks concerned with analysis of genomic mixtures using sequencing data. High-throughput sequencing technologies generate enormous amounts of short fragments (reads) which essentially oversample components of a mixture; the representation redundancy enables reconstruction of the components (haplotypes, viral strains). The reconstruction problem, known to be NP-hard, boils down to grouping together reads originating from the same component in a mixture. Existing methods struggle to solve this problem with required level of accuracy and low runtimes; the problem is becoming increasingly more challenging as the number and length of the components increase. This paper proposes a read clustering method based on a convolutional auto-encoder designed to first project sequenced fragments to a low-dimensional space and then estimate the probability of the read origin using learned embedded features. The components are reconstructed by finding consensus sequences that agglomerate reads from the same origin. Mini-batch stochastic gradient descent and dimension reduction of reads allow the proposed method to efficiently deal with massive numbers of long reads. Experiments on simulated, semi-experimental and experimental data demonstrate the ability of the proposed method to accurately reconstruct haplotypes and viral quasispecies, often demonstrating superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. Source codes are available at https://github.com/WuLoli/CAECseq.

paragraphs: Sequencing a genomic mixture produces many fragments drawn from different underlying sequences. Reconstructing haplotypes or viral strains therefore requires deciding which fragments came from the same source. Repeated coverage supplies useful evidence, but the grouping problem is computationally difficult and becomes more challenging as mixture components grow in number and length.

The paper proposes a convolutional auto-encoder that maps sequencing reads into a lower-dimensional representation. From these learned features, the method estimates the probability that each read belongs to a particular source. It then combines reads assigned to the same source into a consensus sequence. This connects representation learning directly to the grouping step needed for reconstruction.

Dimensionality reduction and mini-batch stochastic gradient descent help the method handle large collections of long reads. Experiments with simulated, semi-experimental, and experimental data show accurate reconstruction of haplotypes and viral mixtures, often outperforming existing methods. The findings support learned read representations as a practical way to improve reconstruction, without claiming that they remove the underlying computational difficulty.
summary.tldr: A convolutional auto-encoder learns compact sequencing-read features that support accurate grouping and reconstruction of haplotypes and viral strains.

title: A Convolutional Auto-Encoder for Haplotype Assembly and Viral Quasispecies Reconstruction

abstract: This paper presents parametric instance classification (PIC) for unsupervised visual feature learning. Unlike the state-of-the-art approaches which do instance discrimination in a dual-branch non-parametric fashion, PIC directly performs a one-branch parametric instance classification, revealing a simple framework similar to supervised classification and without the need to address the information leakage issue. We show that the simple PIC framework can be as effective as the state-of-the-art approaches, i.e. SimCLR and MoCo v2, by adapting several common component settings used in the state-of-the-art approaches. We hope that the PIC framework can serve as a simple baseline to facilitate future study. The code and network configurations are available at \url{https://github.com/bl0/PIC}.

title: Parametric Instance Classification for Unsupervised Visual Feature learning

abstract: We introduce a general framework for designing and training neural network layers whose forward passes can be interpreted as solving non-smooth convex optimization problems, and whose architectures are derived from an optimization algorithm. We focus on convex games, solved by local agents represented by the nodes of a graph and interacting through regularization functions. This approach is appealing for solving imaging problems, as it allows the use of classical image priors within deep models that are trainable end to end. The priors used in this presentation include variants of total variation, Laplacian regularization, bilateral filtering, sparse coding on learned dictionaries, and non-local self similarities. Our models are fully interpretable as well as parameter and data efficient. Our experiments demonstrate their effectiveness on a large diversity of tasks ranging from image denoising and compressed sensing for fMRI to dense stereo matching.

For imaging, this provides a way to incorporate established image priors into models trained end to end. The authors describe the resulting models as interpretable and efficient in their use of parameters and data. Their experiments cover image denoising, compressed sensing for fMRI, and dense stereo matching. The range of applications supports the framework's flexibility: different imaging assumptions can shape the model's computations while its parameters remain learnable from data.
summary.tldr: The framework turns convex optimization and image priors into interpretable neural layers that can be trained end to end.

title: A Flexible Framework for Designing Trainable Priors with Adaptive Smoothing and Game Encoding

abstract: Due to its decentralized nature, Federated Learning (FL) lends itself to adversarial attacks in the form of backdoors during training. The goal of a backdoor is to corrupt the performance of the trained model on specific sub-tasks (e.g., by classifying green cars as frogs). A range of FL backdoor attacks have been introduced in the literature, but also methods to defend against them, and it is currently an open question whether FL systems can be tailored to be robust against backdoors. In this work, we provide evidence to the contrary. We first establish that, in the general case, robustness to backdoors implies model robustness to adversarial examples, a major open problem in itself. Furthermore, detecting the presence of a backdoor in a FL model is unlikely assuming first-order oracles or polynomial time. We couple our theoretical results with a new family of backdoor attacks, which we refer to as edge-case backdoors. An edge-case backdoor forces a model to misclassify on seemingly easy inputs that are however unlikely to be part of the training, or test data, i.e., they live on the tail of the input distribution. We explain how these edge-case backdoors can lead to unsavory failures and may have serious repercussions on fairness. We further exhibit that, with careful tuning at the side of the adversary, one can insert them across a range of machine learning tasks (e.g., image classification, OCR, text prediction, sentiment analysis), and bypass state-of-the-art defense mechanisms.

Such failures may have fairness consequences because rarely encountered inputs can be targeted even when routine evaluation misses them.
summary.tldr: Theoretical obstacles and attacks on rare inputs expose serious challenges for defending federated learning against backdoors.

title: Attack of the Tails: Yes, You Really Can Backdoor Federated Learning

abstract: Understanding the inner workings of complex machine learning models is a long-standing problem and most recent research has focused on local interpretability. To assess the role of individual input features in a global sense, we explore the perspective of defining feature importance through the predictive power associated with each feature. We introduce two notions of predictive power (model-based and universal) and formalize this approach with a framework of additive importance measures, which unifies numerous methods in the literature. We then propose SAGE, a model-agnostic method that quantifies predictive power while accounting for feature interactions. Our experiments show that SAGE can be calculated efficiently and that it assigns more accurate importance values than other methods.

paragraphs: Explaining one prediction and explaining a feature's overall contribution are different interpretability tasks. This paper focuses on the latter, defining global feature importance through predictive power. The guiding question is how much each input feature contributes to useful prediction across the problem, rather than how it affects only one particular model output.

The authors distinguish model-based and universal notions of predictive power and organize feature attribution within a framework of additive importance measures. This framework unifies numerous existing methods. They then introduce SAGE, a model-agnostic approach that quantifies predictive power while accounting for feature interactions, recognizing that the usefulness of one feature can depend on other available features.

Experiments show that SAGE can be computed efficiently and assigns more accurate importance values than the compared methods. The contribution is both conceptual and practical: it provides a common basis for relating feature-importance methods and an estimator designed to reflect interacting contributions. Its global perspective makes the resulting importance values about overall predictive usefulness rather than isolated explanations of individual cases.
summary.tldr: SAGE measures global feature importance through predictive power while accounting for interactions among features.

title: Understanding Global Feature Contributions With Additive Importance Measures

abstract: In today’s clinical practice, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is routinely accelerated through subsampling of the associated Fourier domain. Currently, the construction of these subsampling strategies - known as experimental design - relies primarily on heuristics. We propose to learn experimental design strategies for accelerated MRI with policy gradient methods. Unexpectedly, our experiments show that a simple greedy approximation of the objective leads to solutions nearly on-par with the more general non-greedy approach. We offer a partial explanation for this phenomenon rooted in greater variance in the non-greedy objective's gradient estimates, and experimentally verify that this variance hampers non-greedy models in adapting their policies to individual MR images. We empirically show that this adaptivity is key to improving subsampling designs.

paragraphs: Accelerated MRI collects only part of the measurements available in the Fourier domain. Deciding which measurements to acquire is an experimental design problem, and existing strategies rely mainly on heuristics. This paper instead learns acquisition strategies using policy gradient methods, treating the measurement design as a policy that can be improved through training.

The experiments compare a general non-greedy approach with a simpler greedy approximation of its objective. Unexpectedly, the greedy version produces solutions nearly as good as those of the more general approach. The authors offer a partial explanation: gradient estimates for the non-greedy objective have greater variance, making the training signal less consistent.

Further experiments show that this variance interferes with the non-greedy models' ability to adapt their policies to individual MR images. Such adaptation is empirically important for improving measurement designs. The result highlights a tension between a more general objective and how effectively that objective can be learned. In these experiments, a simpler approximation retains much of the performance while supporting useful image-specific adaptation.
summary.tldr: Learned greedy MRI sampling performs nearly as well as a more general approach, partly because noisier gradients hinder the latter's adaptation to individual images.

title: Experimental design for MRI by greedy policy search

abstract: Recently, there has been extensive research interest in training deep networks to denoise images without clean reference.However, the representative approaches such as Noise2Noise, Noise2Void, Stein's unbiased risk estimator (SURE), etc. seem to differ from one another and it is difficult to find the coherent mathematical structure. To address this, here we present a novel approach, called Noise2Score, which reveals a missing link in order to unite these seemingly different approaches.Specifically, we show that image denoising problems without clean images can be addressed by finding the mode of the posterior distribution and that the Tweedie's formula offers an explicit solution through the score function (i.e. the gradient of loglikelihood). Our method then uses the recent finding that the score function can be stably estimated from the noisy images using the amortized residual denoising autoencoder, the method of which is closely related to Noise2Noise or Nose2Void. Our Noise2Score approach is so universal that the same network training can be used to remove noises from images that are corrupted by any exponential family distributions and noise parameters. Using extensive experiments with Gaussian, Poisson, and Gamma noises, we show that Noise2Score significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art self-supervised denoising methods in the benchmark data set such as (C)BSD68, Set12, and Kodak, etc.

Noise2Score seeks a common structure linking these approaches. It connects denoising to posterior inference and uses Tweedie's formula to express the solution through a score function, the gradient of a log-likelihood.

The method estimates that score directly from noisy images using an amortized residual denoising autoencoder. The authors relate this estimation procedure to existing approaches such as Noise2Noise and Noise2Void. Separating score estimation from the noise-specific denoising calculation allows the same network training to support noise distributions and parameter choices within the exponential family.

Experiments cover Gaussian, Poisson, and Gamma noise on standard image benchmarks. The authors report substantial improvements over state-of-the-art self-supervised denoising methods in those evaluations. The contribution combines a mathematical connection between existing methods with a practical denoising procedure, showing how learning from noisy observations can support multiple noise models without requiring clean training targets.
summary.tldr: Noise2Score learns a score function from noisy images and uses Tweedie's formula to support denoising across exponential-family noise models.

title: Noise2Score: Tweedie’s Approach to Self-Supervised Image Denoising without Clean Images

abstract: Approximate Bayesian inference estimates descriptors of an intractable target distribution - in essence, an optimization problem within a family of distributions. For example, Langevin dynamics (LD) extracts asymptotically exact samples from a diffusion process because the time evolution of its marginal distributions constitutes a curve that minimizes the KL-divergence via steepest descent in the Wasserstein space. Parallel to LD, Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD) similarly minimizes the KL, albeit endowed with a novel Stein-Wasserstein distance, by deterministically transporting a set of particle samples, thus de-randomizes the stochastic diffusion process. We propose de-randomized kernel-based particle samplers to all diffusion-based samplers known as MCMC dynamics. Following previous work in interpreting MCMC dynamics, we equip the Stein-Wasserstein space with a fiber-Riemannian Poisson structure, with the capacity of characterizing a fiber-gradient Hamiltonian flow that simulates MCMC dynamics. Such dynamics discretizes into generalized SVGD (GSVGD), a Stein-type deterministic particle sampler, with particle updates coinciding with applying the diffusion Stein operator to a kernel function. We demonstrate empirically that GSVGD can de-randomize complex MCMC dynamics, which combine the advantages of auxiliary momentum variables and Riemannian structure, while maintaining the high sample quality from an interacting particle system.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference often requires approximating a probability distribution that cannot be handled directly. Diffusion-based sampling methods move random samples through time toward that target. Stein variational gradient descent offers a related approach: it moves a collection of interacting particles deterministically while reducing a measure of discrepancy called KL divergence.

This paper extends that connection beyond Langevin dynamics to the broader class of diffusion-based MCMC dynamics. The authors introduce a geometric structure that describes their evolution in a space of probability distributions. summary.tldr: GSVGD translates diffusion-based MCMC dynamics into deterministic kernel-based particle updates, with empirical evidence of high sample quality.

title: De-randomizing MCMC dynamics with the diffusion Stein operator

abstract: We establish generalization error bounds for stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD) with constant learning rate under the assumptions of dissipativity and smoothness, a setting that has received increased attention in the sampling/optimization literature. Unlike existing bounds for SGLD in non-convex settings, ours are time-independent and decay to zero as the sample size increases. Using the framework of uniform stability, we establish time-independent bounds by exploiting the Wasserstein contraction property of the Langevin diffusion, which also allows us to circumvent the need to bound gradients using Lipschitz-like assumptions. Our analysis also supports variants of SGLD that use different discretization methods, incorporate Euclidean projections, or use non-isotropic noise.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics combines gradient-based updates with randomness. This paper studies its generalization error in nonconvex problems when the learning rate stays constant, assuming smoothness and dissipativity. Those conditions define the setting in which the guarantees hold.

The main result is a bound that does not depend on the amount of training time and approaches zero as the sample size grows. Compared with time-dependent bounds, it gives control that does not become weaker simply because the algorithm runs longer.

The proof uses uniform stability, which examines how changing a training sample affects the learning procedure. The authors exploit a Wasserstein contraction property of the corresponding Langevin diffusion to control that sensitivity. This also avoids needing gradient bounds imposed through Lipschitz-like assumptions.

The analysis extends to variants using different discretizations, Euclidean projections, and non-isotropic noise. Its significance is a generalization guarantee that remains useful over time while accommodating several algorithmic forms, within the stated smoothness and dissipativity setting.
summary.tldr: Under smoothness and dissipativity, constant-rate SGLD admits generalization bounds that are independent of training time and vanish with growing sample size.

title: Time-independent Generalization Bounds for SGLD in Non-convex Settings

abstract: A few years ago, the first CNN surpassed human performance on ImageNet. However, it soon became clear that machines lack robustness on more challenging test cases, a major obstacle towards deploying machines "in the wild" and towards obtaining better computational models of human visual perception. Here we ask: Are we making progress in closing the gap between human and machine vision? To answer this question, we tested human observers on a broad range of out-of-distribution (OOD) datasets, recording 85,120 psychophysical trials across 90 participants. We then investigated a range of promising machine learning developments that crucially deviate from standard supervised CNNs along three axes: objective function (self-supervised, adversarially trained, CLIP language-image training), architecture (e.g. vision transformers), and dataset size (ranging from 1M to 1B).Our findings are threefold. (1.) The longstanding distortion robustness gap between humans and CNNs is closing, with the best models now exceeding human feedforward performance on most of the investigated OOD datasets. (2.) There is still a substantial image-level consistency gap, meaning that humans make different errors than models. In contrast, most models systematically agree in their categorisation errors, even substantially different ones like contrastive self-supervised vs. standard supervised models. (3.) In many cases, human-to-model consistency improves when training dataset size is increased by one to three orders of magnitude. Our results give reason for cautious optimism: While there is still much room for improvement, the behavioural difference between human and machine vision is narrowing. In order to measure future progress, 17 OOD datasets with image-level human behavioural data and evaluation code are provided as a toolbox and benchmark at: https://github.com/bethgelab/model-vs-human/

paragraphs: High accuracy on ImageNet does not establish human-like robustness on unfamiliar images. This study compares human and machine vision across a broad collection of out-of-distribution datasets. It gathers 85,120 psychophysical trials from 90 participants and evaluates models differing in training objectives, architecture, and training-set size.

The results separate two questions: how often a system is correct and whether it makes mistakes on the same images as people. The strongest models exceed human feedforward performance on most tested out-of-distribution datasets, indicating progress on distortion robustness. Models often agree with one another’s categorization mistakes even when their training approaches differ substantially. Increasing training-set size by one to three orders of magnitude improves human-model consistency in many cases. The findings therefore support cautious optimism about narrowing behavioral differences, while preserving the distinction between robust accuracy and human-like errors. The released benchmark combines 17 out-of-distribution datasets with image-level human responses and evaluation code to measure both aspects of future progress.
summary.tldr: Leading vision models narrow the human robustness gap on tested datasets, but their image-level mistakes still differ substantially from people’s.

title: Partial success in closing the gap between human and machine vision

abstract: Low-rank Tucker and CP tensor decompositions are powerful tools in data analytics. The widely used alternating least squares (ALS) method, which solves a sequence of over-determined least squares subproblems, is costly for large and sparse tensors. We propose a fast and accurate sketched ALS algorithm for Tucker decomposition, which solves a sequence of sketched rank-constrained linear least squares subproblems. Theoretical sketch size upper bounds are provided to achieve $O(\epsilon)$ relative error for each subproblem with two sketching techniques, TensorSketch and leverage score sampling. Experimental results show that this new ALS algorithm, combined with a new initialization scheme based on the randomized range finder, yields decomposition accuracy comparable to the standard higher-order orthogonal iteration (HOOI) algorithm. The new algorithm achieves up to $22.0\%$ relative decomposition residual improvement compared to the state-of-the-art sketched randomized algorithm for Tucker decomposition of various synthetic and real datasets. This Tucker-ALS algorithm is further used to accelerate CP decomposition, by using randomized Tucker compression followed by CP decomposition of the Tucker core tensor. Experimental results show that this algorithm not only converges faster, but also yields more accurate CP decompositions.

paragraphs: Low-rank tensor decompositions represent multidimensional data in a more compact form, but computing them can be expensive. Alternating least squares repeatedly solves large least-squares problems, making it costly for large, sparse tensors. This paper develops a randomized version for Tucker decomposition that replaces those subproblems with smaller sketches.

The sketched subproblems include a rank constraint. For TensorSketch and leverage-score sampling, the authors provide upper bounds on sketch sizes sufficient to obtain relative subproblem error proportional to a chosen accuracy parameter. They also introduce an initialization method based on a randomized range finder. Together, these components achieve decomposition accuracy comparable to standard higher-order orthogonal iteration in experiments.

Across synthetic and real datasets, the method improves the relative decomposition residual by up to 22.0% over a leading sketched Tucker algorithm. The authors also use randomized Tucker compression before performing CP decomposition on the smaller core tensor. Experiments show faster convergence and more accurate CP decompositions. The theoretical guarantees concern individual sketched subproblems, while the overall decomposition improvements are empirical findings.
summary.tldr: Randomized sketching and initialization accelerate Tucker decomposition and also improve CP decomposition through Tucker compression.

title: Fast and accurate randomized algorithms for low-rank tensor decompositions

abstract: Domain-specific data is the crux of the successful transfer of machine learning systems from benchmarks to real life. In simple problems such as image classification, crowdsourcing has become one of the standard tools for cheap and time-efficient data collection: thanks in large part to advances in research on aggregation methods. However, the applicability of crowdsourcing to more complex tasks (e.g., speech recognition) remains limited due to the lack of principled aggregation methods for these modalities. The main obstacle towards designing aggregation methods for more advanced applications is the absence of training data, and in this work, we focus on bridging this gap in speech recognition. For this, we collect and release CrowdSpeech --- the first publicly available large-scale dataset of crowdsourced audio transcriptions. Evaluation of existing and novel aggregation methods on our data shows room for improvement, suggesting that our work may entail the design of better algorithms. At a higher level, we also contribute to the more general challenge of developing the methodology for reliable data collection via crowdsourcing. In that, we design a principled pipeline for constructing datasets of crowdsourced audio transcriptions in any novel domain. We show its applicability on an under-resourced language by constructing VoxDIY --- a counterpart of CrowdSpeech for the Russian language. We also release the code that allows a full replication of our data collection pipeline and share various insights on best practices of data collection via crowdsourcing.
originalAbstract: Domain-specific data is the crux of the successful transfer of machine learning systems from benchmarks to real life. In simple problems such as image classification, crowdsourcing has become one of the standard tools for cheap and time-efficient data collection: thanks in large part to advances in research on aggregation methods. However, the applicability of crowdsourcing to more complex tasks (e.g., speech recognition) remains limited due to the lack of principled aggregation methods for these modalities. The main obstacle towards designing aggregation methods for more advanced applications is the absence of training data, and in this work, we focus on bridging this gap in speech recognition. For this, we collect and release CrowdSpeech --- the first publicly available large-scale dataset of crowdsourced audio transcriptions. Evaluation of existing and novel aggregation methods on our data shows room for improvement, suggesting that our work may entail the design of better algorithms. At a higher level, we also contribute to the more general challenge of developing the methodology for reliable data collection via crowdsourcing. In that, we design a principled pipeline for constructing datasets of crowdsourced audio transcriptions in any novel domain. We show its applicability on an under-resourced language by constructing VoxDIY --- a counterpart of CrowdSpeech for the Russian language. We also release the code that allows a full replication of our data collection pipeline and share various insights on best practices of data collection via crowdsourcing.

paragraphs: CrowdSpeech addresses a difficulty in collecting speech data through crowdsourcing: combining contributors’ transcriptions into reliable results. Crowdsourcing is established for simpler tasks such as image classification, but the authors argue that speech lacks sufficiently developed aggregation methods. Developing those methods is itself hindered by a shortage of suitable training data.

The paper introduces a large public dataset of crowdsourced audio transcriptions and evaluates both existing and new aggregation approaches on it. Those evaluations show room for improvement. The dataset therefore serves as material for learning aggregation methods and as a common basis for comparing how well different methods combine crowd contributions.

The authors also design a repeatable collection pipeline for new domains and demonstrate it by creating VoxDIY for Russian, described here as an under-resourced language. They release code for reproducing the full pipeline and share collection practices. This extends the contribution beyond one dataset to a methodology for constructing further speech transcription resources through crowdsourcing.
summary.tldr: CrowdSpeech and VoxDIY provide crowdsourced transcription data and a reproducible collection pipeline to support better aggregation methods.

title: CrowdSpeech and Vox DIY: Benchmark Dataset for Crowdsourced Audio Transcription

abstract: Semi-supervised learning (SSL) provides a powerful framework for leveraging unlabeled data. Existing SSL typically requires all classes have labels. However, in many real-world applications, there may exist some classes that are difficult to label or newly occurred classes that cannot be labeled in time, resulting in there are unseen classes in unlabeled data. Unseen classes will be misclassified as seen classes, causing poor classification performance. The performance of seen classes is also harmed by the existence of unseen classes. This limits the practical and wider application of SSL. To address this problem, this paper proposes a new SSL approach that can classify not only seen classes but also unseen classes. Our approach consists of two modules: unseen class classification and learning pace synchronization. Specifically, we first enable the SSL methods to classify unseen classes by exploiting pairwise similarity between examples and then synchronize the learning pace between seen and unseen classes by proposing an adaptive threshold with distribution alignment. Extensive empirical results show our approach achieves significant performance improvement in both seen and unseen classes compared with previous studies.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning combines labeled and unlabeled examples, but commonly assumes that every class appears in the labeled set. When unlabeled data includes additional classes, those examples can be assigned incorrectly to known classes. The resulting confusion can damage performance on both the previously labeled classes and the unseen ones.

This paper proposes a method with two components. The first uses pairwise similarity between examples to enable classification of unseen classes. The second coordinates the learning pace for seen and unseen classes through an adaptive threshold with distribution alignment. This addresses both the absence of labels for some classes and the imbalance in how the two groups are learned.

The reported experiments show significant improvements for both seen and unseen classes compared with previous studies. The contribution is a semi-supervised approach that explicitly accommodates classes absent from the labeled data, rather than forcing all examples into the known categories. Its two-part design reflects the finding that recognizing unseen classes and coordinating their learning with known classes are related needs.
summary.tldr: Pairwise similarity and synchronized learning improve semi-supervised classification when unlabeled data contains classes absent from the labeled set.

title: Robust Semi-Supervised Learning when Not All Classes have Labels

abstract: Unsupervised Domain Adaptation demonstrates great potential to mitigate domain shifts by transferring models from labeled source domains to unlabeled target domains. While Unsupervised Domain Adaptation has been applied to a wide variety of complex vision tasks, only few works focus on lane detection for autonomous driving. This can be attributed to the lack of publicly available datasets. To facilitate research in these directions, we propose CARLANE, a 3-way sim-to-real domain adaptation benchmark for 2D lane detection. CARLANE encompasses the single-target datasets MoLane and TuLane and the multi-target dataset MuLane. These datasets are built from three different domains, which cover diverse scenes and contain a total of 163K unique images, 118K of which are annotated. In addition we evaluate and report systematic baselines, including our own method, which builds upon Prototypical Cross-domain Self-supervised Learning. We find that false positive and false negative rates of the evaluated domain adaptation methods are high compared to those of fully supervised baselines. This affirms the need for benchmarks such as CARLANE to further strengthen research in Unsupervised Domain Adaptation for lane detection. CARLANE, all evaluated models and the corresponding implementations are publicly available at https://carlanebenchmark.github.io.

paragraphs: A lane detector trained on labeled simulation images must cope with different visual conditions when applied to real roads. Unsupervised domain adaptation addresses this by transferring learning from a labeled source to an unlabeled target. CARLANE provides a benchmark for studying this transfer in lane detection, an area with relatively few existing studies and publicly available datasets.

The benchmark covers three domains and contains 163,000 unique images, including 118,000 annotated images. MoLane and TuLane support single-target adaptation, while MuLane supports adaptation to multiple targets. This organization makes it possible to examine both transfer into one target domain and the broader challenge of handling several target domains.

The authors systematically evaluate baseline methods, including their own approach based on Prototypical Cross-domain Self-supervised Learning. The evaluated adaptation methods have high false-positive and false-negative rates compared with fully supervised baselines. These findings identify a substantial remaining performance gap. Public datasets, evaluated models, and implementations provide a shared basis for investigating that gap.
summary.tldr: CARLANE benchmarks simulation-to-real lane detection across multiple domains and reveals substantial errors relative to fully supervised methods.

title: CARLANE: A Lane Detection Benchmark for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation from Simulation to multiple Real-World Domains

abstract: Machine learning technologies have been used in a wide range of practical systems.In practical situations, it is natural to expect the input-output pairs of a machine learning model to satisfy some requirements.However, it is difficult to obtain a model that satisfies requirements by just learning from examples.A simple solution is to add a module that checks whether the input-output pairs meet the requirements and then modifies the model's outputs. Such a module, which we call a {\em concurrent verifier} (CV), can give a certification, although how the generalizability of the machine learning model changes using a CV is unclear. This paper gives a generalization analysis of learning with a CV. We analyze how the learnability of a machine learning model changes with a CV and show a condition where we can obtain a guaranteed hypothesis using a verifier only in the inference time.We also show that typical error bounds based on Rademacher complexity will be no larger than that of the original model when using a CV in multi-class classification and structured prediction settings.

paragraphs: A model trained from examples may still produce outputs that violate requirements imposed by its application. A concurrent verifier checks an input-output pair and modifies the output to meet those requirements. This paper studies what happens to learning and generalization when such a verifier becomes part of the prediction system.

The analysis asks how adding the verifier changes learnability and whether it must participate during training. The authors establish a condition under which a guaranteed hypothesis can be obtained while using the verifier only at inference time. This is a conditional result: it identifies circumstances in which verification can be attached to prediction without needing to be used throughout learning.

For multi-class classification and structured prediction, the authors also show that typical error bounds based on Rademacher complexity do not become larger when a concurrent verifier is used. This connects output certification to statistical generalization analysis. The finding concerns the stated theoretical bounds, giving a reason that enforcing requirements through a verifier need not worsen those bounds in the analyzed settings.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies conditions for inference-time verification guarantees and shows that standard complexity-based error bounds need not increase.

title: Generalization Analysis on Learning with a Concurrent Verifier

abstract: Recent advances in neural models have shown great results for virtual try-on (VTO) problems, where a 3D representation of a garment is deformed to fit a target body shape. However, current solutions are limited to a single garment layer, and cannot address the combinatorial complexity of mixing different garments. Motivated by this limitation, we investigate the use of neural fields for mix-and-match VTO, and identify and solve a fundamental challenge that existing neural-field methods cannot address: the interaction between layered neural fields. To this end, we propose a neural model that untangles layered neural fields to represent collision-free garment surfaces. The key ingredient is a neural untangling projection operator that works directly on the layered neural fields, not on explicit surface representations. Algorithms to resolve object-object interaction are inherently limited by the use of explicit geometric representations, and we show how methods that work directly on neural implicit representations could bring a change of paradigm and open the door to radically different approaches.

paragraphs: Virtual try-on deforms a three-dimensional garment representation to fit a target body. Combining several garments introduces another problem: the layers must interact without their surfaces colliding. This paper studies that challenge for neural fields, focusing on the complexity created when different garments are mixed and matched.

ULNeF proposes a neural model that untangles layered fields to represent collision-free garment surfaces. Its central component is a neural projection operator applied directly to the layered neural fields. Handling the interaction at this level avoids making an explicit surface representation the object on which the untangling operation must work.

The distinction matters because the paper identifies interactions between layers as a fundamental challenge for existing neural-field methods. Its contribution is a mechanism for addressing those interactions within the implicit representation itself, extending the approach beyond a single garment layer. The authors further argue that direct operations on neural representations could enable substantially different approaches to object interaction, presenting that broader impact as a possibility opened by the method.
summary.tldr: ULNeF untangles layered neural fields directly to represent collision-free garments for mix-and-match virtual try-on.

title: ULNeF: Untangled Layered Neural Fields for Mix-and-Match Virtual Try-On

abstract: Despite the success of generative adversarial networks (GANs) in generating visually appealing images, they are notoriously challenging to train. In order to stabilize the learning dynamics in minimax games, we propose a novel recursive reasoning algorithm: Level $k$ Gradient Play (Lv.$k$ GP) algorithm. Our algorithm does not require sophisticated heuristics or second-order information, as do existing algorithms based on predictive updates. We show that as k increases, Lv.$k$ GP converges asymptotically towards an accurate estimation of players' future strategy.Moreover, we justify that Lv.$\infty$ GP naturally generalizes a line of provably convergent game dynamics which rely on predictive updates. Furthermore, we provide its local convergence property in nonconvex-nonconcave zero-sum games and global convergence in bilinear and quadratic games. By combining Lv.$k$ GP with Adam optimizer, our algorithm shows a clear advantage in terms of performance and computational overhead compared to other methods. Using a single Nvidia RTX3090 GPU and 30 times fewer parameters than BigGAN on CIFAR-10, we achieve an FID of 10.17 for unconditional image generation within 30 hours, allowing GAN training on common computational resources to reach state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Training adversarial models involves interacting players whose updates can destabilize one another. The paper introduces Level k Gradient Play to stabilize minimax learning through recursive reasoning about future strategies. The method uses gradients without requiring second-order information or the sophisticated heuristics associated with some predictive-update approaches.

As the reasoning level k increases, the authors show that the method approaches an accurate estimate of the players' future strategies. Its infinite-level form generalizes a family of provably convergent predictive game dynamics. The convergence results distinguish settings: local convergence is established for nonconvex-nonconcave zero-sum games, while global convergence is established for bilinear and quadratic games.

Combined with Adam, the method shows reported advantages in performance and computational overhead. For unconditional CIFAR-10 generation, the authors report an FID of 10.17 within 30 hours on one Nvidia RTX3090, using 30 times fewer parameters than BigGAN. This experiment supports the practicality of the approach on common computing resources, while the theoretical guarantees retain their stated game-specific scope.
summary.tldr: Level k Gradient Play recursively anticipates opponents' strategies, with setting-specific convergence guarantees and practical gains in GAN training.

title: Recursive Reasoning in Minimax Games: A Level $k$ Gradient Play Method

abstract: The increasing size and complexity of modern ML systems has improved their predictive capabilities but made their behavior harder to explain. Many techniques for model explanation have been developed in response, but we lack clear criteria for assessing these techniques. In this paper, we cast model explanation as the causal inference problem of estimating causal effects of real-world concepts on the output behavior of ML models given actual input data. We introduce CEBaB, a new benchmark dataset for assessing concept-based explanation methods in Natural Language Processing (NLP). CEBaB consists of short restaurant reviews with human-generated counterfactual reviews in which an aspect (food, noise, ambiance, service) of the dining experience was modified. Original and counterfactual reviews are annotated with multiply-validated sentiment ratings at the aspect-level and review-level. The rich structure of CEBaB allows us to go beyond input features to study the effects of abstract, real-world concepts on model behavior. We use CEBaB to compare the quality of a range of concept-based explanation methods covering different assumptions and conceptions of the problem, and we seek to establish natural metrics for comparative assessments of these methods.

paragraphs: An explanation method needs a clear target against which its claims can be assessed. This paper frames that target as a causal question: how does changing a real-world concept affect a model's output on actual input data? It introduces CEBaB to make this question concrete for concept-based explanations of language models.

The dataset contains short restaurant reviews and human-written counterfactual versions that modify an aspect of the dining experience, such as food, noise, ambiance, or service. Both the original reviews and their edited counterparts receive sentiment annotations at the aspect and whole-review levels. These ratings undergo multiple validations, giving the benchmark structure beyond an isolated review and a single overall label.

This design supports studying the effects of meaningful concepts rather than only individual input features. The authors use CEBaB to compare explanation methods with different assumptions and interpretations of the explanation problem. They also seek natural metrics for comparing those methods. The contribution is an evaluation setting that links proposed explanations to controlled conceptual changes and observed model behavior.
summary.tldr: CEBaB uses human-written counterfactual restaurant reviews to evaluate explanations of how real-world concepts affect NLP model outputs.

title: CEBaB: Estimating the Causal Effects of Real-World Concepts on NLP Model Behavior

abstract: This paper considers the challenging tasks of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) under partial observability, where each agent only sees her own individual observations and actions that reveal incomplete information about the underlying state of system. This paper studies these tasks under the general model of multiplayer general-sum Partially Observable Markov Games (POMGs), which is significantly larger than the standard model of Imperfect Information Extensive-Form Games (IIEFGs). We identify a rich subclass of POMGs---weakly revealing POMGs---in which sample-efficient learning is tractable. In the self-play setting, we prove that a simple algorithm combining optimism and Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) is sufficient to find approximate Nash equilibria, correlated equilibria, as well as coarse correlated equilibria of weakly revealing POMGs, in a polynomial number of samples when the number of agents is small. In the setting of playing against adversarial opponents, we show that a variant of our optimistic MLE algorithm is capable of achieving sublinear regret when being compared against the optimal maximin policies. To our best knowledge, this work provides the first line of sample-efficient results for learning POMGs.

paragraphs: Learning in a multi-agent environment becomes harder when each agent sees only incomplete information about the underlying state. This paper studies multiplayer general-sum partially observable Markov games, a model broader than standard imperfect-information extensive-form games. It identifies weakly revealing games as a rich subclass where learning can be sample-efficient.

For self-play, the proposed algorithm combines optimism with maximum likelihood estimation. The authors prove that it can find approximate Nash, correlated, and coarse correlated equilibria using a polynomial number of samples when the number of agents is small. These guarantees establish that limited observation does not preclude efficient learning within the specified subclass and agent-count condition.

The paper also considers play against adversarial opponents. A variant of the optimistic estimation algorithm achieves sublinear regret relative to optimal maximin policies, meaning its cumulative shortfall against that benchmark grows slower than the number of rounds. Together, the results address both learning among interacting agents and learning against opponents. The authors describe them as, to their knowledge, the first sample-efficient results for learning partially observable Markov games.
summary.tldr: Optimistic maximum-likelihood learning provides sample-efficient equilibrium guarantees for weakly revealing partially observable games with few agents.

title: Sample-Efficient Reinforcement Learning of Partially Observable Markov Games

abstract: In this paper, we study Lipschitz bandit problems with batched feedback, where the expected reward is Lipschitz and the reward observations are communicated to the player in batches. We introduce a novel landscape-aware algorithm, called Batched Lipschitz Narrowing (BLiN), that optimally solves this problem. Specifically, we show that for a $T$-step problem with Lipschitz reward of zooming dimension $d_z$, our algorithm achieves theoretically optimal (up to logarithmic factors) regret rate $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(T^{\frac{d_z+1}{d_z+2}}\right)$ using only $ \mathcal{O} \left( \log\log T\right) $ batches. We also provide complexity analysis for this problem. Our theoretical lower bound implies that $\Omega(\log\log T)$ batches are necessary for any algorithm to achieve the optimal regret. Thus, BLiN achieves optimal regret rate using minimal communication.

We introduce a novel landscape-aware algorithm, called Batched Lipschitz Narrowing (BLiN), that optimally solves this problem. Specifically, we show that for a $T$-step problem with Lipschitz reward of zooming dimension $d_z$, our algorithm achieves theoretically optimal (up to logarithmic factors) regret rate $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(T^{\frac{d_z+1}{d_z+2}}\right)$ using only $ \mathcal{O} \left( \log\log T\right) $ batches. paragraphs: In a Lipschitz bandit problem, expected rewards vary smoothly enough that nearby choices have related rewards. This paper studies what happens when observations arrive in batches rather than after every choice. The learner must make decisions between feedback deliveries, creating a tradeoff between learning effectively and limiting the number of communication rounds.

The proposed Batched Lipschitz Narrowing algorithm, BLiN, takes the reward landscape into account. For a horizon of T steps and zooming dimension dz, the authors prove regret of order T raised to (dz + 1)/(dz + 2), up to logarithmic factors. They show that this rate is theoretically optimal and requires only order log log T feedback batches.

A matching lower-bound argument shows that any algorithm needs at least order log log T batches to attain optimal regret. This makes the communication claim especially strong: BLiN achieves both the optimal regret rate, within logarithmic factors, and the necessary order of batch count. The result identifies how infrequently feedback can be delivered without sacrificing the target learning rate in this problem.
summary.tldr: BLiN achieves optimal Lipschitz-bandit regret up to logarithmic factors using the minimum asymptotic number of feedback batches.

title: Lipschitz Bandits with Batched Feedback

abstract: Score-based generative modeling (SGM) is a highly successful approach for learning a probability distribution from data and generating further samples. We prove the first polynomial convergence guarantees for the core mechanic behind SGM: drawing samples from a probability density $p$ given a score estimate (an estimate of $\nabla \ln p$) that is accurate in $L^2(p)$. Compared to previous works, we do not incur error that grows exponentially in time or that suffers from a curse of dimensionality. Our guarantee works for any smooth distribution and depends polynomially on its log-Sobolev constant. Using our guarantee, we give a theoretical analysis of score-based generative modeling, which transforms white-noise input into samples from a learned data distribution given score estimates at different noise scales. Our analysis gives theoretical grounding to the observation that an annealed procedure is required in practice to generate good samples, as our proof depends essentially on using annealing to obtain a warm start at each step. Moreover, we show that a predictor-corrector algorithm gives better convergence than using either portion alone.

paragraphs: Score-based generation relies on estimates of the score, the gradient of a distribution's log density, to guide sampling. This paper establishes polynomial convergence guarantees when the score estimate is accurate in the distribution-weighted squared-error sense. The guarantee applies to smooth distributions and depends polynomially on their log-Sobolev constant.

The analysis avoids the exponential growth of error over time and the curse of dimensionality present in earlier guarantees. It then studies the full generative procedure, which starts from white noise and uses score estimates at multiple noise levels to approach the learned data distribution. This connects a sampling guarantee to the mechanism used in score-based modeling.

Annealing plays an essential role in the proof: progressing through noise levels supplies a suitable starting distribution for each next step. This gives theoretical support to the practical importance of that gradual procedure, without establishing that every possible method must use it. The authors also show that combining predictor and corrector steps yields better convergence than either component alone.
summary.tldr: The paper proves polynomial sampling guarantees from accurate score estimates and explains the benefits of annealing and predictor-corrector sampling.

title: Convergence for score-based generative modeling with polynomial complexity

abstract: Over the past few years, numerous computational models have been developed to solve Optimal Transport (OT) in a stochastic setting, where distributions are represented by samples and where the goal is to find the closest map to the ground truth OT map, unknown in practical settings. So far, no quantitative criterion has yet been put forward to tune the parameter of these models and select maps that best approximate the ground truth. To perform this task, we propose to leverage the Brenier formulation of OT. Theoretically, we show that this formulation guarantees that, up to sharp a distortion parameter depending on the smoothness/strong convexity and a statistical deviation term, the selected map achieves the lowest quadratic error to the ground truth. This criterion, estimated via convex optimization, enables parameter tuning and model selection among entropic regularization of OT, input convex neural networks and smooth and strongly convex nearest-Brenier (SSNB) models.We also use this criterion to question the use of OT in Domain-Adaptation (DA). In a standard DA experiment, it enables us to identify the potential that is closest to the true OT map between the source and the target. Yet, we observe that this selected potential is far from being the one that performs best for the downstream transfer classification task.

paragraphs: When distributions are represented by samples, optimal transport methods try to estimate an unknown transport map. Choosing parameters or selecting among candidate maps is difficult because the true map is unavailable. This paper proposes a quantitative selection criterion based on the Brenier formulation of optimal transport.

The theoretical guarantee relates the selected map's quadratic error to the best candidate's error, with a distortion factor depending on smoothness and strong convexity and an additional statistical deviation term. The criterion is estimated through convex optimization. It supports comparisons among entropically regularized transport, input convex neural networks, and smooth, strongly convex nearest-Brenier models.

The authors also examine what this selection criterion means for domain adaptation. In a standard experiment, it identifies the potential closest to the true transport map between source and target distributions. Yet that potential is far from the best for downstream transfer classification. This finding separates accuracy at estimating the transport map from success on the subsequent task, showing that the two objectives need not select the same solution.
summary.tldr: A Brenier-based criterion selects accurate transport maps, while an experiment shows that transport accuracy need not yield the best transfer classifier.

title: Parameter tuning and model selection in Optimal Transport with semi-dual Brenier formulation

abstract: Masked Autoencoders (MAE) have shown great potentials in self-supervised pre-training for language and 2D image transformers. However, it still remains an open question on how to exploit masked autoencoding for learning 3D representations of irregular point clouds. In this paper, we propose Point-M2AE, a strong Multi-scale MAE pre-training framework for hierarchical self-supervised learning of 3D point clouds. Unlike the standard transformer in MAE, we modify the encoder and decoder into pyramid architectures to progressively model spatial geometries and capture both fine-grained and high-level semantics of 3D shapes. For the encoder that downsamples point tokens by stages, we design a multi-scale masking strategy to generate consistent visible regions across scales, and adopt a local spatial self-attention mechanism during fine-tuning to focus on neighboring patterns. By multi-scale token propagation, the lightweight decoder gradually upsamples point tokens with complementary skip connections from the encoder, which further promotes the reconstruction from a global-to-local perspective. Extensive experiments demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance of Point-M2AE for 3D representation learning. With a frozen encoder after pre-training, Point-M2AE achieves 92.9% accuracy for linear SVM on ModelNet40, even surpassing some fully trained methods. By fine-tuning on downstream tasks, Point-M2AE achieves 86.43% accuracy on ScanObjectNN, +3.36% to the second-best, and largely benefits the few-shot classification, part segmentation and 3D object detection with the hierarchical pre-training scheme. Code is available at https://github.com/ZrrSkywalker/Point-M2AE.

paragraphs: Point-M2AE adapts masked autoencoding to irregular 3D point clouds. The goal is to learn useful shape representations through self-supervised reconstruction. summary.tldr: Point-M2AE learns hierarchical 3D representations through multiscale masked reconstruction, improving reported classification and other point-cloud tasks.

title: Point-M2AE: Multi-scale Masked Autoencoders for Hierarchical Point Cloud Pre-training

abstract: Policy constraint methods to offline reinforcement learning (RL) typically utilize parameterization or regularization that constrains the policy to perform actions within the support set of the behavior policy. The elaborative designs of parameterization methods usually intrude into the policy networks, which may bring extra inference cost and cannot take full advantage of well-established online methods. Regularization methods reduce the divergence between the learned policy and the behavior policy, which may mismatch the inherent density-based definition of support set thereby failing to avoid the out-of-distribution actions effectively. This paper presents Supported Policy OpTimization (SPOT), which is directly derived from the theoretical formalization of the density-based support constraint. SPOT adopts a VAE-based density estimator to explicitly model the support set of behavior policy and presents a simple but effective density-based regularization term, which can be plugged non-intrusively into off-the-shelf off-policy RL algorithms. SPOT achieves the state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks for offline RL. Benefiting from the pluggable design, offline pretrained models from SPOT can also be applied to perform online fine-tuning seamlessly.
