paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning trains from previously collected behavior, so choosing actions outside that behavior's support is a central concern. Existing constraints can require intrusive policy architectures or encourage overall similarity to the behavior policy. The paper argues that distributional similarity may not match the density-based meaning of support closely enough to exclude unsupported actions.

Supported Policy Optimization, or SPOT, starts from a theoretical formulation of the density-based support constraint. It uses a variational autoencoder as a density estimator to model the behavior policy's support, then adds a regularization term based on that density. The regularizer can be inserted into existing off-policy reinforcement learning algorithms without intrusive changes to their policy networks.

SPOT achieves state-of-the-art performance on the standard offline reinforcement learning benchmarks reported in the paper. Its pluggable design also allows offline-pretrained models to proceed to online fine-tuning seamlessly. The contribution connects the constraint's mathematical definition to a practical training mechanism, while preserving compatibility with established algorithms and subsequent learning through interaction.
summary.tldr: SPOT uses learned behavior densities to regularize offline policies toward supported actions, achieving strong benchmark results and supporting online fine-tuning.

title: Supported Policy Optimization for Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In academic recruitment settings, including faculty hiring and PhD admissions, committees aim to maximize the overall quality of recruited candidates, but there is uncertainty about whether a candidate would accept an offer if given one. Previous work has considered algorithms that make offers sequentially and are subject to a hard budget constraint. We argue that these modeling choices may be inconsistent with the practice of academic recruitment. Instead, we restrict ourselves to a single batch of offers, and we treat the target number of positions as a soft constraint, so we risk overshooting or undershooting the target. Specifically, our objective is to select a subset of candidates that maximizes the overall expected value associated with candidates who accept, minus an expected penalty for deviating from the target. We first analyze the guarantees provided by natural greedy heuristics, showing their desirable properties despite the simplicity. Depending on the structure of the penalty function, we further develop algorithms that provide fully polynomial-time approximation schemes and constant-factor approximations to this objective. Empirical evaluation of our algorithms corroborates these theoretical results.

paragraphs: Recruitment committees must choose whom to make offers to without knowing who will accept. The paper models situations such as faculty hiring and doctoral admissions using one batch of offers. It treats the desired number of recruits as a soft target, allowing the final number of acceptances to fall above or below it.

The objective balances the expected total value of candidates who accept against an expected penalty for missing the recruitment target. This places uncertainty about acceptance directly into the selection problem. It also captures a trade-off that a strict cap cannot express: pursuing a valuable group of recruits while accepting some risk of overfilling or underfilling the available positions.

The authors analyze simple greedy strategies and establish desirable guarantees for them. Depending on the form of the penalty function, they also develop fully polynomial-time approximation schemes and constant-factor approximation algorithms. Empirical evaluations support the theoretical results. The guarantees therefore depend on the penalty structure, while the overall contribution is a recruitment model and algorithms that explicitly accommodate uncertain batch outcomes.
summary.tldr: The paper develops recruitment algorithms that balance expected candidate value against the risk of exceeding or missing a hiring target.

title: Recruitment Strategies That Take a Chance

abstract: We are now witnessing significant progress of deep learning methods in a variety of tasks (or datasets) of proteins. However, there is a lack of a standard benchmark to evaluate the performance of different methods, which hinders the progress of deep learning in this field. In this paper, we propose such a benchmark called PEER, a comprehensive and multi-task benchmark for Protein sEquence undERstanding. PEER provides a set of diverse protein understanding tasks including protein function prediction, protein localization prediction, protein structure prediction, protein-protein interaction prediction, and protein-ligand interaction prediction. We evaluate different types of sequence-based methods for each task including traditional feature engineering approaches, different sequence encoding methods as well as large-scale pre-trained protein language models. In addition, we also investigate the performance of these methods under the multi-task learning setting. Experimental results show that large-scale pre-trained protein language models achieve the best performance for most individual tasks, and jointly training multiple tasks further boosts the performance. The datasets and source codes of this benchmark will be open-sourced soon.

paragraphs: PEER addresses the lack of a common benchmark for evaluating methods that learn from protein sequences. Progress across separate datasets is difficult to compare without a shared evaluation collection. The benchmark brings together several types of protein understanding so that different approaches can be assessed across a broader range of tasks.

Its tasks cover protein function, localization, and structure, along with protein-protein and protein-ligand interactions. The authors evaluate traditional feature-engineering methods, different sequence encoders, and large pretrained protein language models. They also examine multitask learning, where a model is trained on several tasks jointly.

The experiments find that large pretrained protein language models perform best on most individual tasks. Joint training across multiple tasks further improves performance. These results provide evidence for both pretrained sequence representations and sharing learning across tasks within the benchmark. PEER's contribution is therefore an evaluation resource together with comparative findings: it creates a common setting for assessing methods and shows which studied approaches work well across its diverse protein problems.
summary.tldr: PEER benchmarks diverse protein-sequence tasks and finds strong performance from pretrained protein language models, with further gains from multitask training.

title: PEER: A Comprehensive and Multi-Task Benchmark for Protein Sequence Understanding

abstract: Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) have quickly become the leading choice for interpretable machine learning. However, unlike uninterpretable methods such as DNNs, they lack expressive power and easy scalability, and are hence not a feasible alternative for real-world tasks. We present a new class of GAMs that use tensor rank decompositions of polynomials to learn powerful, {\em inherently-interpretable} models. Our approach, titled Scalable Polynomial Additive Models (SPAM) is effortlessly scalable and models {\em all} higher-order feature interactions without a combinatorial parameter explosion. SPAM outperforms all current interpretable approaches, and matches DNN/XGBoost performance on a series of real-world benchmarks with up to hundreds of thousands of features. We demonstrate by human subject evaluations that SPAMs are demonstrably more interpretable in practice, and are hence an effortless replacement for DNNs for creating interpretable and high-performance systems suitable for large-scale machine learning.Source code is available at \href{https://github.com/facebookresearch/nbm-spam}{\ttfamily github.com/facebookresearch/nbm-spam}.

paragraphs: Generalized additive models are used for interpretable prediction, but the paper argues that their expressiveness and scalability can restrict practical use. Scalable Polynomial Additive Models, or SPAM, aim to retain an inherently interpretable model structure while handling richer relationships among many input features.

SPAM uses tensor rank decompositions of polynomials. This representation allows the model to account for higher-order feature interactions without a combinatorial explosion in parameters. Those interactions matter because a prediction can depend on combinations of features, rather than only on separate feature contributions. The decomposition provides the paper's route to combining interaction modeling with scalability.

On a series of real-world benchmarks containing up to hundreds of thousands of features, SPAM outperforms the compared interpretable approaches and matches the performance of deep neural networks and XGBoost. Human-subject evaluations also support improved practical interpretability. Together, the results show that this polynomial model class can offer competitive predictive performance and understandable structure at large feature counts in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: SPAM uses decomposed polynomials to model feature interactions at scale while matching strong predictors on reported benchmarks.

title: Scalable Interpretability via Polynomials

abstract: The Bradley-Terry-Luce (BTL) model is a classic and very popular statistical approach for eliciting a global ranking among a collection of items using pairwise comparison data. In applications in which the comparison outcomes are observed as a time series, it is often the case that data are non-stationary, in the sense that the true underlying ranking changes over time. In this paper we are concerned with localizing the change points in a high-dimensional BTL model with piece-wise constant parameters. We propose novel and practicable algorithms based on dynamic programming that can consistently estimate the unknown locations of the change points. We provide consistency rates for our methodology that depend explicitly on the model parameters, the temporal spacing between two consecutive change points and the magnitude of the change. We corroborate our findings with extensive numerical experiments and a real-life example.

paragraphs: Pairwise comparisons provide observations about which of two items is preferred or wins, while the Bradley–Terry–Luce model combines those observations into a global ranking. When comparisons arrive over time, a single fixed ranking may no longer describe the data. This paper asks how to locate the times when the underlying ranking changes abruptly.

The analysis uses a high-dimensional model whose parameters are piecewise constant: they remain fixed within each time segment and change at unknown boundaries. The authors develop practical algorithms based on dynamic programming to estimate those boundaries. This makes the timing of changes an explicit inference target, rather than forcing one ranking to summarize the entire sequence.

The paper establishes consistency and gives rates that explicitly depend on model parameters, the spacing between successive changes, and the size of each change. These dependencies connect estimation accuracy to the structure of the changing process. Extensive numerical experiments and a real-life example support the theoretical findings, grounding the proposed change-localization methods in both controlled and applied settings.
summary.tldr: Dynamic-programming algorithms consistently locate abrupt ranking changes in a piecewise-constant Bradley–Terry–Luce model.

title: Detecting Abrupt Changes in Sequential Pairwise Comparison Data

abstract: We introduce the problem of Bayesian optimization with cost-varying variable subsets (BOCVS) where in each iteration, the learner chooses a subset of query variables and specifies their values while the rest are randomly sampled. Each chosen subset has an associated cost. This presents the learner with the novel challenge of balancing between choosing more informative subsets for more directed learning versus leaving some variables to be randomly sampled to reduce incurred costs. This paper presents a novel Gaussian process upper confidence bound-based algorithm for solving the BOCVS problem that is provably no-regret. We analyze how the availability of cheaper control sets helps in exploration and reduces overall regret. We empirically show that our proposed algorithm can find significantly better solutions than comparable baselines with the same budget.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization when controlling an experiment's inputs has a cost. At each step, the learner chooses which variables to control and assigns their values. The remaining variables are sampled randomly. Different subsets carry different costs, so the learner must decide both what settings to try and how much control to purchase.

This creates a tradeoff between directing an evaluation and conserving the available budget. Choosing an informative subset can make learning more targeted, while leaving variables random can make an evaluation cheaper. The authors introduce this problem as Bayesian optimization with cost-varying variable subsets and develop an algorithm based on Gaussian processes and upper confidence bounds.

The algorithm has a theoretical no-regret guarantee, and the analysis examines how cheaper control subsets can support exploration and reduce accumulated regret. Empirically, the method finds significantly better solutions than comparable baselines under equal budgets. The contribution is to make the cost of controlling variables part of the optimization decision itself, alongside the choice of their values.
summary.tldr: The proposed Bayesian optimization method balances informative input control against its cost and offers a no-regret guarantee.

title: Bayesian Optimization with Cost-varying Variable Subsets

abstract: We derive the first finite-time logarithmic Bayes regret upper bounds for Bayesian bandits. In a multi-armed bandit, we obtain $O(c_\Delta \log n)$ and $O(c_h \log^2 n)$ upper bounds for an upper confidence bound algorithm, where $c_h$ and $c_\Delta$ are constants depending on the prior distribution and the gaps of bandit instances sampled from it, respectively. The latter bound asymptotically matches the lower bound of Lai (1987). Our proofs are a major technical departure from prior works, while being simple and general. To show the generality of our techniques, we apply them to linear bandits. Our results provide insights on the value of prior in the Bayesian setting, both in the objective and as a side information given to the learner. They significantly improve upon existing $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n})$ bounds, which have become standard in the literature despite the logarithmic lower bound of Lai (1987).

paragraphs: Bayesian bandit analysis evaluates learning performance over problem instances drawn from a prior distribution. The paper studies Bayes regret, which measures accumulated decision loss under that averaging. Its main contribution is finite-time upper bounds with logarithmic dependence on the number of rounds, substantially sharpening the square-root-style guarantees commonly used in this literature.

For an upper confidence bound algorithm in multi-armed bandits, the authors obtain bounds of O(cΔ log n) and O(ch log² n). The constants capture information about reward gaps in instances drawn from the prior and about the prior distribution itself. The second bound asymptotically matches a known lower bound, connecting a finite-time guarantee to an established limit.

The authors also apply their proof techniques to linear bandits to demonstrate their broader applicability. Their analysis distinguishes two roles for a prior: it defines how performance is averaged, and it can supply information to the learner. This distinction helps clarify how prior knowledge enters Bayesian learning guarantees and why the resulting bounds can be substantially tighter.
summary.tldr: The paper proves finite-time logarithmic and squared-logarithmic Bayes regret bounds and extends its analysis to linear bandits.

title: Finite-Time Logarithmic Bayes Regret Upper Bounds

abstract: Recently, learning with soft labels has been shown to achieve better performance than learning with hard labels in terms of model generalization, calibration, and robustness. However, collecting pointwise labeling confidence for all training examples can be challenging and time-consuming in real-world scenarios. This paper delves into a novel weakly supervised binary classification problem called confidence-difference (ConfDiff) classification. Instead of pointwise labeling confidence, we are given only unlabeled data pairs with confidence difference that specifies the difference in the probabilities of being positive. We propose a risk-consistent approach to tackle this problem and show that the estimation error bound achieves the optimal convergence rate. We also introduce a risk correction approach to mitigate overfitting problems, whose consistency and convergence rate are also proven. Extensive experiments on benchmark data sets and a real-world recommender system data set validate the effectiveness of our proposed approaches in exploiting the supervision information of the confidence difference.

paragraphs: Training a binary classifier with probability labels can provide richer supervision than assigning each example a definite positive or negative label. Obtaining those probabilities separately for every example can be difficult. This paper studies an alternative: unlabeled pairs accompanied by the difference between their probabilities of belonging to the positive class.

The proposed confidence-difference classification method uses this relative information to learn a classifier. Its risk-consistency result establishes that the approach targets the intended classification risk, and its estimation-error bound has an optimal convergence rate. Thus, the paper gives a theoretical basis for learning from probability differences rather than requiring individual confidence labels.

The authors also develop a risk correction intended to reduce overfitting, with proofs of consistency and convergence rate for the corrected approach. Experiments on benchmark datasets and a real-world recommender-system dataset support the usefulness of both methods. The central finding is that differences in confidence contain supervision that can be exploited through a principled learning objective.
summary.tldr: Confidence-difference classification learns binary classifiers from pairwise probability differences, with consistency guarantees and a correction to mitigate overfitting.

title: Binary Classification with Confidence Difference

abstract: Expressive human pose and shape estimation (EHPS) unifies body, hands, and face motion capture with numerous applications. Despite encouraging progress, current state-of-the-art methods still depend largely on a confined set of training datasets. In this work, we investigate scaling up EHPS towards the first generalist foundation model (dubbed SMPLer-X), with up to ViT-Huge as the backbone and training with up to 4.5M instances from diverse data sources. With big data and the large model, SMPLer-X exhibits strong performance across diverse test benchmarks and excellent transferability to even unseen environments. 1) For the data scaling, we perform a systematic investigation on 32 EHPS datasets, including a wide range of scenarios that a model trained on any single dataset cannot handle. More importantly, capitalizing on insights obtained from the extensive benchmarking process, we optimize our training scheme and select datasets that lead to a significant leap in EHPS capabilities. 2) For the model scaling, we take advantage of vision transformers to study the scaling law of model sizes in EHPS. Moreover, our finetuning strategy turn SMPLer-X into specialist models, allowing them to achieve further performance boosts. Notably, our foundation model SMPLer-X consistently delivers state-of-the-art results on seven benchmarks such as AGORA (107.2 mm NMVE), UBody (57.4 mm PVE), EgoBody (63.6 mm PVE), and EHF (62.3 mm PVE without finetuning).

This paper investigates how far the field can progress by scaling both training data and model capacity. The resulting generalist model, SMPLer-X, uses vision-transformer backbones up to ViT-Huge and as many as 4.5 million training instances.

The authors report state-of-the-art results on seven benchmarks and show that additional finetuning can turn the generalist model into stronger specialists. These findings support the value of broad, carefully selected training data combined with larger models, while also demonstrating a route from general-purpose estimation to task-specific improvements.
summary.tldr: SMPLer-X scales diverse training data and vision transformers to improve unified body, hand, and face estimation across benchmarks and unseen environments.

title: SMPLer-X: Scaling Up Expressive Human Pose and Shape Estimation

abstract: Denoising diffusion models are a powerful type of generative models used to capture complex distributions of real-world signals. However, their applicability is limited to scenarios where training samples are readily available, which is not always the case in real-world applications. For example, in inverse graphics, the goal is to generate samples from a distribution of 3D scenes that align with a given image, but ground-truth 3D scenes are unavailable and only 2D images are accessible. To address this limitation, we propose a novel class of denoising diffusion probabilistic models that learn to sample from distributions of signals that are never directly observed. Instead, these signals are measured indirectly through a known differentiable forward model, which produces partial observations of the unknown signal. Our approach involves integrating the forward model directly into the denoising process. A key contribution of our work is the integration of a differentiable forward model into the denoising process. This integration effectively connects the generative modeling of observations with the generative modeling of the underlying signals, allowing for end-to-end training of a conditional generative model over signals. During inference, our approach enables sampling from the distribution of underlying signals that are consistent with a given partial observation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on three challenging computer vision tasks. For instance, in the context of inverse graphics, our model enables direct sampling from the distribution of 3D scenes that align with a single 2D input image.
originalAbstract: Denoising diffusion models are a powerful type of generative models used to capture complex distributions of real-world signals. However, their applicability is limited to scenarios where training samples are readily available, which is not always the case in real-world applications. For example, in inverse graphics, the goal is to generate samples from a distribution of 3D scenes that align with a given image, but ground-truth 3D scenes are unavailable and only 2D images are accessible. To address this limitation, we propose a novel class of denoising diffusion probabilistic models that learn to sample from distributions of signals that are never directly observed. Instead, these signals are measured indirectly through a known differentiable forward model, which produces partial observations of the unknown signal. Our approach involves integrating the forward model directly into the denoising process. A key contribution of our work is the integration of a differentiable forward model into the denoising process. This integration effectively connects the generative modeling of observations with the generative modeling of the underlying signals, allowing for end-to-end training of a conditional generative model over signals. During inference, our approach enables sampling from the distribution of underlying signals that are consistent with a given partial observation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on three challenging computer vision tasks. For instance, in the context of inverse graphics, our model enables direct sampling from the distribution of 3D scenes that align with a single 2D input image.

paragraphs: Diffusion models usually learn from examples of the signals they will generate. In inverse problems, those signals may never be directly available: a dataset might contain images while the desired outputs are underlying three-dimensional scenes. The paper studies how to learn a distribution over such hidden signals from indirect measurements.

The approach assumes a known, differentiable forward model that turns an underlying signal into a partial observation. It integrates this model into denoising, linking generation of observable data to generation of the hidden signals. This connection enables end-to-end training of a conditional generative model without directly observing the target signals.

At inference time, the model samples underlying signals consistent with a supplied partial observation. The authors demonstrate the approach on three computer vision tasks, including sampling three-dimensional scenes compatible with a single image. The emphasis on a distribution matters: the method produces possible underlying explanations of an observation, rather than treating the inverse problem as necessarily having one unique answer.
summary.tldr: Integrating a known differentiable forward model into diffusion enables learning to generate hidden signals from indirect observations alone.

title: Diffusion with Forward Models: Solving Stochastic Inverse Problems Without Direct Supervision

abstract: We study the best arm identification problem in combinatorial semi-bandits in the fixed confidence setting. We present Perturbed Frank-Wolfe Sampling (P-FWS), an algorithm that (i) runs in polynomial time, (ii) achieves the instance-specific minimal sample complexity in the high confidence regime, and (iii) enjoys polynomial sample complexity guarantees in the moderate confidence regime. To our best knowledge, existing algorithms cannot achieve (ii) and (iii) simultaneously in vanilla bandits. With P-FWS, we close the computational-statistical gap in best arm identification in combinatorial semi-bandits. The design of P-FWS starts from the optimization problem that defines the information-theoretical and instance-specific sample complexity lower bound. P-FWS solves this problem in an online manner using, in each round, a single iteration of the Frank-Wolfe algorithm. Structural properties of the problem are leveraged to make the P-FWS successive updates computationally efficient. In turn, P-FWS only relies on a simple linear maximization oracle.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to identify the best choice in a combinatorial semi-bandit while meeting a specified confidence level. An effective method must satisfy two demands: gather enough evidence to make a reliable decision and keep the computation needed to choose observations manageable. Optimizing one demand alone does not resolve the full problem.

Perturbed Frank-Wolfe Sampling, or P-FWS, begins with the optimization problem defining the information-theoretic sampling lower bound for the particular instance. It works on that problem as observations arrive, taking one Frank-Wolfe iteration per round. The authors use structural properties to make these updates efficient, with access needed only to a linear maximization oracle.

P-FWS runs in polynomial time and reaches the instance-specific minimum sample complexity in the high-confidence regime. It also provides polynomial sample complexity guarantees at moderate confidence. The combination matters because an asymptotically optimal method could otherwise have weak guarantees away from that regime. The authors report that prior methods did not simultaneously achieve the two sampling properties even for ordinary bandits.
summary.tldr: P-FWS combines polynomial computation with asymptotically optimal sampling and polynomial moderate-confidence guarantees for combinatorial best-arm identification.

title: Closing the Computational-Statistical Gap in Best Arm Identification for Combinatorial Semi-bandits

abstract: In this paper, we present StyleTTS 2, a text-to-speech (TTS) model that leverages style diffusion and adversarial training with large speech language models (SLMs) to achieve human-level TTS synthesis. StyleTTS 2 differs from its predecessor by modeling styles as a latent random variable through diffusion models to generate the most suitable style for the text without requiring reference speech, achieving efficient latent diffusion while benefiting from the diverse speech synthesis offered by diffusion models. Furthermore, we employ large pre-trained SLMs, such as WavLM, as discriminators with our novel differentiable duration modeling for end-to-end training, resulting in improved speech naturalness. StyleTTS 2 surpasses human recordings on the single-speaker LJSpeech dataset and matches it on the multispeaker VCTK dataset as judged by native English speakers. Moreover, when trained on the LibriTTS dataset, our model outperforms previous publicly available models for zero-shot speaker adaptation. This work achieves the first human-level TTS on both single and multispeaker datasets, showcasing the potential of style diffusion and adversarial training with large SLMs. The audio demos and source code are available at https://styletts2.github.io/.

paragraphs: Text-to-speech must choose expressive speaking characteristics as well as pronounce the words. StyleTTS 2 represents style as a latent random variable generated by diffusion, allowing it to select a suitable style from text without requiring reference speech.

The model also uses pretrained speech language models, including WavLM, as discriminators. A differentiable duration-modeling component enables end-to-end adversarial training, with the goal of improving perceived speech naturalness while keeping latent diffusion efficient.

Native-English-speaker judgments rate the system above human recordings on LJSpeech and comparable to them on VCTK. Trained on LibriTTS, it also outperforms earlier publicly available models for zero-shot speaker adaptation. These human-level claims refer to particular perceptual evaluations and datasets; they do not establish superiority to human speech in all conditions. The abstract provides no listener counts or numerical rating scales.
summary.tldr: StyleTTS 2 combines latent style diffusion with speech-model adversarial training for natural speech synthesis.

title: StyleTTS 2: Towards Human-Level Text-to-Speech through Style Diffusion and Adversarial Training with Large Speech Language Models

abstract: Modern neural language models that are widely used in various NLP tasks risk memorizing sensitive information from their training data.Understanding this memorization is important in real world applications and also from a learning-theoretical perspective. An open question in previous studies of language model memorization is how to filter out ``common'' memorization. In fact, most memorization criteria strongly correlate with the number of occurrences in the training set, capturing memorized familiar phrases, public knowledge, templated texts, or other repeated data.We formulate a notion of counterfactual memorization which characterizes how a model's predictions change if a particular document is omitted during training.We identify and study counterfactually-memorized training examples in standard text datasets.We estimate the influence of each memorized training example on the validation set and on generated texts, showing how this can provide direct evidence of the source of memorization at test time.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to distinguish a language model's dependence on particular training documents from its familiarity with widely repeated material. Existing memorization criteria often track how frequently text occurs in training. That can flag public knowledge, familiar phrases, or templates, making it difficult to understand whether a particular document was responsible for what the model learned.

The authors define counterfactual memorization through a different question: how would the model's predictions change if a specific document had been left out of training? This focuses on the effect of that document's inclusion. It provides a way to investigate memorization through changes in predictions rather than treating the ability to reproduce common text as sufficient evidence of document-specific dependence.

They identify and examine examples with this property in standard text datasets. They also estimate how memorized training examples influence validation predictions and generated text. These estimates can provide direct evidence connecting memorization observed at test time to its training source, helping clarify a phenomenon relevant to both sensitive information and learning theory.
summary.tldr: Counterfactual memorization measures how omitting a training document changes predictions, helping trace memorized behavior to specific sources.

title: Counterfactual Memorization in Neural Language Models

abstract: Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) allows to update pre-trained models to changing data distributions at deployment time. While early work tested these algorithms for individual fixed distribution shifts, recent work proposed and applied methods for continual adaptation over long timescales. To examine the reported progress in the field, we propose the Continually Changing Corruptions (CCC) benchmark to measure asymptotic performance of TTA techniques. We find that eventually all but one state-of-the-art methods collapse and perform worse than a non-adapting model, including models specifically proposed to be robust to performance collapse. In addition, we introduce a simple baseline, "RDumb", that periodically resets the model to its pretrained state. RDumb performs better or on par with the previously proposed state-of-the-art in all considered benchmarks.Our results show that previous TTA approaches are neither effective at regularizing adaptation to avoid collapse nor able to outperform a simplistic resetting strategy.

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation updates a pretrained model as its deployment data changes. Success on one fixed distribution shift does not establish whether those updates remain useful over a long sequence of changes. This paper introduces the Continually Changing Corruptions benchmark to examine the long-run behavior of adaptation methods.

On this benchmark, all but one of the evaluated state-of-the-art methods eventually collapse and perform worse than a model that does not adapt. This includes methods specifically proposed to resist performance collapse. The finding makes evaluation duration consequential: an adaptation procedure's eventual behavior can undermine the benefit suggested by shorter-term results.

The authors also introduce RDumb, a simple baseline that periodically restores the model to its pretrained state. It matches or exceeds previously proposed state-of-the-art methods on every benchmark considered. Within those evaluations, periodic resetting proves more effective than the tested approaches' attempts to regulate ongoing adaptation, challenging the evidence for progress in maintaining useful continual test-time updates.
summary.tldr: Long-run evaluations expose collapse in most tested adaptation methods, while periodic resetting matches or beats prior methods across the considered benchmarks.

title: RDumb: A simple approach that questions our progress in continual test-time adaptation

abstract: We consider a fair resource allocation problem in the no-regret setting against an unrestricted adversary. The objective is to allocate resources equitably among several agents in an online fashion so that the difference of the aggregate $\alpha$-fair utilities of the agents achieved by an optimal static clairvoyant allocation and the online policy grows sublinearly with time. The problem inherits its difficulty from the non-separable nature of the global $\alpha$-fairness function. Previously, it was shown that no online policy could achieve a sublinear standard regret in this problem. In this paper, we propose an efficient online resource allocation policy, called Online Fair Allocation ($\texttt{OFA}$), that achieves sublinear $c_\alpha$-approximate regret with approximation factor $c_\alpha=(1-\alpha)^{-(1-\alpha)}\leq 1.445,$ for $0\leq \alpha < 1$. Our upper bound on the $c_\alpha$-regret for this problem exhibits a surprising \emph{phase transition} phenomenon -- transitioning from a power-law to a constant at the critical exponent $\alpha=\frac{1}{2}.$ Our result also resolves an open problem in designing an efficient no-regret policy for the online job scheduling problem in certain parameter regimes. Along the way, we introduce new algorithmic and analytical techniques, including greedy estimation of the future gradients for non-additive global reward functions and bootstrapping second-order regret bounds, which may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: This paper studies allocating resources fairly over time against an unrestricted adversary. Performance is compared with the best fixed allocation chosen with knowledge of the entire sequence. The objective uses aggregate α-fair utilities, whose global, non-separable structure makes decisions difficult to evaluate independently. Earlier results rule out sublinear standard regret for this problem.

The proposed Online Fair Allocation policy instead achieves sublinear approximate regret. For 0 ≤ α < 1, its approximation factor is (1−α) raised to the power −(1−α), which is at most 1.445. The guarantee relaxes the comparison with the hindsight benchmark, allowing the regret to grow more slowly than time despite the impossibility for standard regret.

The upper bound exhibits a phase transition at α = 1/2, changing from power-law growth to a constant. The result also resolves an online job-scheduling question in certain parameter regimes. Supporting techniques include estimating future gradients for non-additive rewards and bootstrapping second-order regret bounds, providing tools for reasoning about these globally coupled objectives.
summary.tldr: Online Fair Allocation achieves sublinear approximate regret for adversarial fair allocation, with a bound that changes regime at α = 1/2.

title: No-regret Algorithms for Fair Resource Allocation

abstract: Deep neural networks have reached human-level performance on many computer vision tasks. However, the objectives used to train these networks enforce only that similar images are embedded at similar locations in the representation space, and do not directly constrain the global structure of the resulting space. Here, we explore the impact of supervising this global structure by linearly aligning it with human similarity judgments. We find that a naive approach leads to large changes in local representational structure that harm downstream performance. Thus, we propose a novel method that aligns the global structure of representations while preserving their local structure. This global-local transform considerably improves accuracy across a variety of few-shot learning and anomaly detection tasks. Our results indicate that human visual representations are globally organized in a way that facilitates learning from few examples, and incorporating this global structure into neural network representations improves performance on downstream tasks.

paragraphs: A neural network can place similar images near one another without organizing its entire representation space in a useful way. This paper investigates whether human similarity judgments can improve that broader organization. The authors focus on linearly aligning neural representations with human judgments, asking how the overall geometry affects subsequent learning tasks.

Their initial approach reveals a tradeoff: naive alignment changes local relationships substantially and harms downstream performance. The proposed global-local transform addresses this by aligning the global structure while preserving local structure. In practical terms, the method seeks to improve the arrangement of the representation space without losing the useful neighborhood relationships that the original network already learned.

The resulting transform considerably improves accuracy across a variety of few-shot learning and anomaly detection tasks. The findings indicate that the global organization of human visual representations can support learning from few examples, and that incorporating this organization benefits neural representations in the evaluated tasks. The paper therefore identifies both a useful source of supervision and a reason that applying it without local preservation can fail.
summary.tldr: Aligning global neural representation structure with human similarity judgments improves downstream tasks when local relationships are preserved.

title: Improving neural network representations using human similarity judgments

abstract: Multimodal learning assumes all modality combinations of interest are available during training to learn cross-modal correspondences. In this paper, we challenge this modality-complete assumption for multimodal learning and instead strive for generalization to unseen modality combinations during inference. We pose the problem of unseen modality interaction and introduce a first solution. It exploits a module that projects the multidimensional features of different modalities into a common space with rich information preserved. This allows the information to be accumulated with a simple summation operation across available modalities. To reduce overfitting to less discriminative modality combinations during training, we further improve the model learning with pseudo-supervision indicating the reliability of a modality’s prediction. We demonstrate that our approach is effective for diverse tasks and modalities by evaluating it for multimodal video classification, robot state regression, and multimedia retrieval. Project website: https://xiaobai1217.github.io/Unseen-Modality-Interaction/.

paragraphs: Multimodal systems combine information from different kinds of inputs. Learning their interactions commonly assumes that the combinations needed at inference also appear during training. This paper studies the more demanding case in which a system must work with combinations of modalities it has never encountered together.

The proposed method projects the multidimensional features of each modality into a common representation while preserving rich information. It then combines the available representations by summation. This shared format lets information from different modalities accumulate through the same operation, providing a mechanism for handling combinations beyond those used during training.

The training procedure also uses pseudo-supervision that indicates the reliability of a modality's prediction. This is intended to reduce overfitting to combinations that are less informative for the task. Evaluations cover multimodal video classification, robot state regression, and multimedia retrieval, demonstrating effectiveness across different tasks and input types. The contribution is both a formulation of unseen modality interaction and an initial method that learns representations designed to combine flexibly.
summary.tldr: A shared representation and reliability-based training enable multimodal models to handle input combinations absent from training.

title: Learning Unseen Modality Interaction

abstract: Modeling the interaction between proteins and ligands and accurately predicting their binding structures is a critical yet challenging task in drug discovery. Recent advancements in deep learning have shown promise in addressing this challenge, with sampling-based and regression-based methods emerging as two prominent approaches. However, these methods have notable limitations. Sampling-based methods often suffer from low efficiency due to the need for generating multiple candidate structures for selection. On the other hand, regression-based methods offer fast predictions but may experience decreased accuracy. Additionally, the variation in protein sizes often requires external modules for selecting suitable binding pockets, further impacting efficiency. In this work, we propose FABind, an end-to-end model that combines pocket prediction and docking to achieve accurate and fast protein-ligand binding. FABind incorporates a unique ligand-informed pocket prediction module, which is also leveraged for docking pose estimation. The model further enhances the docking process by incrementally integrating the predicted pocket to optimize protein-ligand binding, reducing discrepancies between training and inference. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, our proposed FABind demonstrates strong advantages in terms of effectiveness and efficiency compared to existing methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/QizhiPei/FABind.

paragraphs: Predicting how a ligand binds to a protein is an important structural modeling problem in drug discovery. Sampling-based methods can be slow because they generate several candidate structures before selecting one. Regression-based methods provide fast predictions but can sacrifice accuracy. Variable protein sizes also create a need to locate suitable binding pockets, sometimes through separate modules.

FABind combines pocket prediction and docking in one end-to-end model. Its pocket predictor uses information about the ligand, and the same module also contributes to estimating the docking pose. Bringing these tasks together allows the model to connect the choice of binding region with the predicted arrangement of the protein and ligand.

The method progressively incorporates its predicted pocket into docking, with the aim of reducing differences between training and inference. Benchmark experiments show strong effectiveness and efficiency advantages over existing methods. The stated contribution is therefore an integrated prediction system that addresses speed and accuracy together, while incorporating pocket selection directly into the binding-structure workflow.
summary.tldr: FABind integrates ligand-informed pocket prediction and docking to deliver fast, accurate protein–ligand binding structures.

title: FABind: Fast and Accurate Protein-Ligand Binding

abstract: Actor-critic (AC) methods are widely used in reinforcement learning (RL), and benefit from the flexibility of using any policy gradient method as the actor and value-based method as the critic. The critic is usually trained by minimizing the TD error, an objective that is potentially decorrelated with the true goal of achieving a high reward with the actor. We address this mismatch by designing a joint objective for training the actor and critic in a decision-aware fashion. We use the proposed objective to design a generic, AC algorithm that can easily handle any function approximation. We explicitly characterize the conditions under which the resulting algorithm guarantees monotonic policy improvement, regardless of the choice of the policy and critic parameterization. Instantiating the generic algorithm results in an actor that involves maximizing a sequence of surrogate functions (similar to TRPO, PPO), and a critic that involves minimizing a closely connected objective. Using simple bandit examples, we provably establish the benefit of the proposed critic objective over the standard squared error. Finally, we empirically demonstrate the benefit of our decision-aware actor-critic framework on simple RL problems.

paragraphs: Actor-critic reinforcement learning divides the work between an actor that chooses actions and a critic that evaluates them. The critic is commonly trained to reduce temporal-difference error, but that training objective may be poorly aligned with improving the actor's reward. This paper directly addresses that possible mismatch between prediction quality and decision quality.

The authors introduce a joint objective that connects actor and critic training. Their generic algorithm accommodates different forms of function approximation, and they identify conditions under which policy performance improves monotonically regardless of the chosen parameterizations. The guarantee depends on those conditions; it does not assert that every actor-critic update automatically improves performance.

A concrete version trains the actor through a sequence of surrogate objectives and trains the critic with a closely related objective. Simple bandit examples establish a provable advantage of the critic objective over standard squared error. Experiments on simple reinforcement learning problems also support the framework, suggesting value in training critics around the decisions their estimates help produce.
summary.tldr: A joint actor-critic objective aligns critic training with policy improvement and provides conditional guarantees across different function approximations.

title: Decision-Aware Actor-Critic with Function Approximation and Theoretical Guarantees

abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization has attracted increasing research attention in recent years, due to its promising experimental results in real-world applications. Interestingly, we find that existing OOD generalization methods are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This motivates us to study OOD adversarial robustness. We first present theoretical analyses of OOD adversarial robustness in two different complementary settings. Motivated by the theoretical results, we design two algorithms to improve the OOD adversarial robustness. Finally, we conduct experiments to validate the effectiveness of our proposed algorithms.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution generalization concerns how models perform when the data they encounter differs from their training setting. This paper examines a further question: how those models behave under adversarial attacks. The authors find that existing methods for out-of-distribution generalization remain vulnerable, making adversarial robustness a separate concern within the broader problem of generalizing beyond training data.

The study develops theoretical analyses in two complementary settings. These analyses motivate two algorithms intended to improve adversarial robustness under distribution shift. The contribution therefore connects a diagnosis of vulnerability with algorithm design: the proposed methods are informed by the theoretical investigation of the combined problem.

Experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms. The stated finding supports improvements in out-of-distribution adversarial robustness, while the initial vulnerability result shows why favorable generalization performance alone does not settle the question of resistance to attacks. The paper brings these two concerns into a shared analysis and evaluation framework rather than treating success at distribution shift as sufficient evidence of adversarial robustness.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies adversarial vulnerabilities in out-of-distribution generalization methods and develops two theoretically motivated algorithms that improve robustness experimentally.

title: On the Adversarial Robustness of Out-of-distribution Generalization Models

abstract: Deep neural networks have been increasingly used in real-world applications, making it critical to ensure their ability to adapt to new, unseen data. In this paper, we study the generalization capability of neural networks trained with (stochastic) gradient flow. We establish a new connection between the loss dynamics of gradient flow and general kernel machines by proposing a new kernel, called loss path kernel. This kernel measures the similarity between two data points by evaluating the agreement between loss gradients along the path determined by the gradient flow. Based on this connection, we derive a new generalization upper bound that applies to general neural network architectures. This new bound is tight and strongly correlated with the true generalization error. We apply our results to guide the design of neural architecture search (NAS) and demonstrate favorable performance compared with state-of-the-art NAS algorithms through numerical experiments.

We apply our results to guide the design of neural architecture search (NAS) and demonstrate favorable performance compared with state-of-the-art NAS algorithms through numerical experiments.

paragraphs: The paper asks how a neural network’s training process can help explain its performance on unseen data. It studies networks trained with gradient flow, including its stochastic form, and connects their changing losses to the theory of kernel machines. This makes the route taken during learning part of the analysis of generalization.

The central construction is the loss path kernel. It measures how similarly two examples’ loss gradients behave along the training path. Instead of describing similarity using only a fixed representation, the kernel incorporates agreement across the learning process. The authors use this connection to derive a generalization upper bound that applies to general neural network architectures.

The paper reports that the bound is tight and strongly correlated with actual generalization error. It also uses the analysis to guide neural architecture search, where candidate network designs must be assessed. Numerical experiments show favorable performance against state-of-the-art search algorithms, giving the theoretical connection a practical application in choosing network architectures.
summary.tldr: A kernel built from loss-gradient agreement along training yields a generalization bound and helps guide neural architecture search.

title: Analyzing Generalization of Neural Networks through Loss Path Kernels

abstract: We study lower bounds on adaptive sensing algorithms for recovering low rank matrices using linear measurements. Given an $n \times n$ matrix $A$, a general linear measurement $S(A)$, for an $n \times n$ matrix $S$, is just the inner product of $S$ and $A$, each treated as $n^2$-dimensional vectors. By performing as few linear measurements as possible on a rank-$r$ matrix $A$, we hope to construct a matrix $\hat{A}$ that satisfies $|A - \hat{A}|\_F^2 \le c |A|\_F^2$, for a small constant $c$. Here $|A|\_F$ denotes the Frobenius norm $(\sum_{i,j} A_{i,j}^2)^{1/2}$. It is commonly assumed that when measuring $A$ with $S$, the response is corrupted with an independent Gaussian random variable of mean $0$ and variance $\sigma^2$. Candès and Plan (IEEE Trans. Inform. Theory 2011) study non-adaptive algorithms for low rank matrix recovery using random linear measurements. They use the restricted isometry property (RIP) of Random Gaussian Matrices to give tractable algorithms to estimate $A$ from the measurements.At the edge of the noise level where recovery is information-theoretically feasible, it is known that their non-adaptive algorithms need to perform $\Omega(n^2)$ measurements, which amounts to reading the entire matrix. An important question is whether adaptivity helps in decreasing the overall number of measurements. While for the related problem of sparse recovery, adaptive algorithms have been extensively studied, as far as we are aware adaptive algorithms and lower bounds on them seem largely unexplored for matrix recovery. We show that any adaptive algorithm that uses $k$ linear measurements in each round and outputs an approximation as in (1) with probability $\ge 9/10$ must run for $t = \Omega(\log(n^2/k)/\log\log n)$ rounds. Our lower bound shows that any adaptive algorithm which uses $n^{2-\beta}$ ($\beta > 0$ is arbitrary constant) linear measurements in each round must run for $\Omega(\log n/\log\log n)$ rounds. Our techniques also readily extend to obtain lower bounds on adaptive algorithms for tensor recovery. Our hard distribution also allows us to give a measurement-vs-rounds trade-off for many sensing problems in numerical linear algebra, such as spectral norm low rank approximation, Frobenius norm low rank approximation, singular vector approximation, and more.

paragraphs: Recovering a low-rank matrix from linear measurements means reconstructing its entries from weighted sums. Here, each measurement is corrupted by independent Gaussian noise, and success means achieving a small relative squared reconstruction error. Near the noise level where recovery remains possible, known non-adaptive methods require measurements on the scale of the matrix's total number of entries.

The paper asks whether choosing later measurements based on earlier responses can avoid that burden. It proves a lower bound on the number of adaptive rounds: an algorithm taking k measurements per round and succeeding with probability at least 9/10 needs Ω(log(n²/k) / log log n) rounds for an n-by-n matrix in the studied setting.

Consequently, using n^(2−β) measurements per round, for any fixed positive β, requires Ω(log n / log log n) rounds. This establishes a trade-off between measurements per round and sequential interaction. The techniques also extend to tensor recovery and related numerical linear algebra tasks, including low-rank and singular-vector approximation.
summary.tldr: Lower bounds show that reducing measurements per round in adaptive matrix recovery requires sufficiently many sequential rounds.

title: Lower Bounds on Adaptive Sensing for Matrix Recovery

abstract: Due to the ease of training, ability to scale, and high sample quality, diffusion models (DMs) have become the preferred option for generative modeling, with numerous pre-trained models available for a wide variety of datasets. Containing intricate information about data distributions, pre-trained DMs are valuable assets for downstream applications. In this work, we consider learning from pre-trained DMs and transferring their knowledge to other generative models in a data-free fashion. Specifically, we propose a general framework called Diff-Instruct to instruct the training of arbitrary generative models as long as the generated samples are differentiable with respect to the model parameters. Our proposed Diff-Instruct is built on a rigorous mathematical foundation where the instruction process directly corresponds to minimizing a novel divergence we call Integral Kullback-Leibler (IKL) divergence. IKL is tailored for DMs by calculating the integral of the KL divergence along a diffusion process, which we show to be more robust in comparing distributions with misaligned supports. We also reveal non-trivial connections of our method to existing works such as DreamFusion \citep{poole2022dreamfusion}, and generative adversarial training. To demonstrate the effectiveness and universality of Diff-Instruct, we consider two scenarios: distilling pre-trained diffusion models and refining existing GAN models. The experiments on distilling pre-trained diffusion models show that Diff-Instruct results in state-of-the-art single-step diffusion-based models. The experiments on refining GAN models show that the Diff-Instruct can consistently improve the pre-trained generators of GAN models across various settings. Our official code is released through \url{https://github.com/pkulwj1994/diff_instruct}.

Diff-Instruct produces state-of-the-art single-step diffusion-based models in the reported distillation experiments and consistently improves pretrained GAN generators across the tested settings. title: Diff-Instruct: A Universal Approach for Transferring Knowledge From Pre-trained Diffusion Models

abstract: Language-based colorization produces plausible and visually pleasing colors under the guidance of user-friendly natural language descriptions. Previous methods implicitly assume that users provide comprehensive color descriptions for most of the objects in the image, which leads to suboptimal performance. In this paper, we propose a unified model to perform language-based colorization with any-level descriptions. We leverage the pretrained cross-modality generative model for its robust language understanding and rich color priors to handle the inherent ambiguity of any-level descriptions. We further design modules to align with input conditions to preserve local spatial structures and prevent the ghosting effect. With the proposed novel sampling strategy, our model achieves instance-aware colorization in diverse and complex scenarios. Extensive experimental results demonstrate our advantages of effectively handling any-level descriptions and outperforming both language-based and automatic colorization methods. The code and pretrained modelsare available at: https://github.com/changzheng123/L-CAD.

paragraphs: Language-guided colorization lets users describe desired colors in natural language. Earlier methods implicitly expect fairly complete color descriptions for most objects, which can hurt performance when instructions are less comprehensive. L-CAD proposes a unified model intended to handle descriptions at varying levels of detail, including the ambiguity that comes with incomplete guidance.

The method uses a pretrained cross-modal generative model for both language understanding and prior knowledge about colors. Additional modules align generation with the input conditions, aiming to preserve local spatial structure and prevent ghosting artifacts. A new sampling strategy supports instance-aware colorization, allowing the model to address individual objects within diverse and complex scenes.

The reported experiments demonstrate effective handling of descriptions at different levels and better performance than both language-based and automatic colorization methods. The approach matters because it combines user guidance with learned color knowledge, reducing dependence on exhaustive instructions. Its structural alignment and sampling components also address how colors are assigned spatially, so the contribution concerns both interpreting the description and producing a coherent colorized image.
summary.tldr: L-CAD combines pretrained diffusion knowledge, structural alignment, and instance-aware sampling to colorize images from descriptions with varying detail.

title: L-CAD: Language-based Colorization with Any-level Descriptions using Diffusion Priors

abstract: Regular expressions (REs) offer one-shot solutions for many networking tasks, e.g., network intrusion detection. However, REs purely rely on expert knowledge and cannot utilize labeled data for better accuracy. Today, neural networks (NNs) have shown superior accuracy and flexibility, thanks to their ability to learn from rich labeled data. Nevertheless, NNs are often incompetent in cold-start scenarios and too complex for deployment on network devices. In this paper, we propose Metis, a general framework that converts REs to network device affordable models for superior accuracy and throughput by taking advantage of REs' expert knowledge and NNs' learning ability. In Metis, we convert REs to byte-level recurrent neural networks (BRNNs) without training. The BRNNs preserve expert knowledge from REs and offer adequate accuracy in cold-start scenarios. When rich labeled data is available, the performance of BRNNs can be improved by training. Furthermore, we design a semi-supervised knowledge distillation to transform the BRNNs into pooling soft random forests (PSRFs) that can be deployed on network devices. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first method to employ model inference as an alternative to RE matching in network scenarios. We collect network traffic data on our campus for three weeks and evaluate Metis on them. Experimental results show that Metis is more accurate than original REs and other baselines, achieving superior throughput when deployed on network devices.

paragraphs: Regular expressions encode expert knowledge for networking tasks such as intrusion detection, but they cannot directly improve from labeled examples. Neural networks can learn from data, yet they can struggle before enough examples are available and may be too costly for network devices. Metis connects these complementary capabilities in a staged framework.

First, Metis converts regular expressions into byte-level recurrent neural networks without training. These networks retain the expert knowledge needed for cold-start operation and can subsequently improve through training when labeled data become available. A semi-supervised knowledge-distillation step then transforms them into pooling soft random forests suitable for deployment on network devices.

The authors evaluate the framework using three weeks of traffic collected on their campus. They report higher accuracy than the original regular expressions and other tested baselines, together with superior throughput on network devices. The results support a path from existing expert rules to trainable models and then to deployable inference systems, combining an immediate starting point with the ability to improve from data.
summary.tldr: Metis converts regular expressions into trainable neural models and distills them into models deployable on network devices.

title: Metis: Understanding and Enhancing In-Network Regular Expressions

abstract: Open-source Large Language Models (LLMs) and their specialized variants, particularly Code LLMs, have recently delivered impressive performance. However, previous Code LLMs are typically fine-tuned on single-source data with limited quality and diversity, which may insufficiently elicit the potential of pre-trained Code LLMs. In this paper, we present AlchemistCoder, a series of Code LLMs with enhanced code generation and generalization capabilities fine-tuned on multi-source data. To achieve this, we pioneer to unveil inherent conflicts among the various styles and qualities in multi-source code corpora and introduce data-specific prompts with hindsight relabeling, termed AlchemistPrompts, to harmonize different data sources and instruction-response pairs. Additionally, we propose incorporating the data construction process into the fine-tuning data as code comprehension tasks, including instruction evolution, data filtering, and code review. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AlchemistCoder holds a clear lead among all models of the same size (6.7B/7B) and rivals or even surpasses larger models (15B/33B/70B), showcasing the efficacy of our method in refining instruction-following capabilities and advancing the boundaries of code intelligence. Source code and models are available at https://github.com/InternLM/AlchemistCoder.

paragraphs: Combining code-training datasets can increase variety, but it also brings together incompatible styles and uneven quality. AlchemistCoder addresses this tension when fine-tuning pretrained code language models. The motivation is that relying on a single data source may leave useful capabilities underdeveloped, while simply pooling sources does not resolve conflicts between their instructions and responses.

The method introduces AlchemistPrompts, prompts tailored to particular data through hindsight relabeling. These prompts help reconcile the differences among sources and their instruction-response pairs. The authors also turn parts of the data-construction process into training material. Instruction evolution, data filtering, and code review become code-comprehension tasks, giving the model additional ways to learn from how examples are constructed and assessed.

The resulting model family is evaluated for code generation and generalization. In the reported experiments, the 6.7-billion- and 7-billion-parameter models lead their same-size comparisons and compete with, or sometimes exceed, larger models. These findings support the value of organizing heterogeneous training data and teaching comprehension alongside generation, rather than treating dataset diversity alone as sufficient.
summary.tldr: AlchemistCoder combines hindsight-based prompts and code-comprehension tasks to improve fine-tuning on heterogeneous code datasets.

title: AlchemistCoder: Harmonizing and Eliciting Code Capability by Hindsight Tuning on Multi-source Data

abstract: High-dimensional Bayesian optimization (BO) tasks such as molecular design often require $>10,$$000$ function evaluations before obtaining meaningful results. While methods like sparse variational Gaussian processes (SVGPs) reduce computational requirements in these settings, the underlying approximations result in suboptimal data acquisitions that slow the progress of optimization. In this paper we modify SVGPs to better align with the goals of BO: targeting informed data acquisition over global posterior fidelity. Using the framework of utility-calibrated variational inference (Lacoste–Julien et al., 2011), we unify GP approximation and data acquisition into a joint optimization problem, thereby ensuring optimal decisions under a limited computational budget. Our approach can be used with any decision-theoretic acquisition function and is readily compatible with trust region methods like TuRBO (Eriksson et al., 2019). We derive efficient joint objectives for the expected improvement (EI) and knowledge gradient (KG) acquisition functions in both the standard and batch BO settings. On a variety of recent high dimensional benchmark tasks in control and molecular design, our approach significantly outperforms standard SVGPs and is capable of achieving comparable rewards with up to $10\times$ fewer function evaluations.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization uses a predictive model to decide which expensive evaluation to perform next. High-dimensional problems can require more than 10,000 evaluations, making scalable predictive models important. Sparse variational Gaussian processes reduce computation, but their approximations can also lead to less useful evaluation choices and slower optimization.

This paper changes what the approximation is trained to accomplish. Instead of prioritizing an accurate posterior distribution everywhere, it prioritizes the decisions needed for optimization. Using utility-calibrated variational inference, the authors jointly optimize the Gaussian-process approximation and the acquisition decision. They derive efficient objectives for expected improvement and knowledge gradient, covering both individual and batch evaluations. The framework also supports decision-theoretic acquisition functions and integration with trust-region methods.

On high-dimensional benchmarks in control and molecular design, the approach significantly outperforms standard sparse variational Gaussian processes. In the reported comparisons, it can reach comparable rewards with up to ten times fewer function evaluations. The central finding is that an approximation designed around the next useful decision can make a limited computational budget more effective.
summary.tldr: Jointly optimizing a Gaussian-process approximation and its acquisition decisions improves evaluation efficiency in tested Bayesian optimization tasks.

title: Approximation-Aware Bayesian Optimization

abstract: Mobility impairment caused by limb loss, aging, stroke, and other movement deficiencies is a significant challenge faced by millions of individuals worldwide. Advanced assistive technologies, such as prostheses and orthoses, have the potential to greatly improve the quality of life for such individuals. A critical component in the design of these technologies is the accurate forecasting of reference joint motion for impaired limbs, which is hindered by the scarcity of joint locomotion data available for these patients. To address this, we propose ReMAP, a novel model repurposing strategy that leverages deep learning's reprogramming property, incorporating network inversion principles and retrieval-augmented mapping. Our approach adapts models originally designed for able-bodied individuals to forecast joint motion in limb-impaired patients without altering model parameters. We demonstrate the efficacy of ReMAP through extensive empirical studies on data from below-knee amputated patients, showcasing significant improvements over traditional transfer learning and fine-tuning methods. These findings have significant implications for advancing assistive technology and mobility for patients with amputations, stroke, or aging.

paragraphs: ReMAP addresses joint-motion forecasting for people with impaired limbs, a component relevant to assistive devices such as prostheses and orthoses. The difficulty is that patient-specific locomotion data are scarce. The paper seeks to make use of models already developed for able-bodied individuals in this more data-limited setting.

The approach combines neural-model reprogramming with network inversion and retrieval-augmented mapping. It adapts an existing model's use for impaired-limb forecasting without changing the model's parameters. This makes repurposing a trained predictor the central adaptation strategy, providing an alternative way to exploit knowledge already present in the model.

Empirical studies using data from patients with below-knee amputations report significant improvements over traditional transfer learning and fine-tuning methods. Those findings support ReMAP for the patient population studied and motivate its potential relevance to assistive technology more broadly. Stroke and aging appear as broader application motivations; the stated empirical evidence comes specifically from below-knee amputation data and concerns motion forecasting rather than demonstrated improvements in patients' mobility.
summary.tldr: ReMAP repurposes fixed models trained on able-bodied motion to improve joint-motion forecasting for patients with below-knee amputations.

title: ReMAP: Neural Model Reprogramming with Network Inversion and Retrieval-Augmented Mapping for Adaptive Motion Forecasting

abstract: We present sDBSCAN, a scalable density-based clustering algorithm in high dimensions with cosine distance. sDBSCAN leverages recent advancements in random projections given a significantly large number of random vectors to quickly identify core points and their neighborhoods, the primary hurdle of density-based clustering. Theoretically, sDBSCAN preserves the DBSCAN’s clustering structure under mild conditions with high probability. To facilitate sDBSCAN, we present sOPTICS, a scalable visual tool to guide the parameter setting of sDBSCAN. We also extend sDBSCAN and sOPTICS to L2, L1, χ2, and Jensen-Shannon distances via random kernel features. Empirically, sDBSCAN is significantly faster and provides higher accuracy than competitive DBSCAN variants on real-world million-point data sets. On these data sets, sDBSCAN and sOPTICS run in a few minutes, while the scikit-learn counterparts and other clustering competitors demand several hours orcannot run on our hardware due to memory constraints. Our code is available at https://github.com/NinhPham/sDbscan.

paragraphs: Density-based clustering becomes expensive when identifying core points and their neighborhoods in large, high-dimensional datasets. sDBSCAN targets this bottleneck for cosine distance using random projections. With a sufficiently large collection of random vectors, it can identify the relevant points and neighborhoods quickly.

The authors prove that sDBSCAN preserves DBSCAN’s clustering structure with high probability under mild conditions. They also introduce sOPTICS, a scalable visualization tool intended to guide parameter choices. Random kernel features extend both methods to several additional distances, including L2, L1, chi-squared, and Jensen-Shannon, broadening the range of data comparisons they can support.

These results connect a conditional structural guarantee with substantial practical scalability gains, making neighborhood discovery the central target of the acceleration rather than changing the clustering objective.
summary.tldr: sDBSCAN uses random projections to accelerate density-based clustering, with conditional structure-preservation guarantees and minute-scale results on million-point datasets.

title: Scalable DBSCAN with Random Projections

abstract: The feasibility of variational quantum algorithms, the most popular correspondent of neural networks on noisy, near-term quantum hardware, is highly impacted by the circuit depth of the involved parametrized quantum circuits (PQCs). Higher depth increases expressivity, but also results in a detrimental accumulation of errors. Furthermore, the number of parameters involved in the PQC significantly influences the performance through the necessary number of measurements to evaluate gradients, which scales linearly with the number of parameters. Motivated by this, we look at deep equilibrium models (DEQs), which mimic an infinite-depth, weight-tied network using a fraction of the memory by employing a root solver to find the fixed points of the network. In this work, we present Quantum Deep Equilibrium Models (QDEQs): a training paradigm that learns parameters of a quantum machine learning model given by a PQC using DEQs. To our knowledge, no work has yet explored the application of DEQs to QML models. We apply QDEQs to find the parameters of a quantum circuit in two settings: the first involves classifying MNIST-4 digits with 4 qubits; the second extends it to 10 classes of MNIST, FashionMNIST and CIFAR. We find that QDEQ is not only competitive with comparable existing baseline models, but also achieves higher performance than a network with 5 times more layers. This demonstrates that the QDEQ paradigm can be used to develop significantly more shallow quantum circuits for a given task, something which is essential for the utility of near-term quantum computers. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/martaskrt/qdeq}.
