paragraphs: Adapting a pretrained model to incoming data can become unstable when observations are not independent and identically distributed. Existing test-time adaptation methods often emphasize their unsupervised training objective while paying less attention to how parameters evolve. This paper studies that evolution directly through a probabilistic description of the adaptation process.

The authors use stochastic differential equations to analyze parameter distributions over time. Under stable, high-performing adaptation conditions, they find that the log-variance of the parameter transition distribution closely follows an inverse-gamma distribution. This observed alignment motivates Structured Inverse-Gamma Model Alignment, or SIGMA, which dynamically regulates parameter evolution to preserve that distributional pattern.

Across diverse models, datasets, and adaptation scenarios, SIGMA consistently improves the tested state-of-the-art adaptation methods. The results support treating update dynamics as an additional source of information for controlling adaptation. The inverse-gamma relationship is presented as a finding associated with successful adaptation, and the algorithm uses that finding to guide parameter changes in non-i.i.d. environments.
summary.tldr: SIGMA improves test-time adaptation by regulating parameter dynamics toward a distributional pattern associated with stable, high-performing adaptation.

title: Parameter Dynamics of Online Machine Learning and Test-time Adaptation

abstract: The meteoric rise of Artificial Intelligence (AI), with its rapidly expanding market capitalization, presents both transformative opportunities and critical challenges. Chief among these is the urgent need for a new, unified paradigm for trustworthy evaluation, as current benchmarks increasingly reveal critical vulnerabilities. Issues like data contamination and selective reporting by model developers fuel hype, while inadequate data quality control can lead to biased evaluations that, even if unintentionally, may favor specific approaches. As a flood of participants enters the AI space, this "Wild West" of assessment makes distinguishing genuine progress from exaggerated claims exceptionally difficult. Such ambiguity blurs scientific signals and erodes public confidence, much as unchecked claims would destabilize financial markets reliant on credible oversight from agencies like Moody's.In high-stakes human examinations (e.g., SAT, GRE), substantial effort is devoted to ensuring fairness and credibility; why settle for less in evaluating AI, especially given its profound societal impact? This position paper argues that a laissez-faire approach is untenable. For true and sustainable AI advancement, we call for a paradigm shift to a unified, live, and quality-controlled benchmarking framework—robust by construction rather than reliant on courtesy or goodwill. Accordingly, we dissect the systemic flaws undermining today’s evaluation ecosystem and distill the essential requirements for next-generation assessments. To concretize this position, we introduce the idea of PeerBench, a community-governed, proctored evaluation blueprint that seeks to improve security and credibility through sealed execution, item banking with rolling renewal, and delayed transparency. Accordingly, we dissect the systemic flaws undermining today’s evaluation ecosystem and distill the essential requirements for next-generation assessments. To concretize this position, we introduce the idea of PeerBench, a community-governed, proctored evaluation blueprint that seeks to improve security and credibility through sealed execution, item banking with rolling renewal, and delayed transparency. PeerBench is presented as a complementary, certificate-grade layer alongside open benchmarks, not a replacement. We discuss trade-offs and limits and call for further research on mechanism design, governance, and reliability guarantees. paragraphs: This position paper argues that AI evaluation needs stronger shared institutions and procedures. The authors frame trustworthy evaluation as a requirement for scientific clarity and public confidence.

They propose PeerBench as a blueprint for community-governed, proctored assessment. Its elements include sealed execution, a bank of evaluation items that is renewed over time, and delayed transparency. Together, these are intended to improve security and credibility through the design of the evaluation process, rather than depending primarily on participants’ goodwill.

summary.tldr: The paper proposes PeerBench, a community-governed evaluation blueprint intended to strengthen credibility alongside existing open benchmarks.

title: Position: Benchmarking is Broken - Don't Let AI be Its Own Judge

abstract: Audio captioning systems face a fundamental challenge: teacher-forcing training creates exposure bias that leads to caption degeneration during inference. While contrastive methods have been proposed as solutions, they typically fail to capture the crucial temporal relationships between acoustic and linguistic modalities. We address this limitation by introducing the unbiased sliced Wasserstein RBF (USW-RBF) kernel with rotary positional embedding, specifically designed to preserve temporal information across modalities. Our approach offers a practical advantage: the kernel enables efficient stochastic gradient optimization, making it computationally feasible for real-world applications. Building on this foundation, we develop a complete audio captioning framework that integrates stochastic decoding to further mitigate caption degeneration. Extensive experiments on AudioCaps and Clotho datasets demonstrate that our method significantly improves caption quality, lexical diversity, and text-to-audio retrieval accuracy. Furthermore, we demonstrate the generalizability of our USW-RBF kernel by applying it to audio reasoning tasks, where it enhances the reasoning capabilities of large audio language models on the CompA-R in terms of correctness and quality. Our kernel also improves the reasoning accuracy of the MMAU-test-mini benchmarks by $4\%$. These results establish our approach as a powerful and generalizable solution for cross-modal alignment challenges in audio-language tasks.

title: Unbiased Sliced Wasserstein Kernels for High-Quality Audio Captioning

abstract: Machine learning is now ubiquitous in societal decision-making, for example in evaluating job candidates or loan applications, and it is increasingly important to take into account how classified agents will react to the learning algorithms. The majority of recent literature on strategic classification has focused on reducing and countering deceptive behaviors by the classified agents, but recent work of Attias et al. identifies surprising properties of learnability when the agents genuinely improve in order to attain the desirable classification, such as smaller generalization error than standard PAC-learning. In this paper we characterize so-called learnability with improvements across multiple new axes. We introduce an asymmetric variant of minimally consistent concept classes and use it to provide an exact characterization of proper learning with improvements in the realizable setting. While prior work studies learnability only under general, arbitrary agent improvement regions, we give positive results for more natural Euclidean ball improvement sets. In particular, we characterize improper learning under a generative assumption on the data distribution. We further show how to learn in more challenging settings, achieving lower generalization error under well-studied bounded noise models and obtaining mistake bounds in realizable and agnostic online learning. We resolve open questions posed by Attias et al. for both proper and improper learning.

paragraphs: Strategic classification often assumes people alter their presentation to obtain favorable decisions. This paper studies a different response: agents genuinely improve. It characterizes learning when such improvement possibilities interact with the classifier, extending earlier results that found unexpectedly favorable generalization behavior.

summary.tldr: Learning theory changes when classified people genuinely improve rather than merely manipulate their features.

title: Conservative classifiers do consistently well with improving agents: characterizing statistical and online learning

abstract: Diffusion models have recently emerged as a powerful approach for trajectory planning. However, their inherently non-sequential nature limits their effectiveness in long-horizon reasoning tasks at test time. The recently proposed Monte Carlo Tree Diffusion (MCTD) offers a promising solution by combining diffusion with tree-based search, achieving state-of-the-art performance on complex planning problems. Despite its strengths, our analysis shows that MCTD incurs substantial computational overhead due to the sequential nature of tree search and the cost of iterative denoising. To address this, we propose Fast-MCTD, a more efficient variant that preserves the strengths of MCTD while significantly improving its speed and scalability. Fast-MCTD integrates two techniques: Parallel MCTD, which enables parallel rollouts via delayed tree updates and redundancy-aware selection; and Sparse MCTD, which reduces rollout length through trajectory coarsening. Experiments show that Fast-MCTD achieves up to 100× speedup over standard MCTD while maintaining or improving planning performance. Remarkably, it even outperforms Diffuser in inference speed on some tasks, despite Diffuser requiring no search and yielding weaker solutions. These results position Fast-MCTD as a practical and scalable solution for diffusion-based inference-time reasoning.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate trajectories for planning, but their non-sequential structure makes long-horizon reasoning at inference time difficult. Monte Carlo Tree Diffusion addresses this by combining trajectory diffusion with tree search. This paper identifies two major computational costs in that combination: sequential search operations and repeated denoising during simulated continuations, or rollouts.

Fast-MCTD tackles both costs. Its parallel component delays tree updates so multiple rollouts can proceed together, while redundancy-aware selection helps manage overlapping search work. Its sparse component coarsens trajectories to shorten rollouts. Together, these changes reduce the overhead of searching and generating candidate plans while retaining the underlying combination of diffusion and tree-based reasoning.

Experiments report speedups of up to 100 times over standard MCTD, with planning performance maintained or improved. On some tasks, Fast-MCTD even runs faster at inference than Diffuser, a method without search that produces weaker solutions in those comparisons. The results show that restructuring search and trajectory resolution can make this form of inference-time planning substantially more practical.
summary.tldr: Fast-MCTD combines parallel search and coarser trajectories for up to 100× faster planning while maintaining or improving reported performance.

title: Fast Monte Carlo Tree Diffusion: 100× Speedup via Parallel and Sparse Planning

abstract: In this paper, we focus on Novel Class Discovery for Point Cloud Segmentation (3D-NCD), aiming to learn a model that can segment unlabeled (novel) 3D classes using only the supervision from labeled (base) 3D classes. The key to this task is to setup the exact correlations between the point representations and their base class labels, as well as the representation correlations between the points from base and novel classes. A coarse or statistical correlation learning may lead to the confusion in novel class inference. lf we impose a causal relationship as a strong correlated constraint upon the learning process, the essential point cloud representations that accurately correspond to the classes should be uncovered. To this end, we introduce a structural causal model (SCM) to re-formalize the 3D-NCD problem and propose a new method, i.e., Joint Learning of Causal Representation and Reasoning. Specifically, we first analyze hidden confounders in the base class representations and the causal relationships between the base and novel classes through SCM. We devise a causal representation prototype that eliminates confounders to capture the causal representations of base classes. A graph structure is then used to model the causal relationships between the base classes' causal representation prototypes and the novel class prototypes, enabling causal reasoning from base to novel classes. Extensive experiments and visualization results on 3D and 2D NCD semantic segmentation demonstrate the superiorities of our method.

paragraphs: Novel class discovery for point-cloud segmentation asks a model to identify unlabeled 3D categories using supervision from labeled base categories. The challenge is to learn representations that connect points to known classes and support inference about unfamiliar ones. The authors argue that coarse statistical associations can create confusion when transferring between these groups.

Their method reformulates the task using a structural causal model. It analyzes hidden confounders in representations of base classes and relationships between base and novel classes. A causal representation prototype is designed to remove confounding influences and capture class-relevant representations. A graph then connects these base-class prototypes with novel-class prototypes, providing the structure for reasoning from known categories to new ones.

Experiments and visualizations on both 3D and 2D novel-class semantic segmentation show advantages for the proposed method. The results support the usefulness of combining representation learning with structured reasoning in these evaluations. The causal formulation supplies the method’s organizing constraints, directing learning toward class-related information and the relationships used to infer unlabeled categories.
summary.tldr: The method combines causal class prototypes with graph-based reasoning to discover unlabeled segmentation categories from labeled base classes.

title: Novel Class Discovery for Point Cloud Segmentation via Joint Learning of Causal Representation and Reasoning

abstract: Virtual screening (VS) is a critical component of modern drug discovery, yet most existing methods—whether physics-based or deep learning-based—are developed around *holo* protein structures with known ligand-bound pockets. Consequently, their performance degrades significantly on *apo* or predicted structures such as those from AlphaFold2, which are more representative of real-world early-stage drug discovery, where pocket information is often missing. In this paper, we introduce an alignment-and-aggregation framework to enable accurate virtual screening under structural uncertainty. Our method comprises two core components: (1) a tri-modal contrastive learning module that aligns representations of the ligand, the *holo* pocket, and cavities detected from structures, thereby enhancing robustness to pocket localization error; and (2) a cross-attention based adapter for dynamically aggregating candidate binding sites, enabling the model to learn from activity data even without precise pocket annotations. We evaluated our method on a newly curated benchmark of *apo* structures, where it significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in blind apo setting, improving the early enrichment factor (EF1\%) from 11.75 to 37.19. Notably, it also maintains strong performance on *holo* structures. These results demonstrate the promise of our approach in advancing first-in-class drug discovery, particularly in scenarios lacking experimentally resolved protein-ligand complexes. Our implementation is publicly available at [https://github.com/Wiley-Z/AANet](https://github.com/Wiley-Z/AANet).

paragraphs: Virtual screening seeks promising drug candidates using protein structures, but many methods assume that the binding pocket is already known from a protein bound to a ligand. Early discovery often has only unbound or predicted structures. AANet addresses this mismatch by learning to screen candidates when the location and structure of the binding site are uncertain.

The framework combines alignment with aggregation. A contrastive learning component brings together representations of ligands, known bound pockets, and cavities detected in protein structures. This aims to make predictions less sensitive to pocket localization errors. A cross-attention adapter then combines information from candidate binding sites, allowing learning from activity measurements without precise pocket annotations.

On a newly assembled benchmark of unbound structures, AANet improves the reported early enrichment factor at 1% from 11.75 to 37.19 in the blind screening setting. It also retains strong performance on bound structures. These findings support the approach’s promise for discovery settings without experimentally resolved protein-ligand complexes, where uncertainty about the pocket is part of the screening problem.
summary.tldr: AANet aligns molecular and pocket representations and combines candidate binding sites to improve virtual screening under structural uncertainty.

title: AANet: Virtual Screening under Structural Uncertainty via Alignment and Aggregation

abstract: In practice, many models from a function class can fit a dataset almost equally well. This collection of near-optimal models is known as the Rashomon set. Prior work has shown that the Rashomon set offers flexibility in choosing models aligned with secondary objectives like interpretability or fairness. However, it is unclear how far this flexibility extends to different trustworthy criteria, especially given that most trustworthy machine learning systems today still rely on complex specialized optimization procedures. *Is the Rashomon set all you need for trustworthy model selection? Can simply searching the Rashomon set suffice to find models that are not only accurate but also fair, stable, robust, or private, without explicitly optimizing for these criteria?*In this paper, we introduce a framework for systematically analyzing trustworthiness within Rashomon sets and conduct extensive experiments on high-stakes tabular datasets. We focus on sparse decision trees, where the Rashomon set can be fully enumerated. Across seven distinct metrics, we find that the Rashomon set almost always contains models that match or exceed the performance of state-of-the-art methods specifically designed to optimize individual trustworthiness criteria. These results suggest that for many practical applications, computing the Rashomon set once can serve as an efficient and effective method for identifying highly accurate and trustworthy models. Our framework can be a valuable tool for both benchmarking Rashomon sets of decision trees and studying the trustworthiness properties of interpretable models.

title: The Rashomon Set Has It All: Analyzing Trustworthiness of Trees under Multiplicity

abstract: The generalization capabilities of vision-language-action (VLA) models to unseen tasks are crucial to achieving general-purpose robotic manipulation in open-world settings. However, the cross-task generalization capabilities of existing VLA models remain significantly underexplored. To address this gap, we introduce **AGNOSTOS**, a novel simulation benchmark designed to rigorously evaluate cross-task zero-shot generalization in manipulation. AGNOSTOS comprises 23 unseen manipulation tasks for test—distinct from common training task distributions—and incorporates two levels of generalization difficulty to assess robustness. Our systematic evaluation reveals that current VLA models, despite being trained on diverse datasets, struggle to generalize effectively to these unseen tasks. To overcome this limitation, we propose **Cross-Task In-Context Manipulation (X-ICM)**, a method that conditions large language models (LLMs) on in-context demonstrations from seen tasks to predict action sequences for unseen tasks. Additionally, we introduce a **dynamics-guided sample selection** strategy that identifies relevant demonstrations by capturing cross-task dynamics. On AGNOSTOS, X-ICM significantly improves cross-task zero-shot generalization performance over leading VLAs, achieving improvements of 6.0\% over $\pi_0$ and 7.9\% over VoxPoser. We believe AGNOSTOS and X-ICM will serve as valuable tools for advancing general-purpose robotic manipulation.

On AGNOSTOS, the proposed method improves cross-task zero-shot generalization, with reported gains of 6.0% over π₀ and 7.9% over VoxPoser. Here, unseen-task prediction still uses demonstrations from seen tasks as context. The results suggest that selecting and reusing relevant experience can help with the transfer difficulties exposed by this simulation benchmark.
summary.tldr: AGNOSTOS exposes unseen-task weaknesses in robot models, while dynamics-guided demonstrations improve cross-task action prediction.

title: Exploring the Limits of Vision-Language-Action Manipulation in Cross-task Generalization

abstract: Table Question Answering (TableQA) combines natural language understanding and structured data reasoning, posing challenges in semantic interpretation and logical inference. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have improved TableQA performance through Direct Prompting and Agent paradigms. However, these models often rely on spurious correlations, as they tend to overfit to token co-occurrence patterns in pretraining corpora, rather than perform genuine reasoning. To address this issue, we propose Causal Intervention TableQA (CIT), which is based on a structural causal graph and applies front-door adjustment to eliminate bias caused by token co-occurrence. CIT formalizes TableQA as a causal graph and identifies token co-occurrence patterns as confounders. By applying front-door adjustment, CIT guides question variant generation and reasoning to reduce confounding effects. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that CIT achieves state-of-the-art performance, demonstrating its effectiveness in mitigating bias. Consistent gains across various LLMs further confirm its generalizability.

paragraphs: Answering questions about tables requires a model to connect language with structured data and logical operations. The paper identifies a source of unreliable answers: language models can lean on word combinations learned during pretraining instead of reasoning from the table. Strong overall language capabilities therefore do not by themselves resolve this source of bias.

Causal Intervention TableQA, or CIT, represents the task using a structural causal graph. Within that formulation, token co-occurrence patterns act as confounders that can distort the relationship between the question and the answer. CIT applies front-door adjustment to guide the generation of question variants and the subsequent reasoning process, aiming to reduce the influence of those misleading patterns.

Experiments across multiple benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance, with consistent gains across different language models. These results support the usefulness of the causal formulation for mitigating bias in TableQA. The contribution is a way to organize question variation and reasoning around an explicit account of why familiar language patterns can interfere with faithful table use.
summary.tldr: CIT uses a causal formulation and front-door adjustment to reduce token co-occurrence bias in language-model table reasoning.

title: Causality Meets the Table: Debiasing LLMs for Faithful TableQA via Front-Door Intervention

abstract: Transformer models have driven breakthroughs across various language tasks by their strong capability to learn rich contextual representations. Scaling them to improve representation, however, often demands substantial memory and compute costs, such as the Key-Value (KV) cache used during auto-regressive decoding. Skip connections offer a promising way to improve representation without bloating resource usage, yet most prior works either improve expressivity while leaving KV costs unchanged, or reduce memory at the cost of weaker representation. In this work, we propose SkipV1Former, a Transformer variant that uses skip connections from the first layer's Value heads to strengthen model representation and reduce KV cache. Specifically, from the second block onward, each layer reuses half of its Value heads from the very first layer, while computing the other half as usual-cutting Value projections and V cache by nearly 50 \%. Theoretically, we show that routing uncompressed first-layer Values into deeper layers restores information lost to compression and accelerates the model’s implicit mesa-optimization-a key pattern of Transformer in auto-regressive tasks. Empirically, across different model scales, SkipV1Former delivers consistent reductions of approximately 25 \% in KV cache while improving perplexity relative to standard Multi-Head Attention (MHA) Transformers and some advanced variants. Moreover, we propose a recipe for uptraining existing MHA Transformer checkpoints to SkipV1Former with only 10-15\% additional compute. Finally, SkipV1Former can seamlessly combine advanced methods like Group-Query Attention and Multi-Latent Attention to achieve further KV cache savings and performance improvement. When combined with YOCO, it cuts KV cache size by nearly 50 \% while still improving performance. The code is available at: https://github.com/Zhoutong-Wu/SkipV1Former.
originalAbstract: Transformer models have driven breakthroughs across various language tasks by their strong capability to learn rich contextual representations. Scaling them to improve representation, however, often demands substantial memory and compute costs, such as the Key-Value (KV) cache used during auto-regressive decoding. Skip connections offer a promising way to improve representation without bloating resource usage, yet most prior works either improve expressivity while leaving KV costs unchanged, or reduce memory at the cost of weaker representation. In this work, we propose SkipV1Former, a Transformer variant that uses skip connections from the first layer's Value heads to strengthen model representation and reduce KV cache. Specifically, from the second block onward, each layer reuses half of its Value heads from the very first layer, while computing the other half as usual-cutting Value projections and V cache by nearly 50 \%. Theoretically, we show that routing uncompressed first-layer Values into deeper layers restores information lost to compression and accelerates the model’s implicit mesa-optimization-a key pattern of Transformer in auto-regressive tasks. Empirically, across different model scales, SkipV1Former delivers consistent reductions of approximately 25 \% in KV cache while improving perplexity relative to standard Multi-Head Attention (MHA) Transformers and some advanced variants. Moreover, we propose a recipe for uptraining existing MHA Transformer checkpoints to SkipV1Former with only 10-15\% additional compute. Finally, SkipV1Former can seamlessly combine advanced methods like Group-Query Attention and Multi-Latent Attention to achieve further KV cache savings and performance improvement. When combined with YOCO, it cuts KV cache size by nearly 50 \% while still improving performance. The code is available at: https://github.com/Zhoutong-Wu/SkipV1Former.

paragraphs: SkipV1Former addresses the memory cost of Transformer generation while aiming to improve representations. Starting with the second block, each layer reuses half of its Value heads from the first layer and computes the remaining half normally. This nearly halves Value projections and the Value cache; the reported reduction in the combined Key-Value cache is approximately 25%.

The theoretical argument is that directly supplying uncompressed first-layer Values to deeper layers restores information lost through compression. The authors also show that this routing accelerates the model’s implicit mesa-optimization, an internal optimization pattern associated with autoregressive tasks. Across model scales, experiments find improved perplexity alongside cache savings compared with standard multi-head attention Transformers and some advanced variants.

Existing multi-head attention checkpoints can be adapted through a proposed uptraining recipe requiring 10–15% additional compute. The architecture also combines with Group-Query Attention and Multi-Latent Attention for further benefits. In combination with YOCO, it nearly halves the KV cache while improving performance. The findings position early-layer Value reuse as a representation change that can also complement other memory-saving techniques.
summary.tldr: SkipV1Former reuses first-layer Value heads to improve perplexity while reducing the combined KV cache by approximately 25%.

title: Improving Model Representation and Reducing KV Cache via Skip Connections with First Value Heads

abstract: This paper addresses the covariate shift problem in the context of nonparametric regression within reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHSs). Covariate shift arises in supervised learning when the input distributions of the training and test data differ, presenting additional challenges for learning. Although kernel methods have optimal statistical properties, their high computational demands in terms of time and, particularly, memory, limit their scalability to large datasets. To address this limitation, the main focus of this paper is to explore the trade-off between computational efficiency and statistical accuracy under covariate shift. We investigate the use of random projections where the hypothesis space consists of a random subspace within a given RKHS. Our results show that, even in the presence of covariate shift, significant computational savings can be achieved without compromising learning performance.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to make kernel regression computationally cheaper when training and test inputs follow different distributions. That mismatch, called covariate shift, complicates learning because the inputs encountered during evaluation need not resemble the training inputs in their frequency or coverage. The central question is whether computational shortcuts can preserve statistical accuracy in this setting.

The authors work with nonparametric regression in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, the function space underlying their kernel method. They investigate random projections that restrict the model’s candidate functions to a randomly chosen subspace. This changes the size of the learning problem while retaining a connection to the original function space.

Their results show that substantial computational savings can be achieved without sacrificing learning performance even under covariate shift. This matters because kernel methods’ statistical advantages can come with substantial time and especially memory requirements. The contribution establishes that distribution mismatch and computational approximation can be addressed together, supporting more scalable use of kernel regression.
summary.tldr: Random subspaces can reduce kernel regression’s computational burden while preserving learning performance under covariate shift.

title: Computational Efficiency under Covariate Shift in Kernel Ridge Regression

abstract: Prohibited item detection based on X-ray images is one of the most effective security inspection methods. However, the foreground-background feature coupling caused by the overlapping phenomenon specific to X-ray images makes general detectors designed for natural images perform poorly. To address this issue, we propose a Category Semantic Prior Contrastive Learning (CSPCL) mechanism, which aligns the class prototypes perceived by the classifier with the content queries to correct and supplement the missing semantic information responsible for classification, thereby enhancing the model sensitivity to foreground features. To achieve this alignment, we design a specific contrastive loss, CSP loss, which comprises the Intra-Class Truncated Attraction (ITA) loss and the Inter-Class Adaptive Repulsion (IAR) loss, and outperforms classic contrastive losses. Specifically, the ITA loss leverages class prototypes to attract intra-class content queries and preserves essential intra-class diversity via a gradient truncation function. The IAR loss employs class prototypes to adaptively repel inter-class content queries, with the repulsion strength scaled by prototype-prototype similarity, thereby improving inter-class discriminability, especially among similar categories. CSPCL is general and can be easily integrated into Deformable DETR-based models. Extensive experiments on the PIXray, OPIXray, PIDray, and CLCXray datasets demonstrate that CSPCL significantly enhances the performance of various state-of-the-art models without increasing inference complexity. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Limingyuan001/CSPCL.

paragraphs: Overlapping objects in X-ray images can entangle foreground and background features, making prohibited items difficult for general image detectors to recognize. CSPCL addresses this by aligning a detector’s content queries with the class prototypes represented by its classifier. The goal is to restore or supplement category information and make the detector more sensitive to foreground objects.

The training objective combines two complementary forces. Intra-Class Truncated Attraction pulls queries toward their own class prototypes while truncating gradients to preserve useful variation within a class. Inter-Class Adaptive Repulsion pushes queries away from other categories. Its strength depends on similarity between class prototypes, helping separate categories that are especially easy to confuse.

The mechanism integrates into models based on Deformable DETR without increasing inference complexity. Experiments on PIXray, OPIXray, PIDray, and CLCXray report significant improvements across several leading detectors, and the proposed loss outperforms classic contrastive losses. The results suggest that improving category structure during training can strengthen X-ray detection without making the deployed detector more computationally complex.
summary.tldr: CSPCL improves X-ray prohibited-item detection by aligning detector queries with class prototypes without adding inference complexity.

title: CSPCL: Category Semantic Prior Contrastive Learning for Deformable DETR-Based Prohibited Item Detectors

abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown impressive video content understanding capabilities but struggle with fine-grained motion comprehension. To comprehensively assess the motion understanding ability of existing MLLMs, we introduce FAVOR-Bench, which comprises 1,776 videos from both ego-centric and third-person perspectives and enables assessment through both close-ended and open-ended tasks. For close-ended evaluation, we carefully design 8,184 multiple-choice question-answer pairs spanning six distinct sub-tasks. For open-ended evaluation, we employ the GPT-assisted evaluation and develop a novel cost-efficient LLM-free assessment method, where the latter can enhance benchmarking interpretability and accessibility. Comprehensive experiments with21 state-of-the-art MLLMs reveal significant limitations in their ability to comprehend and describe detailed temporal dynamics in video motions. To alleviate this limitation, we further build FAVOR-Train, a dataset of 17,152 videos with fine-grained motion annotations. Finetuning Qwen2.5-VL on FAVOR-Train yields consistent improvements on motion-related tasks across TVBench, MotionBenchand our FAVOR-Bench. Our assessment results demonstrate that the proposed FAVOR-Bench and FAVOR-Train provide valuable tools for the community to develop more powerful video understanding models.

paragraphs: Understanding a video's general content does not necessarily mean understanding the details of its motion. FAVOR-Bench evaluates how well multimodal language models comprehend and describe those temporal details. It contains 1,776 videos from first-person and third-person viewpoints, with both multiple-choice questions and tasks that require freely generated answers.

The closed-ended portion includes 8,184 question-answer pairs across six subtasks. For open-ended answers, the authors use GPT-assisted evaluation and introduce a less costly assessment method that does not require a language model. The latter is intended to make evaluation more interpretable and accessible. Testing 21 leading models reveals substantial weaknesses in detailed motion comprehension and description.

The paper also supplies FAVOR-Train, containing 17,152 videos annotated for fine-grained motion. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-VL on this dataset produces consistent gains on motion-related tasks in TVBench, MotionBench, and FAVOR-Bench. Together, the evaluation and training datasets provide a way to identify specific motion-understanding gaps and evidence that targeted training can improve the tested model's performance beyond the new benchmark itself.
summary.tldr: FAVOR-Bench exposes weaknesses in detailed video-motion understanding, while FAVOR-Train improves a tested model across three motion-related benchmarks.

title: FAVOR-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Fine-Grained Video Motion Understanding

abstract: Randomized experiments are the preferred approach for evaluating the effects of interventions, but they are costly and often yield estimates with substantial uncertainty. On the other hand, in silico experiments leveraging foundation models offer a cost-effective alternative that can potentially attain higher statistical precision. However, the benefits of in silico experiments come with a significant risk: statistical inferences are not valid if the models fail to accurately predict experimental responses to interventions. In this paper, we propose a novel approach that integrates the predictions from multiple foundation models with experimental data while preserving valid statistical inference. Our estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal, with asymptotic variance no larger than the standard estimator based on experimental data alone. Importantly, these statistical properties hold even when model predictions are arbitrarily biased. Empirical results across several randomized experiments show that our estimator offers substantial precision gains, equivalent to a reduction of up to 20\% in the sample size needed to match the same precision as the standard estimator based on experimental data alone.

paragraphs: Randomized experiments provide evidence about intervention effects, but collecting enough observations for precise estimates can be expensive. Foundation models can predict experimental responses cheaply, yet inaccurate predictions can undermine statistical conclusions. This paper develops an estimator that combines predictions from multiple foundation models with actual experimental observations while retaining valid inference.

The theoretical contribution is that the estimator remains consistent and asymptotically normal even when model predictions are arbitrarily biased. Its asymptotic variance is no greater than that of the standard estimator using experimental data alone. These are large-sample guarantees: they establish that integrating predictions need not sacrifice the estimator’s limiting statistical properties, even when the predictive models are systematically wrong.

Across several randomized experiments, the combined estimator achieves substantial precision improvements. The largest reported gain corresponds to needing up to 20% fewer observations to match the standard estimator’s precision. The approach therefore uses foundation models to make experimental evidence more informative while keeping real randomized data central to the validity of the conclusions.
summary.tldr: Combining foundation-model predictions with randomized data improves precision while preserving asymptotic validity even with arbitrarily biased predictions.

title: Efficient Randomized Experiments Using Foundation Models

abstract: There is growing interest in leveraging mechanistic interpretability and controllability to better understand and influence the internal dynamics of large language models (LLMs). However, current methods face fundamental challenges in reliably localizing and manipulating feature representations. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as a promising direction for feature extraction at scale, yet they, too, are limited by incomplete feature isolation and unreliable monosemanticity. To systematically quantify these limitations, we introduce Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric to quantify feature monosemanticity in latent representation. Building on these insights, we propose Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that conditions latent representations on labeled concepts during training. We demonstrate that reliable localization and disentanglement of target concepts within the latent space improve interpretability, detection of behavior, and control. Specifically, our evaluations on toxicity detection, writing style identification, and privacy attribute recognition show that G-SAE not only enhances monosemanticity but also enables more effective and fine-grained steering with less quality degradation. Our findings provide actionable guidelines for measuring and advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs.

paragraphs: Understanding and controlling a language model depends partly on locating internal representations of particular concepts. Sparse autoencoders can extract features from model activations, but those features do not always isolate concepts reliably. This paper addresses monosemanticity: the extent to which a feature has a clear, specific meaning instead of mixing several meanings together.

The authors introduce Feature Monosemanticity Score to quantify that property in latent representations. They then propose Guided Sparse Autoencoders, which condition representations on labeled concepts during training. The method uses explicit concept information to help locate and separate target representations, connecting measurement of feature clarity with a training procedure intended to improve it.

Evaluations cover toxicity detection, writing-style identification, and privacy-attribute recognition. In these settings, the guided approach improves monosemanticity and supports more effective, finer-grained steering with less degradation in output quality. The results link better concept isolation to practical gains in recognizing and influencing model behavior. The work therefore offers both a measurement tool and a supervised way to make extracted representations more useful for interpretation and control.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces a monosemanticity metric and concept-guided sparse autoencoders that improve feature isolation and fine-grained model steering.

title: Measuring and Guiding Monosemanticity

abstract: Developing effective multimodal fusion approaches has become increasingly essential in many real-world scenarios, such as health care and finance. The key challenge is how to preserve the feature expressiveness in each modality while learning cross-modal interactions. Previous approaches primarily focus on the cross-modal alignment, while over-emphasis on the alignment of marginal distributions of modalities may impose excess regularization and obstruct meaningful representations within each modality. The Dirichlet process (DP) mixture model is a powerful Bayesian non-parametric method that can amplify the most prominent features by its richer-gets-richer property, which allocates increasing weights to them. Inspired by this unique characteristic of DP, we propose a new DP-driven multimodal learning framework that automatically achieves an optimal balance between prominent intra-modal representation learning and cross-modal alignment. Specifically, we assume that each modality follows a mixture of multivariate Gaussian distributions and further adopt DP to calculate the mixture weights for all the components. This paradigm allows DP to dynamically allocate the contributions of features and select the most prominent ones, leveraging its richer-gets-richer property, thus facilitating multimodal feature fusion. Extensive experiments on several multimodal datasets demonstrate the superior performance of our model over other competitors. Ablation analysis further validates the effectiveness of DP in aligning modality distributions and its robustness to changes in key hyperparameters. Code is anonymously available at https://github.com/HKU-MedAI/DPMM.git

paragraphs: Combining multiple modalities requires preserving useful information within each source while learning relationships between sources. This paper argues that emphasizing distribution alignment too strongly can interfere with that balance. Making modalities look similar can impose excessive regularization, weakening distinctive representations that would otherwise help the combined model.

The proposed framework uses a Dirichlet process mixture to assign contributions to different feature components. It assumes each modality can be represented by a mixture of multivariate Gaussian distributions. The Dirichlet process determines component weights through its richer-gets-richer behavior, giving greater emphasis to prominent components. This provides an adaptive mechanism for balancing strong representations within a modality with alignment across modalities.

Experiments across several multimodal datasets report better performance than the compared methods. Ablation studies also support the Dirichlet process component's role in distribution alignment and show robustness to changes in key hyperparameters. The findings suggest that fusion benefits from selectively strengthening useful modality-specific structure, alongside learning shared relationships, within the proposed mixture-based modeling approach.
summary.tldr: A Dirichlet process mixture strengthens prominent features while balancing modality-specific representations with cross-modal alignment.

title: Amplifying Prominent Representations in Multimodal Learning via Variational Dirichlet Process

abstract: We develop a generic approach to form smooth versions of basic mathematical operations like multiplication, composition, change of measure, and conditional expectation, among others. Operations which result in functions outside the reproducing kernel Hilbert space (such as the product of two RKHS functions) are approximated via a natural cost function, such that the solution is guaranteed to be in the targeted RKHS. This approximation problem is reduced to a regression problem using an adjoint trick, and solved in a vector-valued RKHS, consisting of continuous, linear, smooth operators which map from an input, real-valued RKHS to the desired target RKHS. Important constraints, such as an almost everywhere positive density, can be enforced or approximated naturally in this framework, using convex constraints on the operators. Finally, smooth operators can be composed to accomplish more complex machine learning tasks, such as the sum rule and kernelized approximate Bayesian inference, where state-of-the-art convergence rates are obtained.

paragraphs: Kernel methods work with functions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, or RKHS. Basic operations can produce a function outside the desired space; multiplying two RKHS functions is one example. This paper develops a general framework for approximating such operations while guaranteeing that the resulting function belongs to a chosen target RKHS.

The framework covers operations including multiplication, composition, changes of measure, and conditional expectation. An adjoint-based transformation turns the approximation task into regression. The regression takes place in a vector-valued RKHS whose elements are continuous linear operators mapping functions from the input space to the target space.

Convex constraints on these operators allow important requirements, such as a density being positive almost everywhere, to be enforced or approximated. Operators can also be composed to perform more complex tasks, including the sum rule and kernelized approximate Bayesian inference. The paper reports state-of-the-art convergence rates for these applications, showing how a common mathematical construction can support both basic operations and larger inference procedures.
summary.tldr: Smooth operators approximate mathematical operations within a target RKHS and compose into kernel-based inference procedures.

title: Smooth Operators

abstract: We developed a flexible framework for modeling the annotation and judgment processes of humans, which we called “normalized gamma construction of a confusion matrix.” This framework enabled us to model three properties: (1) the abilities of humans, (2) a confusion matrix with labeling, and (3) the difficulty with which items are correctly annotated. We also provided the concept of “latent confusion analysis (LCA),” whose main purpose was to analyze the principal confusions behind human annotations and judgments. It is assumed in LCA that confusion matrices are shared between persons, which we called “latent confusions”, in tribute to the “latent topics” of topic modeling. We aim at summarizing the workers’ confusion matrices with the small number of latent principal confusion matrices because many personal confusion matrices is difficult to analyze. We used LCA to analyze latent confusions regarding the effects of radioactivity on fish and shellfish following the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster in 2011.

paragraphs: Human annotations can reflect differences in ability, differences in item difficulty, and recurring patterns of confusion among labels. The paper introduces a normalized gamma construction for confusion matrices that can represent all three. A confusion matrix describes which labels or judgments tend to be mistaken for others.

The authors then develop latent confusion analysis to summarize the main patterns behind many individual annotators’ judgments. Its stated assumption is that confusion matrices are shared across people. These shared patterns, called latent confusions, play a summarizing role analogous to latent topics in topic modeling.

The motivation is interpretability: inspecting a separate confusion matrix for every worker can become difficult, while a small collection of principal confusion matrices offers a more compact account. The authors apply the approach to judgments about radioactivity’s effects on fish and shellfish following the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster. The application illustrates the intended use of the framework: analyzing the structure of human confusion through shared patterns while accounting for ability and item difficulty.
summary.tldr: Latent confusion analysis summarizes human judgment patterns through shared confusion matrices while modeling annotator ability and item difficulty.

title: Latent Confusion Analysis by Normalized Gamma Construction

abstract: A popular machine learning strategy is the transfer of a representation (i.e. a feature extraction function) learned on a source task to a target task. Examples include the re-use of neural network weights or word embeddings. We develop sufficient conditions for the success of this approach. If the representation learned from the source task is fixed, we identify conditions on how the tasks relate to obtain an upper bound on target task risk via a VC dimension-based argument. We then consider using the representation from the source task to construct a prior, which is fine-tuned using target task data. We give a PAC-Bayes target task risk bound in this setting under suitable conditions. We show examples of our bounds using feedforward neural networks. Our results motivate a practical approach to weight transfer, which we validate with experiments.

paragraphs: Reusing a feature representation learned on one task is a common way to approach another task. Neural-network weights and word embeddings are examples. This paper asks when such transfer can be justified theoretically, developing sufficient conditions that connect a source representation to bounds on prediction risk for the target task.

The first setting keeps the transferred representation fixed. Here, the authors identify conditions on the relationship between tasks and use a VC-dimension argument to bound target risk. The second setting uses the source representation to construct a prior that is then fine-tuned with target data. Under suitable conditions, a PAC-Bayes analysis bounds risk in this setting.

The paper illustrates its bounds using feedforward neural networks and derives a practical weight-transfer approach that it validates experimentally. The two analyses distinguish retaining source features from adapting them using new evidence. Their conditions are sufficient for the stated guarantees, providing theoretical support for transfer in those circumstances without claiming that transfer succeeds only when those conditions hold.
summary.tldr: The paper gives sufficient conditions and target-risk bounds for transferring representations, both fixed and fine-tuned.

title: Risk Bounds for Transferring Representations With and Without Fine-Tuning

abstract: Bayesian optimization is an efficient way to optimize expensive black-box functions such as designing a new product with highest quality or hyperparameter tuning of a machine learning algorithm. However, it has a serious limitation when the parameter space is high-dimensional as Bayesian optimization crucially depends on solving a global optimization of a surrogate utility function in the same sized dimensions. The surrogate utility function, known commonly as acquisition function is a continuous function but can be extremely sharp at high dimension - having only a few peaks marooned in a large terrain of almost flat surface. Global optimization algorithms such as DIRECT are infeasible at higher dimensions and gradient-dependent methods cannot move if initialized in the flat terrain. We propose an algorithm that enables local gradient-dependent algorithms to move through the flat terrain by using a sequence of gross-to-finer Gaussian process priors on the objective function as we leverage two underlying facts - a) there exists a large enough length-scales for which the acquisition function can be made to have a significant gradient at any location in the parameter space, and b) the extrema of the consecutive acquisition functions are close although they are different only due to a small difference in the length-scales. Theoretical guarantees are provided and experiments clearly demonstrate the utility of the proposed method at high dimension using both benchmark test functions and real-world case studies.

Theoretical guarantees are provided and experiments clearly demonstrate the utility of the proposed method at high dimension using both benchmark test functions and real-world case studies.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization chooses evaluations of an expensive function by optimizing a cheaper acquisition function. In high dimensions, that second optimization can become difficult: the acquisition surface may contain a few narrow peaks separated by broad, nearly flat regions. Gradient-based methods can struggle to move when initialized in those flat areas.

The proposed method works through a sequence of Gaussian process priors, progressing from coarse to finer descriptions by changing length scales. It uses the fact that sufficiently large length scales can provide a significant acquisition gradient at any location. It also relies on nearby length-scale settings producing acquisition functions whose extrema remain close.

These properties let local gradient-based optimization move through initially uninformative regions and then follow a progressively refined acquisition surface. The authors provide theoretical guarantees and evaluate the approach using benchmark functions and real-world case studies. The experiments demonstrate its usefulness in high dimensions, addressing the acquisition-optimization bottleneck within Bayesian optimization rather than only the cost of evaluating the original function.
summary.tldr: A coarse-to-fine sequence of Gaussian process priors helps gradient-based acquisition optimization navigate flat regions in high-dimensional Bayesian optimization.

title: High Dimensional Bayesian Optimization with Elastic Gaussian Process

abstract: Stein variational gradient decent (SVGD) has been shown to be a powerful approximate inference algorithm for complex distributions. However, the standard SVGD requires calculating the gradient of the target density and cannot be applied when the gradient is unavailable. In this work, we develop a gradient-free variant of SVGD (GF-SVGD), which replaces the true gradient with a surrogate gradient, and corrects the introduced bias by re-weighting the gradients in a proper form. We show that our GF-SVGD can be viewed as the standard SVGD with a special choice of kernel, and hence directly inherits all the theoretical properties of SVGD. We shed insights on the empirical choice of the surrogate gradient and further, propose an annealed GF-SVGD that consistently outperforms a number of recent advanced gradient-free MCMC methods in our empirical studies.

That requirement prevents its direct use when those gradients are unavailable. This paper introduces GF-SVGD, a variant that replaces the unavailable target gradient with a surrogate.

Using a surrogate can introduce bias, so the method reweights the gradients in a form designed to correct it. The authors show that the resulting algorithm can be interpreted as ordinary SVGD with a particular kernel choice. This relationship is central to their analysis: GF-SVGD directly inherits SVGD's theoretical properties through that interpretation.

The paper also discusses empirical choices of surrogate gradient and proposes an annealed version of GF-SVGD. In the reported empirical studies, the annealed method consistently outperforms several recent gradient-free MCMC methods. The contribution therefore includes both a principled way to replace target gradients and an experimentally successful inference variant, with the comparative performance claim grounded in the studies conducted.
summary.tldr: GF-SVGD substitutes reweighted surrogate gradients for unavailable target gradients while retaining a theoretical connection to standard SVGD.

title: Stein Variational Gradient Descent Without Gradient

abstract: We provide theoretical and empirical evidence that using tighter evidence lower bounds (ELBOs) can be detrimental to the process of learning an inference network by reducing the signal-to-noise ratio of the gradient estimator. Our results call into question common implicit assumptions that tighter ELBOs are better variational objectives for simultaneous model learning and inference amortization schemes. Based on our insights, we introduce three new algorithms: the partially importance weighted auto-encoder (PIWAE), the multiply importance weighted auto-encoder (MIWAE), and the combination importance weighted autoencoder (CIWAE), each of which includes the standard importance weighted auto-encoder (IWAE) as a special case. We show that each can deliver improvements over IWAE, even when performance is measured by the IWAE target itself. Furthermore, our results suggest that PIWAE may be able to deliver simultaneous improvements in the training of both the inference and generative networks.

This paper challenges that assumption when training a generative model and an inference network together. It shows theoretically and empirically that tightening the bound can weaken the inference network's learning signal.

The mechanism is a reduction in the signal-to-noise ratio of the gradient estimator. A bound can more closely approximate its target while providing less useful gradients for learning the inference network. This separates the quality of an objective as an approximation from its effectiveness as a tool for training both networks.

The authors introduce PIWAE, MIWAE, and CIWAE, each containing standard IWAE as a special case. All three can improve over IWAE, including when assessed using IWAE's own target. The results further suggest that PIWAE may improve training of both the inference and generative networks simultaneously. That simultaneous benefit remains a suggested possibility in the stated findings.
summary.tldr: Tighter variational bounds can weaken inference-network gradients, motivating three alternatives that can outperform IWAE.

title: Tighter Variational Bounds are Not Necessarily Better

abstract: Integrating logical reasoning within deep learning architectures has been a major goal of modern AI systems. In this paper, we propose a new direction toward this goal by introducing a differentiable (smoothed) maximum satisfiability (MAXSAT) solver that can be integrated into the loop of larger deep learning systems. Our (approximate) solver is based upon a fast coordinate descent approach to solving the semidefinite program (SDP) associated with the MAXSAT problem. We show how to analytically differentiate through the solution to this SDP and efficiently solve the associated backward pass. We demonstrate that by integrating this solver into end-to-end learning systems, we can learn the logical structure of challenging problems in a minimally supervised fashion. In particular, we show that we can learn the parity function using single-bit supervision (a traditionally hard task for deep networks) and learn how to play 9x9 Sudoku solely from examples. We also solve a “visual Sudoku” problem that maps images of Sudoku puzzles to their associated logical solutions by combining our MAXSAT solver with a traditional convolutional architecture. Our approach thus shows promise in integrating logical structures within deep learning.

Making this component differentiable allows training signals to pass through the reasoning step, so the surrounding system can be learned end to end.

The approximate solver uses fast coordinate descent on a semidefinite program associated with the satisfiability problem. The authors derive how to differentiate through its solution analytically and compute the backward pass efficiently. This provides a concrete mechanism for combining a structured logical computation with neural-network training.

The demonstrations include learning parity with single-bit supervision and learning to solve 9-by-9 Sudoku from examples. A visual Sudoku system combines the solver with a convolutional architecture to map puzzle images to logical solutions. These results show that the integrated approach can learn challenging logical structure with limited forms of supervision. They support the promise of differentiable reasoning components while retaining the paper's characterization of the solver as approximate.
summary.tldr: SATNet makes an approximate satisfiability solver differentiable, enabling end-to-end systems that learn tasks including parity and visual Sudoku.

title: SATNet: Bridging deep learning and logical reasoning using a differentiable satisfiability solver

abstract: In this paper, we propose the Self-Attention Generative Adversarial Network (SAGAN) which allows attention-driven, long-range dependency modeling for image generation tasks. Traditional convolutional GANs generate high-resolution details as a function of only spatially local points in lower-resolution feature maps. In SAGAN, details can be generated using cues from all feature locations. Moreover, the discriminator can check that highly detailed features in distant portions of the image are consistent with each other. Furthermore, recent work has shown that generator conditioning affects GAN performance. Leveraging this insight, we apply spectral normalization to the GAN generator and find that this improves training dynamics. The proposed SAGAN performs better than prior work, boosting the best published Inception score from 36.8 to 52.52 and reducing Fréchet Inception distance from 27.62 to 18.65 on the challenging ImageNet dataset. Visualization of the attention layers shows that the generator leverages neighborhoods that correspond to object shapes rather than local regions of fixed shape.

paragraphs: Self-Attention Generative Adversarial Networks address the difficulty of coordinating distant parts of a generated image. Traditional convolutional GANs generate fine details from spatially local information in lower-resolution features. SAGAN adds self-attention so that a detail can draw on cues from all feature locations, allowing image generation to account more directly for long-range relationships.

The discriminator also benefits from this broader view: it can assess whether detailed features in distant image regions agree with one another. Separately, the authors apply spectral normalization to the generator and find improved training dynamics. The approach therefore addresses both spatial coordination in generated images and the behavior of the adversarial training process.

On ImageNet, the paper reports an Inception score increase from 36.8 to 52.52 and a Fréchet Inception distance decrease from 27.62 to 18.65 relative to the best published results cited. Attention visualizations show neighborhoods corresponding to object shapes, supporting the interpretation that the generator uses image-dependent relationships beyond fixed local regions.
summary.tldr: SAGAN combines long-range self-attention with generator spectral normalization to improve image generation and training dynamics.

title: Self-Attention Generative Adversarial Networks

abstract: Ordered Weighted $L_{1}$ (OWL) regularized regression is a new regression analysis for high-dimensional sparse learning. Proximal gradient methods are used as standard approaches to solve OWL regression. However, it is still a burning issue to solve OWL regression due to considerable computational cost and memory usage when the feature or sample size is large. In this paper, we propose the first safe screening rule for OWL regression by exploring the order of the primal solution with the unknown order structure via an iterative strategy, which overcomes the difficulties of tackling the non-separable regularizer. It effectively avoids the updates of the parameters whose coefficients must be zero during the learning process. More importantly, the proposed screening rule can be easily applied to standard and stochastic proximal gradient methods. Moreover, we prove that the algorithms with our screening rule are guaranteed to have identical results with the original algorithms. Experimental results on a variety of datasets show that our screening rule leads to a significant computational gain without any loss of accuracy, compared to existing competitive algorithms.

paragraphs: Ordered Weighted L1 regression supports sparse learning with many features, but solving it can require substantial computation and memory. Standard proximal gradient methods repeatedly update parameters during optimization. This paper asks which updates can safely be avoided because the corresponding coefficients must be zero, reducing work without changing the result of the original algorithm.

The difficulty is that the regularizer couples coefficients through their ordering, so they cannot simply be handled independently. The proposed screening rule uses an iterative strategy to explore the ordering of the primal solution even though that structure is initially unknown. It then excludes parameters certified to have zero coefficients from further updates. The rule can be incorporated into both standard and stochastic proximal gradient methods.

The authors prove that algorithms equipped with the screening rule retain identical results to their original versions. Experiments across multiple datasets report significant computational gains without loss of accuracy relative to competitive algorithms. The key distinction is the certification behind the removal: computational savings come from avoiding updates that the optimization result does not need.
summary.tldr: Safe screening accelerates OWL regression by skipping coefficients certified to be zero while preserving the original algorithms' results.

title: Fast OSCAR and OWL Regression via Safe Screening Rules

abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) methods often rely on the assumption that the objective function is well-behaved, but in practice, this is seldom true for real-world objectives even if noise-free observations can be collected. Common approaches, which try to model the objective as precisely as possible, often fail to make progress by spending too many evaluations modeling irrelevant details. We address this issue by proposing surrogate models that focus on the well-behaved structure in the objective function, which is informative for search, while ignoring detrimental structure that is challenging to model from few observations. First, we demonstrate that surrogate models with appropriate noise distributions can absorb challenging structures in the objective function by treating them as irreducible uncertainty. Secondly, we show that a latent Gaussian process is an excellent surrogate for this purpose, comparing with Gaussian processes with standard noise distributions. We perform numerous experiments on a range of BO benchmarks and find that our approach improves reliability and performance when faced with challenging objective functions.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization uses a surrogate model to guide the search for good objective values. This paper argues that trying to reproduce every detail of a difficult objective can waste evaluations on structure that does little to help the search. Such difficulties can arise even when observations themselves contain no measurement noise.

The proposed surrogates focus on well-behaved structure that is informative for optimization. Appropriate noise distributions absorb challenging parts of the objective as irreducible uncertainty. This changes the role of noise in the model: it can represent structure that is unhelpful or difficult to learn from a small number of observations, even for a noise-free objective.

The authors show that a latent Gaussian process is particularly effective for this purpose through comparisons with Gaussian processes using standard noise distributions. Across numerous Bayesian-optimization benchmarks, the approach improves reliability and performance on challenging objectives. The finding supports designing the surrogate around useful search guidance, with the treatment of difficult structure becoming a deliberate modeling choice.
summary.tldr: Surrogates that absorb difficult objective structure as uncertainty improve Bayesian optimization reliability and performance in experiments.

title: Modulating Surrogates for Bayesian Optimization

abstract: Existing multi-armed bandit (MAB) models make two implicit assumptions: an arm generates a payoff only when it is played, and the agent observes every payoff that is generated. This paper introduces synchronization bandits, a MAB variant where all arms generate costs at all times, but the agent observes an arm’s instantaneous cost only when the arm is played. Synchronization MABs are inspired by online caching scenarios such as Web crawling, where an arm corresponds to a cached item and playing the arm means downloading its fresh copy from a server. We present MirrorSync, an online learning algorithm for synchronization bandits, establish an adversarial regret of $O(T^{2/3})$ for it, and show how to make it practical.

This paper introduces synchronization bandits, a MAB variant where all arms generate costs at all times, but the agent observes an arm’s instantaneous cost only when the arm is played. Synchronization MABs are inspired by online caching scenarios such as Web crawling, where an arm corresponds to a cached item and playing the arm means downloading its fresh copy from a server. We present MirrorSync, an online learning algorithm for synchronization bandits, establish an adversarial regret of $O(T^{2/3})$ for it, and show how to make it practical.

paragraphs: A cached copy can become costly to keep outdated even when nobody refreshes it. This differs from standard multi-armed bandit models, where an option produces a payoff when selected and that payoff is observed. The paper introduces synchronization bandits to capture situations where costs continue to arise between actions.

In this model, every arm generates costs continuously, but the learner observes an arm's instantaneous cost only when selecting it. For web crawling, an arm represents a cached item and selecting it means downloading a fresh copy. The learner must therefore make refresh decisions with only intermittent observations of the costs those decisions address.

The authors propose MirrorSync and establish an adversarial regret bound of order T to the two-thirds over a horizon T. This sublinear bound means the guaranteed regret grows more slowly than the horizon. They also describe how to make the algorithm practical. The contribution combines a model tailored to ongoing, partly hidden synchronization costs with an online algorithm that has a formal performance guarantee.
summary.tldr: Synchronization bandits model ongoing cache costs with intermittent feedback, and MirrorSync achieves an adversarial regret bound of order T to the two-thirds.

title: Online Learning for Active Cache Synchronization

abstract: Submodular functions have been studied extensively in machine learning and data mining. In particular, the optimization of submodular functions over the integer lattice (integer submodular functions) has recently attracted much interest, because this domain relates naturally to many practical problem settings, such as multilabel graph cut, budget allocation and revenue maximization with discrete assignments. In contrast, the use of these functions for probabilistic modeling has received surprisingly little attention so far. In this work, we firstly propose the Generalized Multilinear Extension, a continuous DR-submodular extension for integer submodular functions. We study central properties of this extension and formulate a new probabilistic model which is defined through integer submodular functions. Then, we introduce a block-coordinate ascent algorithm to perform approximate inference for this class of models and finally, we demonstrate its effectiveness and viability on several real-world social connection graph datasets with integer submodular objectives.

paragraphs: Integer submodular functions describe objectives over discrete quantities, extending the setting beyond simple set membership. Such objectives arise in problems including budget allocation, multilabel graph cuts, and revenue maximization with discrete assignments. This paper develops their use in probabilistic modeling, an area the authors identify as receiving less attention than optimization.

The first contribution is a Generalized Multilinear Extension: a continuous extension of integer submodular functions that has a diminishing-returns property. The authors study its central mathematical properties and introduce a probabilistic model defined through integer submodular functions. The continuous formulation provides a connection between the discrete structure of the model and the machinery used to work with it.

For approximate inference, the paper introduces a block-coordinate ascent algorithm, which updates blocks of variables in turn. Evaluations on real-world social connection graphs with integer submodular objectives demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness and viability. The contribution combines a model class, an extension with useful mathematical structure, and an inference procedure, bringing integer-valued submodular objectives into a probabilistic framework.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces probabilistic integer submodular models, a continuous extension, and a block-coordinate method for approximate inference.

title: From Sets to Multisets: Provable Variational Inference for Probabilistic Integer Submodular Models

abstract: We propose a novel algorithm for online meta learning where task instances are sequentially revealed with limited supervision and a learner is expected to meta learn them in each round, so as to allow the learner to customize a task-specific model rapidly with little task-level supervision. A fundamental concern arising in online meta-learning is the scalability of memory as more tasks are viewed over time. Heretofore, prior works have allowed for perfect recall leading to linear increase in memory with time. Different from prior works, in our method, prior task instances are allowed to be deleted. We propose to leverage prior task instances by means of a fixed-size state-vector, which is updated sequentially. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that our proposed memory efficient online learning (MOML) method suffers sub-linear regret with convex loss functions and sub-linear local regret for nonconvex losses. On benchmark datasets we show that our method can outperform prior works even though they allow for perfect recall.

Heretofore, prior works have allowed for perfect recall leading to linear increase in memory with time. Different from prior works, in our method, prior task instances are allowed to be deleted.
