paragraphs: Online meta-learning receives tasks sequentially and must learn how to adapt quickly using little supervision for each task. Retaining every previous task makes memory usage grow with time. This paper proposes a method that can delete past task instances while continuing to use information gained from them.

The method, called MOML, maintains a fixed-size state vector and updates it as tasks arrive. This vector provides the mechanism for carrying prior task information forward without perfect recall. The contribution targets a central scalability issue: the learner's accumulated experience need not require keeping an ever-growing collection of task instances.

The theoretical analysis establishes sublinear regret for convex losses and sublinear local regret for nonconvex losses. These are distinct guarantees, with the nonconvex result stated in terms of local regret. Benchmark experiments show that MOML can outperform earlier methods even when those methods retain all past tasks. The findings therefore support both memory efficiency and competitive learning behavior, showing that discarding task instances need not prevent strong performance in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: MOML summarizes past tasks in a fixed-size state, providing regret guarantees and sometimes outperforming online meta-learners with perfect recall.

title: Memory Efficient Online Meta Learning

abstract: Contextual bandit algorithms have become widely used for recommendation in online systems (e.g. marketplaces, music streaming, news), where they now wield substantial influence on which items get shown to users. This raises questions of fairness to the items — and to the sellers, artists, and writers that benefit from this exposure. We argue that the conventional bandit formulation can lead to an undesirable and unfair winner-takes-all allocation of exposure. To remedy this problem, we propose a new bandit objective that guarantees merit-based fairness of exposure to the items while optimizing utility to the users. We formulate fairness regret and reward regret in this setting and present algorithms for both stochastic multi-armed bandits and stochastic linear bandits. We prove that the algorithms achieve sublinear fairness regret and reward regret. Beyond the theoretical analysis, we also provide empirical evidence that these algorithms can allocate exposure to different arms effectively.

To remedy this problem, we propose a new bandit objective that guarantees merit-based fairness of exposure to the items while optimizing utility to the users. We formulate fairness regret and reward regret in this setting and present algorithms for both stochastic multi-armed bandits and stochastic linear bandits. paragraphs: Recommendation algorithms determine which items receive attention and, consequently, which sellers, artists, or writers benefit from being seen. The paper argues that a conventional bandit objective can concentrate exposure on a winner in an undesirable way. It introduces an objective that incorporates merit-based fairness to items while still optimizing user utility.

The authors formalize two forms of regret: one tracks fairness and the other tracks reward. Keeping both quantities explicit makes it possible to study whether an algorithm learns to provide useful recommendations while also allocating exposure appropriately. They develop algorithms for stochastic multi-armed bandits and stochastic linear bandits within this setting.

The theoretical results establish sublinear growth of both fairness regret and reward regret. This means that each cumulative shortfall grows more slowly than the number of decisions, so its average per decision diminishes. Empirical results also support effective exposure allocation across arms. The fairness claim is tied to the paper's merit-based objective, which makes item exposure a direct part of learning.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces bandit algorithms that balance user reward with merit-based item exposure and achieve sublinear regret for both objectives.

title: Fairness of Exposure in Stochastic Bandits

abstract: Supervised learning in artificial neural networks typically relies on backpropagation, where the weights are updated based on the error-function gradients and sequentially propagated from the output layer to the input layer. Although this approach has proven effective in a wide domain of applications, it lacks biological plausibility in many regards, including the weight symmetry problem, the dependence of learning on non-local signals, the freezing of neural activity during error propagation, and the update locking problem. Alternative training schemes have been introduced, including sign symmetry, feedback alignment, and direct feedback alignment, but they invariably rely on a backward pass that hinders the possibility of solving all the issues simultaneously. Here, we propose to replace the backward pass with a second forward pass in which the input signal is modulated based on the error of the network. We show that this novel learning rule comprehensively addresses all the above-mentioned issues and can be applied to both fully connected and convolutional models. We test this learning rule on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100. These results help incorporate biological principles into machine learning.

Although this approach has proven effective in a wide domain of applications, it lacks biological plausibility in many regards, including the weight symmetry problem, the dependence of learning on non-local signals, the freezing of neural activity during error propagation, and the update locking problem. Alternative training schemes have been introduced, including sign symmetry, feedback alignment, and direct feedback alignment, but they invariably rely on a backward pass that hinders the possibility of solving all the issues simultaneously. Here, we propose to replace the backward pass with a second forward pass in which the input signal is modulated based on the error of the network. We show that this novel learning rule comprehensively addresses all the above-mentioned issues and can be applied to both fully connected and convolutional models. We test this learning rule on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100. These results help incorporate biological principles into machine learning.

paragraphs: Backpropagation assigns credit for a network's errors by sending gradient information backward through its layers. Although effective, it has features that are difficult to reconcile with biological learning. The paper highlights weight symmetry, dependence on nonlocal signals, frozen activity during error propagation, and restrictions on when updates can occur.

The proposed learning rule replaces the backward pass with another forward pass. In that second pass, the network's input is modified according to its error. This changes the route by which error information influences learning. The authors argue that alternatives such as feedback alignment retain a backward pass and therefore do not simultaneously resolve all the listed issues.

The authors show that their rule addresses these concerns and can train both fully connected and convolutional models. They test it on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100. The contribution is a concrete alternative for credit assignment that incorporates biological principles into network training, with applicability demonstrated across the stated architectures and image-classification datasets.
summary.tldr: An error-modulated second forward pass provides a learning rule that addresses several biological-plausibility problems of backpropagation.

title: Error-driven Input Modulation: Solving the Credit Assignment Problem without a Backward Pass

abstract: Since reinforcement learning algorithms are notoriously data-intensive, the task of sampling observations from the environment is usually split across multiple agents. However, transferring these observations from the agents to a central location can be prohibitively expensive in terms of the communication cost, and it can also compromise the privacy of each agent’s local behavior policy. In this paper, we consider a federated reinforcement learning framework where multiple agents collaboratively learn a global model, without sharing their individual data and policies. Each agent maintains a local copy of the model and updates it using locally sampled data. Although having N agents enables the sampling of N times more data, it is not clear if it leads to proportional convergence speedup. We propose federated versions of on-policy TD, off-policy TD and Q-learning, and analyze their convergence. For all these algorithms, to the best of our knowledge, we are the first to consider Markovian noise and multiple local updates, and prove a linear convergence speedup with respect to the number of agents. To obtain these results, we show that federated TD and Q-learning are special cases of a general framework for federated stochastic approximation with Markovian noise, and we leverage this framework to provide a unified convergence analysis that applies to all the algorithms.
originalAbstract: Since reinforcement learning algorithms are notoriously data-intensive, the task of sampling observations from the environment is usually split across multiple agents. However, transferring these observations from the agents to a central location can be prohibitively expensive in terms of the communication cost, and it can also compromise the privacy of each agent’s local behavior policy. In this paper, we consider a federated reinforcement learning framework where multiple agents collaboratively learn a global model, without sharing their individual data and policies. Each agent maintains a local copy of the model and updates it using locally sampled data. Although having N agents enables the sampling of N times more data, it is not clear if it leads to proportional convergence speedup. We propose federated versions of on-policy TD, off-policy TD and Q-learning, and analyze their convergence. For all these algorithms, to the best of our knowledge, we are the first to consider Markovian noise and multiple local updates, and prove a linear convergence speedup with respect to the number of agents. To obtain these results, we show that federated TD and Q-learning are special cases of a general framework for federated stochastic approximation with Markovian noise, and we leverage this framework to provide a unified convergence analysis that applies to all the algorithms.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often needs many observations, making it attractive to collect experience with multiple agents. Sending all that experience to a central location can be expensive and expose local behavior policies. This paper considers agents that instead maintain local model copies and collaborate on a global model without sharing their individual data or policies.

The authors develop federated versions of on-policy temporal-difference learning, off-policy temporal-difference learning, and Q-learning. Their analysis includes multiple local updates and Markovian sampling, where observations arise from a dependent sequence. This matters because collecting N times as much data with N agents does not by itself establish that learning converges N times faster.

For all three algorithms, the authors prove a convergence speedup linear in the number of agents within their analyzed framework. They obtain a unified proof by expressing the algorithms as instances of federated stochastic approximation with Markovian noise. The contribution connects distributed data collection to a convergence guarantee while explicitly accounting for dependence in the sampled experience.
summary.tldr: Federated TD and Q-learning achieve provable linear speedup with agent count in an analysis that includes Markovian sampling and multiple local updates.

title: Federated Reinforcement Learning: Linear Speedup Under Markovian Sampling

abstract: Recently, certifiable robust training methods via bound propagation have been proposed for training neural networks with certifiable robustness guarantees. However, no neural architectures with regular convolution and linear layers perform better in the certifiable training than the plain CNNs, since the output bounds for the deep explicit models increase quickly as their depth increases. And such a phenomenon significantly hinders certifiable training. Meanwhile, the Deep Equilibrium Model (DEQ) is more representative and robust due to their equivalent infinite depth and controllable global Lipschitz. But no work has been proposed to explore whether DEQ can show advantages in certified training. In this work, we aim to tackle the problem of DEQ’s certified training. To obtain the output bound based on the bound propagation scheme in the implicit model, we first involve the adjoint DEQ for bound approximation. Furthermore, we also use the weight orthogonalization method and other tricks specified for DEQ to stabilize the certifiable training. With our approach, we can obtain the certifiable DEQ called CerDEQ. Our CerDEQ can achieve state-of-the-art performance compared with models using regular convolution and linear layers on $\ell_\infty$ tasks with $\epsilon=8/255$: $64.72%$ certified error for CIFAR-$10$ and $94.45%$ certified error for Tiny ImageNet.

For deep explicit networks, these bounds can grow rapidly with depth, making training difficult. This paper investigates whether deep equilibrium models can offer a useful alternative, drawing on their effective infinite depth and controllable global Lipschitz behavior.

The main challenge is obtaining output bounds for an implicit model within a bound-propagation approach. The authors introduce an adjoint deep equilibrium model to approximate those bounds. The authors report state-of-the-art performance within the comparison class of models using regular convolution and linear layers. These results demonstrate a way to bring implicit equilibrium architectures into certified training despite the difficulty of computing their bounds.
summary.tldr: CerDEQ enables certified training of deep equilibrium models through adjoint-based bound approximation and training stabilization.

title: CerDEQ: Certifiable Deep Equilibrium Model

abstract: We study the effects of constrained optimization formulations and Frank-Wolfe algorithms for obtaining interpretable neural network predictions. Reformulating the Rate-Distortion Explanations (RDE) method for relevance attribution as a constrained optimization problem provides precise control over the sparsity of relevance maps. This enables a novel multi-rate as well as a relevance-ordering variant of RDE that both empirically outperform standard RDE and other baseline methods in a well-established comparison test. We showcase several deterministic and stochastic variants of the Frank-Wolfe algorithm and their effectiveness for RDE.

paragraphs: This paper studies how the optimization formulation behind an explanation method affects the explanations it produces. Its starting point is Rate-Distortion Explanations, or RDE, which assigns relevance to input features for a neural network’s prediction. The authors reformulate RDE as a constrained optimization problem so that the sparsity of its relevance maps can be controlled precisely.

Sparsity concerns how many input features an explanation marks as relevant. Explicit control over it gives the method a direct handle on how selective an explanation should be. The reformulation also enables two extensions: a multi-rate version and a version that orders features by relevance. These provide additional ways to express which parts of an input matter for a prediction.

The authors investigate both deterministic and stochastic variants of the Frank-Wolfe algorithm for solving these explanation problems. In an established comparison test, both new RDE variants empirically outperform standard RDE and other baselines. The contribution links an optimization choice to concrete explanation capabilities and measured improvements in that evaluation, rather than presenting sparsity control as an end in itself.
summary.tldr: A constrained RDE formulation gives precise sparsity control and enables explanation variants that outperform standard RDE and other baselines in the reported test.

title: Interpretable Neural Networks with Frank-Wolfe: Sparse Relevance Maps and Relevance Orderings

abstract: Variational approximations to Gaussian processes (GPs) typically use a small set of inducing points to form a low-rank approximation to the covariance matrix. In this work, we instead exploit a sparse approximation of the precision matrix. We propose variational nearest neighbor Gaussian process (VNNGP), which introduces a prior that only retains correlations within $K$ nearest-neighboring observations, thereby inducing sparse precision structure. Using the variational framework, VNNGP’s objective can be factorized over both observations and inducing points, enabling stochastic optimization with a time complexity of $O(K^3)$. Hence, we can arbitrarily scale the inducing point size, even to the point of putting inducing points at every observed location. We compare VNNGP to other scalable GPs through various experiments, and demonstrate that VNNGP (1) can dramatically outperform low-rank methods, and (2) is less prone to overfitting than other nearest neighbor methods.

paragraphs: Scalable variational Gaussian processes commonly rely on a small set of inducing points to build a low-rank covariance approximation. This paper takes a different route by approximating the precision matrix, the inverse of the covariance matrix, with sparse structure. The aim is to support many inducing points without making their total number the central computational bottleneck.

The proposed variational nearest neighbor Gaussian process introduces a prior that retains correlations within K nearest-neighboring observations. This produces the sparse precision structure. Its variational objective separates over both observations and inducing points, allowing stochastic optimization with O(K^3) time complexity. The construction permits increasing the inducing-point set even to one point at every observed location.

Experiments compare VNNGP with other scalable Gaussian-process methods. The authors show that it can substantially outperform low-rank approaches and is less prone to overfitting than other nearest-neighbor methods in those comparisons. The findings support combining local dependence structure with variational inference as a scalable alternative to restricting the model to a small inducing-point set.
summary.tldr: VNNGP combines sparse nearest-neighbor dependence with variational inference to scale Gaussian processes to large inducing-point sets.

title: Variational nearest neighbor Gaussian process

abstract: Learning accurate predictive models of real-world dynamic phenomena (e.g., climate, biological) remains a challenging task. One key issue is that the data generated by both natural and artificial processes often comprise time series that are irregularly sampled and/or contain missing observations. In this work, we propose the Neural Continuous-Discrete State Space Model (NCDSSM) for continuous-time modeling of time series through discrete-time observations. NCDSSM employs auxiliary variables to disentangle recognition from dynamics, thus requiring amortized inference only for the auxiliary variables. Leveraging techniques from continuous-discrete filtering theory, we demonstrate how to perform accurate Bayesian inference for the dynamic states. We propose three flexible parameterizations of the latent dynamics and an efficient training objective that marginalizes the dynamic states during inference. Empirical results on multiple benchmark datasets across various domains show improved imputation and forecasting performance of NCDSSM over existing models.

paragraphs: Many time series describe processes that evolve continuously even though measurements arrive at irregular times or are missing. This paper introduces the Neural Continuous-Discrete State Space Model, or NCDSSM, to model that combination directly. It represents continuous-time dynamics while learning from discrete observations, targeting both missing-value estimation and future prediction.

The model introduces auxiliary variables to separate recognition from the underlying dynamics. Consequently, amortized inference is needed only for those auxiliary variables. For the dynamic states, the authors use methods from continuous-discrete filtering to perform Bayesian inference. This division assigns different inference machinery to different parts of the model instead of handling every latent quantity through the same mechanism.

The paper provides three flexible ways to parameterize latent dynamics and a training objective that marginalizes the dynamic states during inference. Across multiple benchmark datasets from different domains, the authors report improved imputation and forecasting compared with existing models. The contribution links a continuous-time description of change with an inference procedure designed for observations that do not follow a regular sampling schedule.
summary.tldr: NCDSSM combines continuous-time dynamics with discrete-observation inference and reports improved forecasting and missing-value estimation on multiple benchmarks.

title: Neural Continuous-Discrete State Space Models for Irregularly-Sampled Time Series

abstract: Transport maps can ease the sampling of distributions with non-trivial geometries by transforming them into distributions that are easier to handle. The potential of this approach has risen with the development of Normalizing Flows (NF) which are maps parameterized with deep neural networks trained to push a reference distribution towards a target. NF-enhanced samplers recently proposed blend (Markov chain) Monte Carlo methods with either (i) proposal draws from the flow or (ii) a flow-based reparametrization. In both cases, the quality of the learned transport conditions performance. The present work clarifies for the first time the relative strengths and weaknesses of these two approaches. Our study concludes that multimodal targets can be reliably handled with flow-based proposals up to moderately high dimensions. In contrast, methods relying on reparametrization struggle with multimodality but are more robust otherwise in high-dimensional settings and under poor training. To further illustrate the influence of target-proposal adequacy, we also derive a new quantitative bound for the mixing time of the Independent Metropolis-Hastings sampler.

paragraphs: Transport maps can make difficult probability distributions easier to sample by transforming their geometry. Normalizing flows learn such maps with neural networks. Flow-assisted Monte Carlo methods use them in two main ways: generating proposed samples directly, or changing the coordinates in which sampling takes place. Both depend on the quality of the learned map.

This paper compares the strengths and weaknesses of those approaches. Its study finds that flow-based proposals can reliably handle targets with multiple modes up to moderately high dimensions. Methods based on reparameterization struggle with multimodality, but otherwise show greater robustness in high-dimensional settings and when the flow has been poorly trained.

These findings make the choice of how to use a flow depend on the target distribution and training quality. The authors also derive a quantitative mixing-time bound for Independent Metropolis-Hastings, connecting sampling behavior to how well the proposal matches the target. Together, the comparison and bound clarify why an approximate learned transport can help differently depending on its role in the sampler.
summary.tldr: Flow-based proposals and flow-based reparameterizations offer different sampling advantages depending on multimodality, dimension, and training quality.

title: On Sampling with Approximate Transport Maps

abstract: This paper studies the fair range clustering problem in which the data points are from different demographic groups and the goal is to pick $k$ centers with the minimum clustering cost such that each group is at least minimally represented in the centers set and no group dominates the centers set. More precisely, given a set of $n$ points in a metric space $(P, d)$ where each point belongs to one of the $\ell$ different demographics (i.e., $P = P_1 \uplus P_2 \uplus \cdots \uplus P_\ell$) and a set of $\ell$ intervals $[\alpha_1, \beta_1], \cdots, [\alpha_\ell, \beta_\ell]$ on desired number of centers from each group, the goal is to pick a set of $k$ centers $C$ with minimum $\ell_p$-clustering cost (i.e., $(\sum_{v\in P} d(v,C)^p)^{1/p}$) such that for each group $i\in \ell$, $|C\cap P_i| \in [\alpha_i, \beta_i]$. In particular, the fair range $\ell_p$-clustering captures fair range $k$-center, $k$-median and $k$-means as its special cases. In this work, we provide an efficient constant factor approximation algorithm for the fair range $\ell_p$-clustering for all values of $p\in [1,\infty)$.

paragraphs: This paper studies clustering when the selected centers must represent different demographic groups within specified ranges. Each data point belongs to one group, and the task is to choose a fixed total number of centers. Every group has a lower and upper bound on how many centers it can contribute, expressing both minimum representation and limits on dominance.

The objective combines these representation requirements with a distance-based clustering cost. Points should be close to their nearest selected center, while the selected centers satisfy all group bounds. The framework accommodates different ways of aggregating distances, connecting the problem to familiar clustering objectives such as k-median and k-means.

The contribution is an efficient algorithm with a constant-factor approximation guarantee for every finite parameter p of at least one in the stated objective family. This means the algorithm offers a bounded relationship to the optimal constrained clustering cost, rather than promising an exact optimum. The fairness requirement concerns representation among centers, making that particular allocation decision part of the optimization itself.
summary.tldr: The paper gives efficient constant-factor approximation algorithms for clustering with lower and upper demographic representation bounds on selected centers.

title: Approximation Algorithms for Fair Range Clustering

abstract: Graph transformers have been competitive on graph classification tasks, but they fail to outperform Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) on node classification, which is a common task performed on large-scale graphs for industrial applications. Meanwhile, existing GNN architectures are limited in their ability to perform equally well on both homophilious and heterophilious graphs as their inductive biases are generally tailored to only one setting. To address these issues, we propose GOAT, a scalable global graph transformer. In GOAT, each node conceptually attends to all the nodes in the graph and homophily/heterophily relationships can be learnt adaptively from the data. We provide theoretical justification for our approximate global self-attention scheme, and show it to be scalable to large-scale graphs. We demonstrate the competitiveness of GOAT on both heterophilious and homophilious graphs with millions of nodes.

paragraphs: Node classification requires predicting properties of individual nodes in a graph. The paper identifies a mismatch in existing models: graph transformers had been competitive for whole-graph classification but less successful against graph neural networks on node classification. Many graph neural networks also favor either graphs connecting similar nodes or graphs connecting dissimilar nodes.

GOAT is a global graph transformer designed to address both concerns. Each node conceptually attends to every other node, allowing information to come from across the graph. The model can learn from data how similarity and dissimilarity relationships should influence predictions. Its approximate global self-attention scheme makes that broad interaction pattern scalable, and the authors provide theoretical justification for the approximation.

The experiments demonstrate competitive performance on both homophilous graphs, where connected nodes tend to be similar, and heterophilous graphs, where they tend to differ. The evaluated graphs include millions of nodes. These findings support global attention as a practical approach to large-scale node classification across both relationship patterns, without establishing that it always outperforms every alternative.
summary.tldr: GOAT makes approximate global attention scalable to million-node graphs and achieves competitive classification across different neighborhood similarity patterns.

title: GOAT: A Global Transformer on Large-scale Graphs

abstract: Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) denotes a powerful family of algorithms for recovering a reward function justifying the behavior demonstrated by an expert agent. A well-known limitation of IRL is the ambiguity in the choice of the reward function, due to the existence of multiple rewards that explain the observed behavior. This limitation has been recently circumvented by formulating IRL as the problem of estimating the feasible reward set, i.e., the region of the rewards compatible with the expert’s behavior. In this paper, we make a step towards closing the theory gap of IRL in the case of finite-horizon problems with a generative model. We start by formally introducing the problem of estimating the feasible reward set, the corresponding PAC requirement, and discussing the properties of particular classes of rewards. Then, we provide the first minimax lower bound on the sample complexity for the problem of estimating the feasible reward set of order ${\Omega}\left( \frac{H^3SA}{\epsilon^2} \left( \log \left(\frac{1}{\delta}\right) + S \right)\right)$, being $S$ and $A$ the number of states and actions respectively, $H$ the horizon, $\epsilon$ the desired accuracy, and $\delta$ the confidence. We analyze the sample complexity of a uniform sampling strategy (US-IRL), proving a matching upper bound up to logarithmic factors. Finally, we outline several open questions in IRL and propose future research directions.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning tries to infer rewards that explain an expert's behavior. The central ambiguity is that multiple reward functions can justify the same decisions. This paper studies estimating the entire feasible reward set, meaning all rewards compatible with the demonstrated behavior.

The analysis concerns finite-horizon problems with access to a generative model. The authors formalize reward-set estimation and its probably approximately correct requirement, connecting desired accuracy and confidence to the number of samples required. They also examine properties of particular reward classes.

Here H is the horizon, S and A count states and actions, ε specifies accuracy, and δ controls the confidence requirement. A uniform sampling algorithm, US-IRL, matches this bound up to logarithmic factors. The paired bounds identify near-matching necessary and sufficient sample requirements in the stated setting, giving a theoretical foundation for learning compatible reward sets.
summary.tldr: For finite-horizon IRL with a generative model, uniform sampling estimates compatible reward sets with sample complexity matching a minimax lower bound up to logarithmic factors.

title: Towards Theoretical Understanding of Inverse Reinforcement Learning

abstract: It is notoriously difficult to train Transformers on small datasets; typically, large pre-trained models are instead used as the starting point. We explore the weights of such pre-trained Transformers (particularly for vision) to attempt to find reasons for this discrepancy. Surprisingly, we find that simply initializing the weights of self-attention layers so that they "look" more like their pre-trained counterparts allows us to train vanilla Transformers faster and to higher final accuracies, particularly on vision tasks such as CIFAR-10 and ImageNet classification, where we see gains in accuracy of over 5% and 4%, respectively. Our initialization scheme is closed form, learning-free, and very simple: we set the product of the query and key weights to be approximately the identity, and the product of the value and projection weights to approximately the negative identity. As this mimics the patterns we saw in pre-trained Transformers, we call the technique "mimetic initialization".

paragraphs: Transformers can be difficult to train on small datasets, making pretrained models attractive starting points. This paper examines pretrained attention weights, especially in vision models, to identify structural patterns that might help explain the advantage. It then turns those observations into a simple initialization scheme.

The scheme sets the product of the query and key weight matrices approximately equal to the identity matrix. It sets the product of the value and projection matrices approximately equal to the negative identity. These relationships imitate patterns found in pretrained Transformers, giving the method its name, mimetic initialization. The construction is closed form and requires no learning to produce the initialization.

The authors report faster training and higher final accuracy for vanilla Transformers, particularly on vision classification tasks. Reported accuracy gains exceed 5% on CIFAR-10 and 4% on ImageNet. The finding shows that these simple relationships among attention weights can provide a useful starting structure. In the evaluated settings, some training benefits associated with the observed pretrained weight patterns can therefore be obtained through initialization alone.
summary.tldr: A learning-free initialization that imitates pretrained attention-weight patterns improves Transformer training speed and final accuracy in evaluated vision tasks.

title: Mimetic Initialization of Self-Attention Layers

abstract: Local graph clustering methods aim to detect small clusters in very large graphs without the need to process the whole graph. They are fundamental and scalable tools for a wide range of tasks such as local community detection, node ranking and node embedding. While prior work on local graph clustering mainly focuses on graphs without node attributes, modern real-world graph datasets typically come with node attributes that provide valuable additional information. We present a simple local graph clustering algorithm for graphs with node attributes, based on the idea of diffusing mass locally in the graph while accounting for both structural and attribute proximities. Using high-dimensional concentration results, we provide statistical guarantees on the performance of the algorithm for the recovery of a target cluster with a single seed node. We give conditions under which a target cluster generated from a fairly general contextual random graph model, which includes both the stochastic block model and the planted cluster model as special cases, can be fully recovered with bounded false positives. Empirically, we validate all theoretical claims using synthetic data, and we show that incorporating node attributes leads to superior local clustering performances using real-world graph datasets.

We present a simple local graph clustering algorithm for graphs with node attributes, based on the idea of diffusing mass locally in the graph while accounting for both structural and attribute proximities. paragraphs: Local graph clustering seeks a small cluster inside a very large graph without processing the entire graph. Existing approaches often emphasize connectivity alone, although nodes may also carry useful attributes. This paper combines those information sources so that cluster discovery reflects both graph structure and similarities between node attributes.

The proposed algorithm diffuses mass locally through the graph while accounting for structural and attribute proximity. Starting from a single seed node, it aims to recover a target cluster. The authors use high-dimensional concentration results to establish statistical performance guarantees under a contextual random graph model that includes stochastic block and planted cluster models.

The theory gives conditions under which the entire target cluster can be recovered while keeping false positives bounded. Full target recovery therefore does not mean that every returned node must belong to the target. Synthetic experiments validate the theoretical claims, and real-world graph experiments show that incorporating attributes improves local clustering. The results support combining connectivity and node information within a scalable local procedure.
summary.tldr: Local weighted diffusion combines graph structure and node attributes, with conditional recovery guarantees and improved empirical clustering.

title: Weighted Flow Diffusion for Local Graph Clustering with Node Attributes: an Algorithm and Statistical Guarantees

abstract: Generalization in Reinforcement Learning (RL) aims to train an agent during training that generalizes to the target environment. In this work, we first point out that RL generalization is fundamentally different from the generalization in supervised learning, and fine-tuning on the target environment is necessary for good test performance. Therefore, we seek to answer the following question: how much can we expect pre-training over training environments to be helpful for efficient and effective fine-tuning? On one hand, we give a surprising result showing that asymptotically, the improvement from pre-training is at most a constant factor. On the other hand, we show that pre-training can be indeed helpful in the non-asymptotic regime by designing a policy collection-elimination (PCE) algorithm and proving a distribution-dependent regret bound that is independent of the state-action space. We hope our theoretical results can provide insight towards understanding pre-training and generalization in RL.

title: On the Power of Pre-training for Generalization in RL: Provable Benefits and Hardness

abstract: In deep learning, often the training process finds an interpolator (a solution with 0 training loss), but the test loss is still low. This phenomenon, known as benign overfitting , is a major mystery that received a lot of recent attention. One common mechanism for benign overfitting is implicit regularization , where the training process leads to additional properties for the interpolator, often characterized by minimizing certain norms. However, even for a simple sparse linear regression problem $y = \beta^{\ast\top} x +\xi$ with sparse $\beta^{\ast}$, neither minimum $\ell_1$ or $\ell_2$ norm interpolator gives the optimal test loss. In this work, we give a different parametrization of the model which leads to a new implicit regularization effect that combines the benefit of $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ interpolators. We show that training our new model via gradient descent leads to an interpolator with near-optimal test loss. Our result is based on careful analysis of the training dynamics and provides another example of implicit regularization effect that goes beyond norm minimization.

paragraphs: A model can fit its training data perfectly yet still predict well on new data, a phenomenon called benign overfitting. This paper studies that behavior in sparse linear regression, where the true coefficient vector has relatively few nonzero entries and observations contain additive noise. The question is what makes a particular exact fit generalize well.

One explanation is implicit regularization: the training procedure favors certain solutions without an explicit penalty selecting them. Such preferences are often described through minimum-norm solutions. However, the authors show that neither the minimum l1-norm nor the minimum l2-norm interpolator attains optimal test loss for the sparse regression problem considered.

The paper introduces a different model parameterization whose gradient-descent dynamics combine benefits associated with those two interpolators. The analysis establishes that training reaches an exact fit with near-optimal test loss. This provides a concrete example in which the route taken during optimization matters for generalization, and the resulting implicit preference goes beyond ordinary norm minimization. The theoretical contribution concerns this sparse linear regression construction.
summary.tldr: A new sparse linear regression parameterization lets gradient descent find an exact training fit with near-optimal test loss through implicit regularization.

title: Implicit Regularization Leads to Benign Overfitting for Sparse Linear Regression

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) and Large Multi-modality Models (LMMs) have demonstrated remarkable decision masking capabilities on a variety of tasks. However, they inherently operate planning within the language space, lacking the vision and spatial imagination ability. In contrast, humans utilize both left and right hemispheres of the brain for language and visual planning during the thinking process. Therefore, we introduce a novel vision-language planning framework in this work to perform concurrent visual and language planning for tasks with inputs of any form. Our framework incorporates visual planning to capture intricate environmental details, while language planning enhances the logical coherence of the overall system. We evaluate the effectiveness of our framework across vision-language tasks, vision-only tasks, and language-only tasks. The results demonstrate the superior performance of our approach, indicating that the integration of visual and language planning yields better contextually aware task execution.

paragraphs: Language models and multimodal models can make decisions across many tasks, but this paper argues that their planning remains centered in language and lacks visual and spatial imagination. The authors propose a framework that performs visual planning and language planning concurrently. It is designed for tasks with different input forms, rather than only tasks that already contain both images and text.

The two planning modes have complementary intended roles. Visual planning captures detailed information about the environment, while language planning supports logical coherence across the overall process. The brain comparison in the title motivates this combination; the substantive proposal is to incorporate both forms of planning into the task-solving framework.

The authors evaluate the approach on vision-language, vision-only, and language-only tasks. They report superior performance, interpreting the results as evidence that combined planning can improve contextually aware execution. Testing all three input categories is relevant to the framework’s intended breadth: its potential value is tied to how it plans, not solely to whether the original task supplies multiple modalities.
summary.tldr: Concurrent visual and language planning improves reported performance across multimodal, vision-only, and language-only tasks.

title: Using Left and Right Brains Together: Towards Vision and Language Planning

abstract: In classic Reinforcement Learning (RL), the agent maximizes an additive objective of the visited states, e.g., a value function. Unfortunately, objectives of this type cannot model many real-world applications such as experiment design, exploration, imitation learning, and risk-averse RL to name a few. This is due to the fact that additive objectives disregard interactions between states that are crucial for certain tasks. To tackle this problem, we introduce Global RL (GRL), where rewards are globally defined over trajectories instead of locally over states. Global rewards can capture negative interactions among states, e.g., in exploration, via submodularity, positive interactions, e.g., synergetic effects, via supermodularity, while mixed interactions via combinations of them. By exploiting ideas from submodular optimization, we propose a novel algorithmic scheme that converts any GRL problem to a sequence of classic RL problems and solves it efficiently with curvature-dependent approximation guarantees. We also provide hardness of approximation results and empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on several GRL instances.

paragraphs: Standard reinforcement learning commonly adds up rewards associated with visited states. That formulation can miss interactions: visiting two states together may be redundant or especially valuable. This paper introduces Global RL, where rewards are defined over complete trajectories so that the objective can account for relationships among the states an agent visits.

The framework represents negative interactions through submodularity, positive interactions through supermodularity, and mixed interactions through combinations of the two. These distinctions let the reward express effects that an additive objective overlooks. The authors then draw on submodular optimization to turn a Global RL problem into a sequence of conventional reinforcement-learning problems.

The resulting algorithmic scheme has approximation guarantees that depend on curvature, so the guarantee varies with the objective's structure. The paper also establishes hardness-of-approximation results and reports effective performance on several Global RL instances. Its contribution is both an expanded reward formulation and a way to approach it through familiar RL subproblems, while recognizing that these broader objectives have computational limits.
summary.tldr: Global RL models interactions across trajectories and solves the resulting objectives through sequences of standard RL problems with curvature-dependent approximation guarantees.

title: Global Reinforcement Learning : Beyond Linear and Convex Rewards via Submodular Semi-gradient Methods

abstract: Variance reduction techniques are designed to decrease the sampling variance, thereby accelerating convergence rates of first-order (FO) and zeroth-order (ZO) optimization methods. However, in composite optimization problems, ZO methods encounter an additional variance called the coordinate-wise variance, which stems from the random gradient estimation. To reduce this variance, prior works require estimating all partial derivatives, essentially approximating FO information. This approach demands $\mathcal{O}(d)$ function evaluations ($d$ is the dimension size), which incurs substantial computational costs and is prohibitive in high-dimensional scenarios. This paper proposes the Zeroth-order Proximal Double Variance Reduction ($\texttt{ZPDVR}$) method, which utilizes the averaging trick to reduce both sampling and coordinate-wise variances. Compared to prior methods, $\texttt{ZPDVR}$ relies solely on random gradient estimates, calls the stochastic zeroth-order oracle (SZO) in expectation $\mathcal{O}(1)$ times per iteration, and achieves the optimal $\mathcal{O}(d(n + \kappa)\log (\frac{1}{\epsilon}))$ SZO query complexity in the strongly convex and smooth setting, where $\kappa$ represents the condition number and $\epsilon$ is the desired accuracy. Empirical results validate $\texttt{ZPDVR}$’s linear convergence and demonstrate its superior performance over other related methods.

paragraphs: Zeroth-order optimization works with function evaluations rather than directly available gradients. In composite optimization, its random gradient estimates create coordinate-wise variance in addition to ordinary sampling variance. Earlier methods reduce this extra variability by estimating every partial derivative, requiring a number of function evaluations proportional to the dimension and making high-dimensional problems expensive.

The paper introduces Zeroth-order Proximal Double Variance Reduction, or ZPDVR. It uses an averaging technique to reduce both sources of variance while relying only on random gradient estimates. Each iteration requires a constant expected number of stochastic zeroth-order oracle calls, avoiding the need to estimate all partial derivatives at every step.

For the strongly convex and smooth setting, the authors establish an optimal total query complexity proportional to d(n + κ) log(1/ε), with κ denoting the condition number and ε the target accuracy. Dimension therefore still appears in the overall cost. Empirical results support linear convergence and show better performance than related methods, linking cheaper individual iterations with a strong total-computation guarantee.
summary.tldr: ZPDVR reduces two sources of gradient-estimation variance, achieving optimal query complexity in the strongly convex, smooth setting with constant expected oracle calls per iteration.

title: Double Variance Reduction: A Smoothing Trick for Composite Optimization Problems without First-Order Gradient

abstract: The multivariate hypergeometric distribution describes sampling without replacement from a discrete population of elements divided into multiple categories. Addressing a gap in the literature, we tackle the challenge of estimating discrete distributions when both the total population size and the category sizes are unknown. Here, we propose a novel solution using the hypergeometric likelihood to solve this estimation problem, even in the presence of severe under-sampling. Our approach accounts for a data generating process where the ground-truth is a mixture of distributions conditional on a continuous latent variable, as seen in collaborative filtering, using the variational autoencoder framework. Empirical data simulation demonstrates that our method outperforms other likelihood functions used to model count data, both in terms of accuracy of population size estimate and learning an informative latent space. We showcase our method’s versatility through applications in NLP, by inferring and estimating the complexity of latent vocabularies in reading passage excerpts, and in biology, by accurately recovering the true number of gene transcripts from sparse single-cell genomics data.

paragraphs: Sampling without replacement reveals only part of a finite population. When that population contains multiple categories, both its total size and the number of elements in each category may be unknown. This paper addresses estimating those quantities using the multivariate hypergeometric distribution, whose likelihood reflects the sampling process directly.

The proposed method handles severe undersampling and also allows the underlying distribution to vary with a continuous latent variable. A variational autoencoder provides the framework for this latent structure. This lets the model account for data generated from a mixture of conditional distributions, a setting the authors connect to collaborative filtering, while estimating the hidden population quantities.

In simulations, the method outperforms other count-data likelihoods in population-size estimation and in learning an informative latent space. Applications illustrate two uses: estimating the complexity of latent vocabularies from reading excerpts and recovering gene-transcript counts from sparse single-cell genomics data. The results connect the choice of sampling likelihood with both better size estimates and useful learned representations.
summary.tldr: A hypergeometric likelihood within a variational autoencoder estimates unknown population and category sizes from severely undersampled data.

title: Estimating Unknown Population Sizes Using the Hypergeometric Distribution

abstract: Current solutions for efficiently constructing large vision-language (VL) models follow a two-step paradigm: projecting the output of pre-trained vision encoders to the input space of pre-trained language models as visual prompts; and then transferring the models to downstream VL tasks via end-to-end parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). However, this paradigm still exhibits inefficiency since it significantly increases the input length of the language models. In this paper, in contrast to integrating visual prompts into inputs, we regard visual prompts as additional knowledge that facilitates language models in addressing tasks associated with visual information. Motivated by the finding that Feed-Forward Network (FFN) of language models acts as "key-value memory", we introduce a novel approach termed memory-space visual prompting (MemVP), wherein visual prompts are concatenated with the weights of FFN for visual knowledge injection. Experimental results across various VL tasks and language models reveal that MemVP significantly reduces the training time and inference latency of the finetuned VL models and surpasses the performance of previous PEFT methods.

paragraphs: A common way to build a vision-language model is to convert a vision encoder’s output into visual prompts placed in a language model’s input. Even when only a small portion of the model is fine-tuned, those prompts increase input length. This creates an efficiency cost during both adaptation and use.

Memory-space visual prompting, or MemVP, introduces visual information through the language model’s feed-forward networks. The approach draws on the view that these networks act as key-value memories. It concatenates visual prompts with their weights, treating the visual information as additional knowledge available to the model when solving a task.

This changes where visual conditioning enters the model and addresses the input-length overhead of conventional visual prompting. Across the evaluated vision-language tasks and language models, MemVP substantially reduces training time and inference latency while outperforming previous parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods. The findings indicate that the location of visual information inside the architecture can matter for both computational efficiency and downstream task performance.
summary.tldr: MemVP injects visual prompts through language-model feed-forward weights, reducing reported training time and inference latency while improving task performance.

title: Memory-Space Visual Prompting for Efficient Vision-Language Fine-Tuning

abstract: Semantic identifier (ID) is an important concept in information retrieval that aims to preserve the semantics of objects such as documents and items inside their IDs. Previous studies typically adopt a two-stage pipeline to learn semantic IDs by first procuring embeddings using off-the-shelf text encoders and then deriving IDs based on the embeddings. However, each step introduces potential information loss, and there is usually an inherent mismatch between the distribution of embeddings within the latent space produced by text encoders and the anticipated distribution required for semantic indexing. It is non-trivial to design a method that can learn the document’s semantic representations and its hierarchical structure simultaneously, given that semantic IDs are discrete and sequentially structured, and the semantic supervision is deficient. In this paper, we introduce LMIndexer, a self-supervised framework to learn semantic IDs with a generative language model. We tackle the challenge of sequential discrete ID by introducing a semantic indexer capable of generating neural sequential discrete representations with progressive training and contrastive learning. In response to the semantic supervision deficiency, we propose to train the model with a self-supervised document reconstruction objective. We show the high quality of the learned IDs and demonstrate their effectiveness on three tasks including recommendation, product search, and document retrieval on five datasets from various domains. Code is available at https://github.com/PeterGriffinJin/LMIndexer.

paragraphs: A semantic identifier aims to encode something about a document or item’s meaning in its ID. Common methods first obtain text embeddings and then convert them into identifiers. Both stages can lose information, and the embedding distribution may be poorly matched to the structure needed for indexing.

LMIndexer learns semantic identifiers using a generative language model. It addresses the difficulty of producing discrete, sequential IDs through progressive training and contrastive learning. This brings semantic representation and hierarchical identifier structure into the same learning framework, rather than relying entirely on representations produced for a separate purpose.

Because direct semantic supervision is limited, the framework learns through a self-supervised document reconstruction objective. Reconstructing the document supplies a training signal for what the identifier should preserve. Evaluations across recommendation, product search, and document retrieval on five datasets show high-quality learned IDs and demonstrate their effectiveness. The contribution is a unified approach to learning identifiers whose structure carries useful semantic information across several retrieval-related tasks.
summary.tldr: LMIndexer learns structured semantic IDs with a generative language model, using document reconstruction and contrastive learning to support retrieval-related tasks.

title: Language Models as Semantic Indexers

abstract: The limitations of purely neural learning have sparked an interest in probabilistic neurosymbolic models, which combine neural networks with probabilistic logical reasoning. As these neurosymbolic models are trained with gradient descent, we study the complexity of differentiating probabilistic reasoning. We prove that although approximating these gradients is intractable in general, it becomes tractable during training. Furthermore, we introduce WeightME, an unbiased gradient estimator based on model sampling. Under mild assumptions, WeightME approximates the gradient with probabilistic guarantees using a logarithmic number of calls to a SAT solver. Lastly, we evaluate the necessity of these guarantees on the gradient. Our experiments indicate that the existing biased approximations indeed struggle to optimize even when exact solving is still feasible.

paragraphs: Probabilistic neurosymbolic models combine neural networks with logical reasoning under uncertainty. Training them by gradient descent requires differentiating through that reasoning process. This paper studies the computational difficulty of obtaining those gradients, making the learning calculation itself the central object of analysis.

The authors prove that approximating the gradients is intractable in general, but becomes tractable during training. They also introduce WeightME, an unbiased estimator based on model sampling. Under mild assumptions, it provides probabilistic guarantees on gradient approximation using a logarithmic number of calls to a SAT solver. The assumptions qualify this computational guarantee.

Experiments investigate whether gradient guarantees matter for optimization in practice. Existing biased approximations struggle even in cases where exact solving remains feasible. This connects the theoretical analysis to a practical concern: an approximation that is easier to compute may still provide a poor training signal. WeightME offers a route toward gradients with explicit statistical properties, while the hardness result explains why unrestricted gradient approximation is a difficult starting point.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes neurosymbolic gradient complexity and introduces an unbiased estimator with conditional probabilistic guarantees.

title: On the Hardness of Probabilistic Neurosymbolic Learning

abstract: Learning meaningful representations of complex objects that can be seen through multiple ($k\geq 3$) views or modalities is a core task in machine learning. Existing methods use losses originally intended for paired views, and extend them to $k$ views, either by instantiating $\tfrac12k(k-1)$ loss-pairs, or by using reduced embeddings, following a one vs. average-of-rest strategy. We propose the multi-marginal matching gap (M3G), a loss that borrows tools from multi-marginal optimal transport (MM-OT) theory to simultaneously incorporate all $k$ views. Given a batch of $n$ points, each seen as a $k$-tuple of views subsequently transformed into $k$ embeddings, our loss contrasts the cost of matching these $n$ ground-truth $k$-tuples with the MM-OT polymatching cost, which seeks $n$ optimally arranged $k$-tuples chosen within these $n\times k$ vectors. While the exponential complexity $O(n^k$) of the MM-OT problem may seem daunting, we show in experiments that a suitable generalization of the Sinkhorn algorithm for that problem can scale to, e.g., $k=3\sim 6$ views using mini-batches of size $64 \sim128$. Our experiments demonstrate improved performance over multiview extensions of pairwise losses, for both self-supervised and multimodal tasks.

paragraphs: An object may be represented through three or more views or modalities. Learning their shared meaning often relies on objectives designed for pairs, either comparing every pair separately or comparing one view with an average of the others. This paper introduces a loss that treats all views jointly, preserving their role in a complete group.

The multi-marginal matching gap compares two costs within a batch. One measures the known groups of embeddings belonging to the same objects. The other finds an optimal arrangement of groups using multi-marginal optimal transport. Contrasting these costs gives the model a training signal based on how the true groupings compare with alternative joint matchings.

The underlying transport problem has exponential complexity in the number of views. Nevertheless, experiments show that a generalized Sinkhorn algorithm can handle three to six views with batches of roughly 64 to 128 examples. The reported results improve on multiview extensions of pairwise losses in both self-supervised and multimodal tasks, supporting the practical value of joint comparisons at these scales.
summary.tldr: M3G learns from multiple views jointly through an optimal-transport matching loss, improving on pairwise-loss extensions in the reported experiments.

title: Contrasting Multiple Representations with the Multi-Marginal Matching Gap

abstract: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM), which performs gradient descent on adversarially perturbed weights, can improve generalization by identifying flatter minima. However, recent studies have shown that SAM may suffer from convergence instability and oscillate around saddle points, resulting in slow convergence and inferior performance. To address this problem, we propose the use of a lookahead mechanism to gather more information about the landscape by looking further ahead, and thus find a better trajectory to converge. By examining the nature of SAM, we simplify the extrapolation procedure, resulting in a more efficient algorithm. Theoretical results show that the proposed method converges to a stationary point and is less prone to saddle points. Experiments on standard benchmark datasets also verify that the proposed method outperforms the SOTAs, and converge more effectively to flat minima.

However, recent studies have shown that SAM may suffer from convergence instability and oscillate around saddle points, resulting in slow convergence and inferior performance. To address this problem, we propose the use of a lookahead mechanism to gather more information about the landscape by looking further ahead, and thus find a better trajectory to converge. By examining the nature of SAM, we simplify the extrapolation procedure, resulting in a more efficient algorithm. paragraphs: Sharpness-Aware Minimization, or SAM, updates a model using gradients evaluated at adversarially perturbed weights. This can improve generalization by directing training toward flatter minima. However, SAM can also become unstable and oscillate around saddle points, slowing convergence and weakening performance. This paper modifies its update process to address that behavior.

The proposed method adds a lookahead mechanism that gathers information farther along the optimization landscape. That additional information helps choose a better trajectory for subsequent updates. By examining SAM’s structure, the authors simplify the extrapolation step, producing a more efficient version of the lookahead procedure rather than simply adding a costly extra operation.

The theoretical analysis establishes convergence to a stationary point and shows reduced susceptibility to saddle points. Experiments on standard benchmarks report better performance than the compared state-of-the-art methods and more effective convergence toward flat minima. The contribution ties improvements in the training path to the geometry SAM already seeks to exploit, while its stated convergence result concerns stationarity.
summary.tldr: A simplified lookahead mechanism improves SAM’s optimization trajectory, with theoretical convergence results and stronger benchmark performance.

title: Improving Sharpness-Aware Minimization by Lookahead

abstract: Chain-of-thought reasoning and scratchpads have emerged as critical tools for enhancing the computational capabilities of transformers. While theoretical results show that polynomial-length scratchpads can extend transformers’ expressivity from $TC^0$ to $PTIME$, their required length remains poorly understood. Empirical evidence even suggests that transformers need scratchpads even for many problems in $TC^0$, such as Parity or Multiplication, challenging optimistic bounds derived from circuit complexity. In this work, we initiate the study of systematic lower bounds for the number of CoT steps across different algorithmic problems, in the hard-attention regime. We study a variety of algorithmic problems, and provide bounds that are tight up to logarithmic factors. Overall, these results contribute to emerging understanding of the power and limitations of chain-of-thought reasoning.

paragraphs: Intermediate scratchpad steps can expand the computational capabilities of transformers, but expressivity alone does not say how long a scratchpad must be. This paper investigates that length requirement. It focuses on lower bounds: statements showing that a model needs at least a certain number of chain-of-thought steps to solve a problem.

The motivation comes from a gap between broad theoretical capability and observed reasoning requirements. Polynomial-length scratchpads can extend expressivity from TC⁰ to PTIME, yet empirical evidence suggests that transformers also need scratchpads for some problems already in TC⁰, including parity and multiplication. Circuit-complexity classifications therefore leave important questions about the amount of intermediate computation unresolved.

The authors systematically study several algorithmic problems in the hard-attention setting and obtain bounds that are tight up to logarithmic factors. This qualification means the characterization retains a logarithmic gap rather than giving an exact step count. The results contribute a more detailed picture of chain-of-thought’s computational cost, identifying limits on how short reasoning sequences can be within the transformer regime under study.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes near-tight lower bounds on chain-of-thought length for algorithmic problems in hard-attention transformers.

title: Lower Bounds for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Hard-Attention Transformers

abstract: Learning from human feedback plays an important role in aligning generative models, such as large language models (LLM). However, the effectiveness of this approach can be influenced by adversaries, who may intentionally provide misleading preferences to manipulate the output in an undesirable or harmful direction. To tackle this challenge, we study a specific model within this problem domain–contextual dueling bandits with adversarial feedback, where the true preference label can be flipped by an adversary. We propose an algorithm namely robust contextual dueling bandits ($\texttt{RCDB}$), which is based on uncertainty-weighted maximum likelihood estimation. Our algorithm achieves an $\tilde O(d\sqrt{T}/\kappa+dC/\kappa)$ regret bound, where $T$ is the number of rounds, $d$ is the dimension of the context, $\kappa$ is the lower bound of the derivative of the link function, and $ 0 \le C \le T$ is the total number of adversarial feedback. We also prove a lower bound to show that our regret bound is nearly optimal, both in scenarios with and without ($C=0$) adversarial feedback. Our work is the first to achieve nearly minimax optimal regret for dueling bandits in the presence of adversarial preference feedback. Additionally, for the sigmoid link function, we develop a novel algorithm that takes into account the effect of local derivatives into maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) analysis through a refined method for estimating the link function’s derivative. This method helps us to eliminate the $\kappa$ dependence in the leading term with respect to $T$, which reduces the exponential dependence on the parameter radius $B$ to a polynomial dependence. We conduct experiments to evaluate our proposed algorithm $\texttt{RCDB}$ against various types of adversarial feedback. Experimental results demonstrate its superiority over the state-of-the-art dueling bandit algorithms in the presence of adversarial feedback.

paragraphs: Preference-based learning can be manipulated when an adversary changes which option is labeled preferable. This paper studies that problem in contextual dueling bandits, where decisions depend on context and feedback compares options. The corruption model allows an adversary to flip preference labels during learning.

The proposed RCDB algorithm uses uncertainty-weighted maximum likelihood estimation. Up to logarithmic factors, its regret bound scales as d times the square root of T divided by kappa, plus d times C divided by kappa. Here d is context dimension, T is the number of rounds, C counts corrupted feedback, and kappa bounds the link function’s derivative from below. A matching lower-bound analysis establishes near-optimality both with and without corruption.

For a sigmoid link, a further algorithm uses refined estimates of local derivatives to remove kappa dependence from the leading term in T. This changes exponential dependence on the parameter radius into polynomial dependence. Experiments with different adversarial feedback patterns report RCDB outperforming state-of-the-art dueling-bandit methods. Together, the theory and evaluation characterize how learning degrades as corrupted feedback increases.
summary.tldr: RCDB learns from adversarially corrupted preference feedback with nearly optimal regret, while a sigmoid-specific refinement improves parameter dependence.

title: Nearly Optimal Algorithms for Contextual Dueling Bandits from Adversarial Feedback

abstract: Language models lack the notion of interchangeable tokens: symbols that are semantically equivalent yet distinct, such as bound variables in formal logic. This limitation prevents generalization to larger vocabularies and hinders the model’s ability to recognize alpha-equivalence, where renaming bound variables preserves meaning. We formalize this machine learning problem and introduce alpha-covariance, a metric for evaluating robustness to such transformations. To tackle this task, we propose a dual-part token embedding strategy: a shared component ensures semantic consistency, while a randomized component maintains token distinguishability. Compared to a baseline that relies on alpha-renaming for data augmentation, our approach demonstrates improved generalization to unseen tokens in linear temporal logic solving, propositional logic assignment prediction, and copying with an extendable vocabulary, while introducing a favorable inductive bias for alpha-equivalence. Our findings establish a foundation for designing language models that can learn interchangeable token representations, a crucial step toward more flexible and systematic reasoning in formal domains. Our code and project page are available at https://necrashter.github.io/interchangeable-token-embeddings

paragraphs: In formal reasoning, symbols can need distinct identities without having distinct semantic roles. Renaming a bound variable can preserve an expression's meaning, a property called alpha-equivalence. The paper argues that language models lack a suitable notion of such interchangeable tokens, making unfamiliar symbols and expanding vocabularies difficult to handle.

The authors formalize this problem and introduce alpha-covariance as a metric for robustness to these transformations. Their embedding design gives each token two components. A shared component represents semantic consistency across interchangeable symbols, while a randomized component keeps individual tokens distinguishable. The design therefore preserves both the common role and the identity information that reasoning tasks require.

Compared with a baseline trained using alpha-renaming as data augmentation, the method generalizes better to unseen tokens in linear temporal logic solving, propositional logic assignment prediction, and copying with an expandable vocabulary. The results support an architectural inductive bias toward alpha-equivalence and show how embedding design can help models handle new symbols systematically.
summary.tldr: Shared and randomized embedding components help models treat symbols as semantically interchangeable while preserving identity and generalizing to unseen tokens.

title: Interchangeable Token Embeddings for Extendable Vocabulary and Alpha-Equivalence

abstract: Streaming generation models are utilized across fields, with the Transducer architecture being popular in industrial applications. However, its input-synchronous decoding mechanism presents challenges in tasks requiring non-monotonic alignments, such as simultaneous translation. In this research, we address this issue by integrating Transducer’s decoding with the history of input stream via a learnable monotonic attention. Our approach leverages the forward-backward algorithm to infer the posterior probability of alignments between the predictor states and input timestamps, which is then used to estimate the monotonic context representations, thereby avoiding the need to enumerate the exponentially large alignment space during training. Extensive experiments show that our MonoAttn-Transducer effectively handles non-monotonic alignments in streaming scenarios, offering a robust solution for complex generation tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/ictnlp/MonoAttn-Transducer.

paragraphs: Streaming generation produces output as input arrives, making the relationship between input order and output order important. Transducer models use input-synchronous decoding, which becomes difficult when a task requires non-monotonic alignments. Simultaneous translation is one such setting. This paper modifies decoding so that the model can use the history of the input stream more effectively.

MonoAttn-Transducer introduces learnable monotonic attention into the decoding process. During training, a forward-backward algorithm infers posterior probabilities for alignments between predictor states and input timestamps. These probabilities are then used to estimate context representations. This provides a way to account for alignment uncertainty without explicitly enumerating an exponentially large set of possible alignments.

The method’s significance is that access to input history helps address non-monotonic generation requirements while keeping alignment-related training tractable. Extensive experiments report that MonoAttn-Transducer handles non-monotonic alignments effectively in streaming scenarios. The stated result supports the proposed combination of history-aware decoding and efficient probabilistic alignment estimation for complex streaming generation tasks.
summary.tldr: MonoAttn-Transducer adds attention over input history and efficient alignment inference to handle non-monotonic streaming generation.

title: Overcoming Non-monotonicity in Transducer-based Streaming Generation

abstract: Density-based mode-seeking methods generate a density-ascending dependency from low-density points towards higher-density neighbors. Current mode-seeking methods identify modes by breaking some dependency connections, but relying heavily on local data characteristics, requiring case-by-case threshold settings or human intervention to be effective for different datasets. To address this issue, we introduce a novel concept called typicality, by exploring the locally defined dependency from a global perspective, to quantify how confident a point would be a mode. We devise an algorithm that effectively and efficiently identifies modes with the help of the global-view typicality. To implement and validate our idea, we design a clustering method called TANGO, which not only leverages typicality to detect modes, but also utilizes graph-cut with an improved path-based similarity to aggregate data into the final clusters. Moreover, this paper also provides some theoretical analysis on the proposed algorithm. Experimental results on several synthetic and extensive real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of TANGO. The code is available at https://github.com/SWJTU-ML/TANGO_code.
