paragraphs: Density-based mode-seeking methods connect lower-density points toward higher-density neighbors, then identify peaks that can organize clusters. Deciding which connections to break often depends heavily on local characteristics. This can require thresholds chosen separately for each dataset or human intervention to obtain useful clusters.

TANGO introduces typicality, a measure of confidence that a point should count as a mode. It derives this measure by examining locally defined dependencies from a global perspective. An accompanying algorithm uses typicality to identify modes efficiently, bringing information from the broader dependency structure into what would otherwise be a locally driven decision.

The clustering procedure then uses graph-cut optimization with an improved path-based similarity to assemble the final groups. The paper includes theoretical analysis of its algorithm and evaluates TANGO on synthetic and extensive real-world datasets, reporting effectiveness and superiority in those experiments. Its contribution joins two stages: identifying representative density peaks through a global view and assigning data to final clusters through graph-based optimization.
summary.tldr: TANGO identifies density modes using globally informed typicality and forms clusters with path-based similarity and graph-cut optimization.

title: TANGO: Clustering with Typicality-Aware Nonlocal Mode-Seeking and Graph-Cut Optimization

abstract: How can we know whether new mechanistic interpretability methods achieve real improvements? In pursuit of lasting evaluation standards, we propose MIB, a Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark, with two tracks spanning four tasks and five models. MIB favors methods that precisely and concisely recover relevant causal pathways or causal variables in neural language models. The circuit localization track compares methods that locate the model components—and connections between them—most important for performing a task (e.g., attribution patching or information flow routes). The causal variable track compares methods that featurize a hidden vector, e.g., sparse autoencoders (SAE) or distributed alignment search (DAS), and align those features to a task-relevant causal variable. Using MIB, we find that attribution and mask optimization methods perform best on circuit localization. For causal variable localization, we find that the supervised DAS method performs best, while SAEs features are not better than neurons, i.e., non-featurized hidden vectors. These findings illustrate that MIB enables meaningful comparisons, and increases our confidence that there has been real progress in the field.

paragraphs: Mechanistic interpretability methods aim to identify how neural networks carry out tasks, but comparing their progress requires shared evaluation standards. MIB introduces a benchmark spanning four tasks and five models. It rewards explanations that recover relevant causal pathways or variables precisely and concisely.

The benchmark has two tracks. Circuit localization evaluates methods that identify important model components and their connections. Causal variable localization evaluates methods that turn hidden vectors into features and align those features with task-relevant causal variables. This separates finding where a computation happens from identifying the variables represented within that computation.

On MIB, attribution and mask optimization methods perform best at circuit localization. The supervised distributed alignment search method performs best at causal variable localization, while sparse autoencoder features do not outperform neurons in that track. These are findings within the benchmark’s tasks and models. They provide concrete comparisons among interpretability approaches and show how a shared evaluation can distinguish improvements in different aspects of causal explanation.
summary.tldr: MIB benchmarks causal circuit and variable localization, revealing distinct strengths among interpretability methods across four tasks and five models.

title: MIB: A Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark

abstract: Recent research has shown an increasing interest in utilizing pre-trained large language models (LLMs) for a variety of time series applications. However, there are three main challenges when using LLMs as foundational models for time series forecasting: (1) Cross-domain generalization. (2) Cross-modality alignment. (3) Error accumulation in autoregressive frameworks. To address these challenges, we proposed LangTime, a language-guided unified model for time series forecasting that incorporates cross-domain pre-training with reinforcement learning-based fine-tuning. Specifically, LangTime constructs Temporal Comprehension Prompts (TCPs), which include dataset-wise and channel-wise instructions, to facilitate domain adaptation and condense time series into a single token, enabling LLMs to understand better and align temporal data. To improve autoregressive forecasting, we introduce TimePPO, a reinforcement learning-based fine-tuning algorithm. TimePPO mitigates error accumulation by leveraging a multidimensional rewards function tailored for time series and a repeat-based value estimation strategy. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LangTime achieves state-of-the-art cross-domain forecasting performance, while TimePPO fine-tuning effectively enhances the stability and accuracy of autoregressive forecasting.

paragraphs: LangTime addresses three obstacles to using pretrained language models for time-series forecasting: transferring across domains, connecting numerical sequences with language representations, and preventing errors from accumulating during autoregressive prediction. The proposed system combines training across domains with reinforcement-learning fine-tuning, assigning different parts of the approach to these related challenges.

Its Temporal Comprehension Prompts contain instructions about the dataset and individual channels. Together with condensing a time series into a single token, these prompts help align temporal data with the language model and support domain adaptation. For autoregressive forecasting, the authors introduce TimePPO, which uses a multidimensional reward function designed for time series and a repeat-based strategy for estimating value.

The experiments report state-of-the-art cross-domain forecasting performance for LangTime. They also show that TimePPO improves the stability and accuracy of autoregressive forecasts while mitigating accumulated error. The approach matters because representing time-series inputs and controlling sequential prediction errors are distinct requirements; the paper brings both into a unified forecasting model.
summary.tldr: LangTime combines language-guided temporal representations with TimePPO fine-tuning to improve cross-domain forecasting and reduce autoregressive error accumulation.

title: LangTime: A Language-Guided Unified Model for Time Series Forecasting with Proximal Policy Optimization

abstract: Efficient sampling of unnormalized probability densities such as the Boltzmann distribution of molecular systems is a longstanding challenge. Next to conventional approaches like molecular dynamics or Markov chain Monte Carlo, variational approaches, such as training normalizing flows with the reverse Kullback-Leibler divergence, have been introduced. However, such methods are prone to mode collapse and often do not learn to sample the full configurational space. Here, we present temperature-annealed Boltzmann generators (TA-BG) to address this challenge. First, we demonstrate that training a normalizing flow with the reverse Kullback-Leibler divergence at high temperatures is possible without mode collapse. Furthermore, we introduce a reweighting-based training objective to anneal the distribution to lower target temperatures. We apply this methodology to three molecular systems of increasing complexity and, compared to the baseline, achieve better results in almost all metrics while requiring up to three times fewer target energy evaluations. For the largest system, our approach is the only method that accurately resolves the metastable states of the system.

paragraphs: Sampling molecular configurations from a Boltzmann distribution is difficult, and learned sampling methods can miss important parts of the configuration space. In particular, normalizing flows trained with reverse Kullback-Leibler divergence can suffer from mode collapse. This paper introduces temperature-annealed Boltzmann generators to improve coverage while controlling the cost of target energy evaluations.

The method first trains a normalizing flow at a high temperature, a setting where the authors demonstrate training without mode collapse. It then uses a reweighting-based objective to move the learned distribution toward a lower target temperature. This separates learning broad configurational coverage from adapting that coverage to the desired target distribution.

Tests on three molecular systems of increasing complexity show improvements over the baseline on almost all metrics, with up to three times fewer target energy evaluations. For the largest tested system, the proposed method is the only compared approach that accurately resolves its metastable states. The results support temperature annealing as an effective strategy for improving both sampling coverage and efficiency in these systems.
summary.tldr: Training at high temperature and reweighting toward lower temperatures improves molecular sampling coverage and reduces target energy evaluations.

title: Temperature-Annealed Boltzmann Generators

abstract: Static systems exhibit diverse structural properties, such as hierarchical, scale-free, and isotropic patterns, where different geometric spaces offer unique advantages. Methods combining multiple geometries have proven effective in capturing these characteristics. However, real-world systems often evolve dynamically, introducing significant challenges in modeling their temporal changes. To overcome this limitation, we propose a unified cross-geometric learning framework for dynamic systems, which synergistically integrates Euclidean and hyperbolic spaces, aligning embedding spaces with structural properties through fine-grained substructure modeling. Our framework further incorporates a temporal state aggregation mechanism and an evolution-driven optimization objective, enabling comprehensive and adaptive modeling of both nodal and relational dynamics over time. Extensive experiments on diverse real-world dynamic graph datasets highlight the superiority of our approach in capturing complex structural evolution, surpassing existing methods across multiple metrics.

paragraphs: Graphs can contain different kinds of structure, including hierarchies and more evenly distributed relationships. Different geometric spaces offer different advantages for representing these patterns. Combining geometries has helped with static graphs, but predicting relationships in evolving systems also requires representing how nodes and connections change over time.

The paper proposes a unified framework that combines Euclidean and hyperbolic spaces for dynamic graphs. It models fine-grained substructures so that the embedding geometry can align with the structure being represented. A temporal state aggregation mechanism brings together information over time, while an evolution-driven optimization objective directs learning toward changes in both nodes and relationships.

These components link structural representation with temporal modeling within one learning framework. Experiments on multiple real-world dynamic graph datasets report improvements over existing methods across several metrics. The findings support the value of adapting geometry to local graph structure while explicitly accounting for evolution, rather than relying only on representations developed for a fixed snapshot.
summary.tldr: A dynamic graph framework combines Euclidean and hyperbolic representations with temporal modeling to improve link prediction.

title: Analytical Construction on Geometric Architectures: Transitioning from Static to Temporal Link Prediction

abstract: The alignment of large language models (LLMs) with human preferences remains a key challenge. While post-training techniques like Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) have achieved notable success, they often experience computational inefficiencies and training instability. In this paper, we propose Feature-level constrained Preference Optimization (FPO), a novel method designed to simplify the alignment process while ensuring stability. FPO leverages pre-trained Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and introduces feature-level constraints, allowing for efficient, sparsity-enforced alignment. Our approach enjoys efficiency by using sparse features activated in a well-trained sparse autoencoder and the quality of sequential KL divergence by using the feature-level offline reference. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that FPO achieves an above 5% absolute improvement in win rate with much lower computational cost compared to state-of-the-art baselines, making it a promising solution for efficient and controllable LLM alignments.

paragraphs: Aligning a language model with human preferences can involve expensive or unstable training. Feature-level constrained Preference Optimization, or FPO, approaches this problem through a pretrained sparse autoencoder. Such an encoder provides a feature representation in which relatively few features are active, giving the alignment procedure a sparse space in which to impose constraints.

FPO uses those active features to make preference optimization more efficient. It also introduces an offline reference at the feature level, which the authors associate with retaining the quality of sequential KL divergence. The approach brings together sparse feature usage and reference-based constraints, with the goal of simplifying alignment while keeping training stable and model changes controllable.

On benchmark datasets, the authors report an absolute win-rate improvement of more than five percentage points over state-of-the-art baselines, alongside substantially lower computational cost. These are empirical results for the evaluated comparisons. The contribution is evidence that constraints built around a well-trained sparse autoencoder can make preference alignment both more effective and less computationally demanding.
summary.tldr: FPO uses pretrained sparse-autoencoder features to constrain preference optimization, reporting better alignment win rates at substantially lower computational cost.

title: Constrain Alignment with Sparse Autoencoders

abstract: This paper focuses on the design of spatial experiments to optimize the amount of information derived from the experimental data and enhance the accuracy of the resulting causal effect estimator. We propose a surrogate function for the mean squared error (MSE) of the estimator, which facilitates the use of classical graph cut algorithms to learn the optimal design. Our proposal offers three key advances: (1) it accommodates moderate to large spatial interference effects; (2) it adapts to different spatial covariance functions; (3) it is computationally efficient. Theoretical results and numerical experiments based on synthetic environments and a dispatch simulator that models a city-scale ridesharing market, further validate the effectiveness of our design. A python implementation of our method is available at https://github.com/Mamba413/CausalGraphCut.

paragraphs: Spatial experiments must account for relationships between locations when estimating causal effects. Treatment at one location can affect outcomes elsewhere, while outcomes at nearby locations can also be correlated. This paper studies how to design experiments around both features so that the resulting data provide more information and support more accurate causal estimates.

The proposed method constructs a surrogate for the estimator’s mean squared error, a measure of estimation accuracy. This substitute objective makes the design problem accessible to classical graph cut algorithms. The central contribution is therefore a connection between statistical design quality and an efficient computational procedure for choosing the design.

The approach accommodates moderate to large interference effects and adapts to different spatial covariance functions, which describe how outcomes vary together across space. The authors support the design with theoretical results and numerical experiments using synthetic environments and a city-scale ridesharing dispatch simulator. These findings support jointly considering interference and correlation when choosing spatial experimental designs.
summary.tldr: A graph cut approach designs spatial experiments around both treatment spillovers and correlated outcomes to improve causal estimation.

title: Balancing Interference and Correlation in Spatial Experimental Designs: A Causal Graph Cut Approach

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle with complex reasoning due to limited diversity and inefficient search. We propose Soft Reasoning, an embedding-based search framework that optimises the embedding of the first token to guide generation. It combines (1) embedding perturbation for controlled exploration and (2) Bayesian optimisation to refine embeddings via a verifier-guided objective, balancing exploration and exploitation. This approach improves reasoning accuracy and coherence while avoiding reliance on heuristic search. Experiments demonstrate superior correctness with minimal computation, making it a scalable, model-agnostic solution.

This makes the initial embedding the object of search, using changes in that representation to steer the solutions subsequently produced by the model.

Perturbations provide exploration, while a verifier-guided objective directs refinement toward promising embeddings. Bayesian optimization balances exploring alternatives with exploiting candidates that already look useful. The verifier therefore has a direct role in shaping the search, connecting candidate generation with feedback about solution quality.

The paper reports improvements in reasoning accuracy and coherence, with experiments showing superior correctness using minimal computation. It presents the approach as scalable and model-agnostic. The central contribution is a controlled search procedure in embedding space that uses explicit verification feedback, offering a way to improve generation without relying on heuristic search to navigate the solution space.
summary.tldr: Soft Reasoning uses verifier-guided Bayesian optimization of the first token’s embedding to improve reasoning search and correctness.

title: Soft Reasoning: Navigating Solution Spaces in Large Language Models through Controlled Embedding Exploration

abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences is commonly done via reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) or, more simply, via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). While DPO is stable and RL-free, it treats preferences as flat winner vs. loser signals and is sensitive to noisy or brittle preferences arising from fragile chains of thought. We propose TUR-DPO, a topology- and uncertainty-aware variant of DPO that rewards how answers are derived, not only what they say, by eliciting lightweight reasoning topologies and combining semantic faithfulness, utility, and topology quality into a calibrated uncertainty signal. A small learnable reward is factorized over these signals and incorporated into an uncertainty-weighted DPO objective that remains RL-free and relies only on a fixed or moving reference policy. Empirically, across open 7–8B models and benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, factual question answering, summarization, and helpful/harmless dialogue, TUR-DPO improves judge win-rates, faithfulness, and calibration relative to DPO while preserving training simplicity and avoiding online rollouts. We further observe consistent gains in multimodal and long-context settings, and show that TUR-DPO matches or exceeds PPO on reasoning-centric tasks while maintaining operational simplicity.

summary.tldr: TUR-DPO incorporates reasoning structure and uncertainty into preference training to improve alignment without online reinforcement-learning rollouts.

title: TUR-DPO: Topology- and Uncertainty-Aware Direct Preference Optimization

abstract: Evaluating survival models under censoring is inherently challenging, yet standard evaluation practices are often applied without explicitly assessing how censoring distorts metric reliability. Performing a large experimental study, we analyze and quantify how survival evaluation metrics are affected in fundamentally different ways by the censoring rate and the censoring mechanism. Using a controlled semi-synthetic framework, we vary both the censoring mechanism (administrative, independent, covariate-dependent) and the censoring rate, and compare standard evaluations based on censored data with oracle evaluations using fully observed event times. This controlled setting enables us to quantify distortions along two complementary axes: numerical bias and preservation of model ranking. Across datasets and metric families, we find that censoring induces systematic, mechanism-dependent distortions. Moderate numerical bias, if not properly addressed, can lead to unreliable model comparison as censoring increases. These findings reveal fundamental limitations of common benchmarking practices and call for more careful interpretation of survival evaluation under realistic censoring.

paragraphs: Survival models predict event timing, but evaluation becomes difficult when some event times are censored and therefore not fully observed. This paper studies how that missing information changes the reliability of evaluation metrics. It distinguishes the amount of censoring from the mechanism that determines which observations are censored.

The authors construct a controlled semi-synthetic study varying administrative, independent, and covariate-dependent censoring at different rates. They compare metrics calculated from censored data with oracle evaluations using fully observed event times. This allows them to measure two separate effects: distortion in the numerical scores and preservation of the ordering between competing models.

Across datasets and metric families, censoring produces systematic distortions that depend on its mechanism. Even moderate numerical bias can undermine model comparison as censoring increases if it is not properly addressed. The findings mean that apparently modest score errors do not necessarily imply dependable rankings. They motivate interpreting survival benchmarks with explicit attention to both the censoring process and the reliability of the resulting comparisons.
summary.tldr: Censoring can distort survival-evaluation scores and model rankings in ways that depend on both its rate and mechanism.

title: When Can We Trust Survival Model Evaluation ?

abstract: Automatic loop invariant generation remains a challenging problem in program verification, particularly for memory-manipulating programs where shape invariants are required to characterize heap-allocated structures and memory layouts. While existing approaches succeed on numerical invariants, they achieve limited accuracy on shape invariants. We hypothesize that this stems from the need to reason about memory state evolution—information that remains implicit in source code. To address this, we ground LLM reasoning in symbolic execution traces that explicitly capture such transitions. We propose Malice, a two-stage framework incorporating these traces: (1) guided multi-step reasoning that predicts invariants via chain-of-thought analysis of traces, and (2) agentic iterative refinement that corrects candidates through verification tool feedback. Evaluated on LIG-MM+, a benchmark featuring common operations on typical memory structures, Malice substantially outperforms existing approaches.

paragraphs: Loop invariants describe properties that remain true as a program repeats a loop, making them useful for verification. For programs that manipulate memory, these properties must often describe the shape of heap-allocated structures and their layout. Existing methods handle numerical relationships more successfully than these structural properties.

MALICE starts from the hypothesis that source code leaves memory-state evolution too implicit for reliable invariant generation. It gives a language model symbolic execution traces that explicitly expose those transitions. A first stage uses guided, multistep reasoning over the traces to propose invariants. A second stage iteratively corrects the candidates using feedback from verification tools.

The design connects two kinds of support: traces make the relevant behavior visible, and verification feedback helps refine proposed properties. On LIG-MM+, a benchmark containing common operations on typical memory structures, MALICE substantially outperforms existing approaches. The reported result supports grounding invariant generation in explicit memory transitions and checking the resulting candidates, rather than relying on source-code interpretation alone.
summary.tldr: MALICE combines symbolic memory traces with verification feedback to improve loop-invariant generation for memory-manipulating programs.

title: MALICE: Memory-aware Loop Invariants Generation on Symbolic Execution Traces

abstract: Accurate 6D pose estimation and tracking are core capabilities for physical AI systems, yet real-world deployment remains brittle and labor-intensive. Many pipelines rely on CAD models, manual masking, or per-object adaptation, and still fail under occlusion or fast motion without a principled way to recognize failure. We propose STORM, a unified framework for reference-conditioned 6D tracking that can operate from a single reference image, with minimal manual input and improved robustness. STORM combines: (i) Hierarchical Spatial Fusion Attention (HSFA), a task-driven reference-query fusion architecture that supports both single-reference and multi-reference conditioning and can optionally use vision-language semantic conditioning to resolve instance ambiguities; and (ii) a BCE-trained tracking verifier whose continuous compatibility logit is used as an energy-like score to detect drift and trigger automatic re-initialization. Experiments on LM-O and YCB-Video show that STORM improves annotation-free pose tracking accuracy over strong baselines and recovers reliably from severe occlusions and rapid viewpoint changes with minimal overhead.

paragraphs: Tracking an object’s position and orientation can become unreliable when it is occluded or moves rapidly. STORM provides a unified reference-conditioned tracking framework that can start from one image with minimal manual input and includes a mechanism for recognizing tracking failure.

It supports either one reference or multiple references and can optionally use vision-language semantic information to resolve ambiguity between object instances. This gives the tracking system several ways to condition its predictions on the object it should follow.

A separately trained tracking verifier produces a continuous compatibility score that acts like an energy signal. STORM uses that signal to detect drift and automatically restart tracking. On LM-O and YCB-Video, experiments show improved annotation-free pose tracking over strong baselines, with reliable recovery from severe occlusion and rapid viewpoint changes at minimal overhead. Recovery is therefore an explicit part of the tracking framework.
summary.tldr: STORM tracks object pose from a single reference image and uses a learned verifier to detect drift and trigger automatic recovery.

title: STORM: Segment, Track, and Object Re-Localization from a Single Image

abstract: Although Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have made remarkable progress, they still struggle with long-video understanding due to the massive memory footprint of KV Caches. Existing methods often resort to disjoint retrieval or attention-based reduction with a uniform layer-wise budget to achieve compression. However, these methods disrupt temporal continuity and ignore the varying information density across network layers. In this work, we reveal that memory allocation should mirror layer-wise semantic density, rather than adhering to a uniform budget. To this end, we introduce EAKV, a training-free entropy-driven adaptive KV compression framework that leverages attention entropy to adaptively allocate compression budgets, selectively preserving critical tokens while distilling redundant contexts into compact contextual anchors, thereby achieving granular memory allocation proportional to semantic density. Extensive experiments on various benchmarks demonstrate that EAKV surpasses existing methods across diverse model architectures and varying parameter scales, yielding improvements ranging from 0.6% to 6.5%.

paragraphs: Long videos create large key-value caches in multimodal language models, making memory a major obstacle to processing extended sequences. Existing compression approaches can break temporal continuity or assign the same memory budget to every layer. EAKV starts from the observation that layers differ in how much semantic information they contain.

The framework uses attention entropy to guide adaptive allocation of cache space without additional training. It preserves critical tokens and condenses redundant context into compact contextual anchors. This gives compression two roles: deciding where memory is most valuable and retaining a compact representation of information that would otherwise be discarded. The allocation is intended to track semantic density across layers.

Experiments across multiple benchmarks, architectures, and model sizes report improvements ranging from 0.6% to 6.5% over existing methods. These findings support adapting compression to the model’s internal information distribution. The contribution is a memory-allocation strategy that combines selective retention with contextual summarization, addressing both uneven layer requirements and the continuity needed for understanding long videos.
summary.tldr: EAKV uses attention entropy to allocate cache memory across layers while preserving important video tokens and compact contextual anchors.

title: EAKV: An Entropy-Driven Adaptive KV Compression Framework for Long Video Understanding

abstract: Robotic policies deployed in real-world environments often encounter post-training faults, where retraining, exploration, or system identification are impractical. We introduce an inference-time, cerebellar-inspired residual control framework that augments a frozen reinforcement learning policy with online corrective actions, enabling fault recovery without modifying base policy parameters. The framework instantiates core cerebellar principles, including high-dimensional pattern separation via fixed feature expansion, parallel microzone-style residual pathways, and local error-driven plasticity with excitatory and inhibitory eligibility traces operating at distinct time scales. These mechanisms enable fast, localized correction under post-training disturbances while avoiding destabilizing global policy updates. A conservative, performance-driven meta-adaptation regulates residual gain and plasticity, preserving nominal behavior and suppressing unnecessary intervention. Experiments on MuJoCo benchmarks under actuator, dynamic, and environmental perturbations show improvements of up to $+66$% on $\texttt{HalfCheetah-v5}$ and $+53$% on $\texttt{Humanoid-v5}$ under moderate faults, with graceful degradation under severe shifts and complementary robustness from consolidating persistent residual corrections into policy parameters.

This paper adds an adaptive corrective controller to a frozen reinforcement learning policy. The authors also find complementary robustness from consolidating persistent corrections into policy parameters, connecting immediate adaptation with longer-term changes to the controller.
summary.tldr: A cerebellum-inspired corrective controller helps frozen robot policies recover from faults through localized online adaptation.

title: Cerebellar-Inspired Residual Control for Fault Recovery: From Inference-Time Adaptation to Structural Consolidation

abstract: Serving Large Language Models (LLMs) can benefit immensely from parallelizing both the model and input requests across multiple devices, but incoming workloads exhibit substantial spatial and temporal heterogeneity. Spatially, workloads comprise heterogeneous requests with varying compute and memory demands. Temporally, workload composition varies over time. Nevertheless, existing systems typically assume spatially uniform and temporally stable workloads, employing a homogeneous, static model deployment. This mismatch between the assumption and real-world spatial-temporal heterogeneity results in suboptimal performance. We present OServe, an LLM serving system with heterogeneous and flexible model deployment that addresses both spatial and temporal heterogeneity. First, OServe introduces a novel workload-aware scheduling algorithm that optimizes heterogeneous model deployments according to real-time workload characteristics. Second, OServe proposes an efficient workload-adaptive switching method that migrates model deployments in response to predicted workload changes. Experiments on real-world traces show that OServe improves performance by up to 2$\times$ (average: 1.5$\times$) compared to state-of-the-art serving systems.

paragraphs: OServe addresses two kinds of variation in language-model serving workloads. The paper proposes heterogeneous, flexible deployments to respond to both sources of variation.

The system has two complementary mechanisms. A workload-aware scheduling algorithm chooses heterogeneous model deployments using current workload characteristics. A workload-adaptive switching method then migrates deployments in response to predicted changes. The first determines an appropriate arrangement for present demand; the second provides a way to move between arrangements as the workload evolves.

These findings support treating deployment configuration as a workload-dependent decision. The benefit comes from coordinating placement and adaptation with demand across devices and over time, with the reported maximum and average describing the evaluated traces rather than a fixed improvement for every request.
summary.tldr: OServe adapts heterogeneous model deployments to current and predicted workloads, reporting an average 1.5× serving performance improvement.

title: OServe: Accelerating LLM Serving via Spatial-Temporal Workload Orchestration

abstract: Machine learning models are increasingly trained or fine-tuned on synthetic data. Recursively training on such data has been observed to significantly degrade performance in a wide range of tasks, often characterized by a progressive drift away from the target distribution. In this work, we theoretically analyze this phenomenon in the setting of score-based diffusion models. For a realistic pipeline where each training round uses a combination of synthetic data and fresh samples from the target distribution, we obtain upper and lower bounds on the accumulated divergence between the generated and target distributions. Notably, to the best of our knowledge, this is the first lower bound on the divergence between the learned and target distributions, even for standard diffusion models. Our results allow us to characterize different regimes of drift, depending on the score estimation error and the proportion of fresh data used in each generation. In a certain regime, the accumulated divergence after several retraining rounds can be expressed as a discounted sum of score estimation errors made at each generation. We also provide empirical results on synthetic data and images to illustrate the theory.

paragraphs: Training repeatedly on model-generated data can cause the learned distribution to drift away from the original target. This paper analyzes that process for score-based diffusion models in a pipeline where every training round mixes synthetic examples with fresh samples from the target distribution.

The authors derive both upper and lower bounds on the accumulated divergence. Upper bounds constrain how large the discrepancy can become, while lower bounds characterize discrepancy that the analysis cannot rule away. They describe their lower bound as, to their knowledge, the first for the difference between learned and target distributions even in standard diffusion models.

The results distinguish drift regimes according to score-estimation error and the share of fresh data introduced each round. In one regime, divergence after repeated training takes the form of a discounted sum of errors from individual generations. This gives a precise way to describe how errors across rounds combine, rather than treating recursive training as uniformly harmful. Experiments on synthetic data and images illustrate the theory and its account of error propagation.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds diffusion-model drift under recursive training and shows how score errors and fresh-data proportions shape its accumulation.

title: Quantifying Error Propagation and Model Collapse in Diffusion Models

abstract: Compositional explanations are a family of methods that aim to describe the spatial alignment between neurons’ receptive field activations and concepts through logical rules, typically computed via a search over all possible concept combinations. Since computing the spatial alignment over the entire state space is computationally infeasible, the literature commonly adopts assumptions related to the structure of the combinations and beam search to restrict the state space. However, beam search cannot provide any theoretical guarantees of optimality, and it remains unclear how close current explanations are to the true optimum. In this theoretical paper, we address this gap by introducing the first framework for computing guaranteed optimal compositional explanations over the entire state space spanned by the adopted assumptions. Specifically, we propose: (i) a decomposition that identifies the factors influencing the spatial alignment, (ii) a heuristic to estimate the alignment at any stage of the search, and (iii) the first algorithm that can compute optimal compositional explanations in a time comparable to exhaustive beam search. Using this framework, we demonstrate that 10-40% of explanations previously obtained with beam search are suboptimal when overlapping concepts are involved. Finally, we evaluate a beam-search variant guided by our proposed decomposition and heuristic, showing that it matches or improves runtime over prior methods while offering greater flexibility in hyperparameters and computational resources.

paragraphs: Compositional explanations describe where a neuron activates using logical combinations of concepts. Finding the combination that best matches its spatial activation pattern requires searching a potentially enormous space. Existing methods commonly restrict that space through structural assumptions and beam search, which cannot guarantee that the best explanation has been found.

This paper introduces a framework that guarantees optimal explanations within the full search space defined by the adopted assumptions. It decomposes the factors affecting spatial alignment and supplies a heuristic for estimating alignment during search. Together, these support an optimal-search algorithm whose runtime is reported as comparable to exhaustive beam search.

It matches or improves earlier runtimes while permitting more flexible choices of hyperparameters and computational resources.
summary.tldr: The framework guarantees optimal neuron explanations within its assumed search space and exposes suboptimal results from beam search.

title: Guaranteed Optimal Compositional Explanations for Neurons

abstract: Mean Field Games (MFGs) provide a powerful framework for modeling the collective behavior of large populations of interacting agents. In this paper, we address the problem of Imitation Learning (IL) in MFGs subject to common noise, where the population distribution evolves stochastically. This stochasticity compels agents to adopt population-aware policies to respond to aggregate shocks. We formulate two distinct learning objectives: recovering a Nash equilibrium and maximizing performance against an expert population. We investigate two imitation proxies: Behavioral Cloning (BC) and Adversarial (ADV) divergence. We then establish finite-sample error bounds showing that minimizing these proxies effectively controls both the policy’s exploitability and its performance gap relative to the expert. Furthermore, we propose a numerical framework using generalized Fictitious Play and Deep Learning to compute expert population-aware policies. Through experiments on three environments we demonstrate that standard population-unaware policies fail to capture the equilibrium dynamics. Our results highlight that learning population-aware policies is crucial to avoid being misled by the randomness inherent in common noise.

paragraphs: Mean-field games model interactions within large populations of agents. When common noise affects the population, its distribution evolves randomly, so agents must respond to aggregate changes. This paper studies how to imitate expert behavior in that setting using policies that account for the population’s state.

The authors distinguish two learning goals: recovering a Nash equilibrium and performing well against an expert population. They analyze behavioral cloning and adversarial divergence as practical imitation objectives. Finite-sample error bounds show that minimizing these objectives controls both exploitability and the performance gap relative to the expert, connecting imitation quality to the two game-theoretic goals.

The paper also develops a numerical framework combining generalized Fictitious Play with deep learning to compute expert population-aware policies. The findings explain why shared randomness matters for imitation: responding appropriately requires information about how the population evolves, alongside the behavior of an individual agent.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes imitation-learning bounds and methods for policies that respond to population changes under common noise.

title: Population-Aware Imitation Learning in Mean-field Games with Common Noise

abstract: Large kernel convolutions offer a scalable alternative to vision transformers for high-resolution 3D volumetric analysis, yet naively increasing kernel size often leads to optimization instability. Motivated by the spatial bias inherent in effective receptive fields (ERFs), we theoretically demonstrate that structurally re-parameterized blocks induce spatially varying learning rates that are crucial for convergence. Leveraging this insight, we introduce Rep3D, a framework that employs a lightweight modulation network to generate receptive-biased scaling masks, adaptively re-weighting kernel updates within a plain encoder architecture. This approach unifies spatial inductive bias with optimization-aware learning, avoiding the complexity of multi-branch designs while ensuring robust local-to-global convergence. Extensive evaluations on five 3D segmentation benchmarks demonstrate that Rep3D consistently outperforms state-of-the-art transformer and fixed-prior baselines. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/leeh43/Rep3D.

paragraphs: Large convolution kernels can capture broad spatial context in high-resolution three-dimensional volumes, offering an alternative to vision transformers. Simply enlarging the kernels, however, can destabilize optimization. This paper investigates that problem through effective receptive fields, focusing on how different spatial positions influence learning rather than treating every kernel location identically.

The theoretical analysis shows that structurally reparameterized blocks induce spatially varying learning rates that are crucial for convergence. Rep3D turns this insight into a lightweight modulation network that generates scaling masks for kernel updates. These masks adaptively reweight learning across spatial positions according to receptive-field bias, while the main model retains a plain encoder architecture.

The framework aims to support stable learning from local to global structure without the complexity of multi-branch designs. Across five three-dimensional segmentation benchmarks, Rep3D consistently outperforms the compared state-of-the-art transformer and fixed-prior baselines. The findings indicate that adapting where and how strongly a large kernel learns can improve its usefulness for volumetric segmentation.
summary.tldr: Rep3D adaptively scales updates across large 3D convolution kernels, improving optimization and segmentation performance on five benchmarks.

title: Spatially-Adaptive Gradient Re-parameterization for 3D Large Kernel Optimization

abstract: Video generation models offer a promising imagination mechanism for robot manipulation by predicting long-horizon future observations, but effectively exploiting these imagined futures for action execution remains challenging. Existing approaches either condition policies on predicted frames or directly decode generated videos into actions, both suffering from a mismatch between visual realism and control relevance. As a result, predicted observations emphasize perceptual fidelity rather than action-centric causes of state transitions, leading to indirect and unstable control. To address this gap, we propose MoLA (Mixture of Latent Actions), a control-oriented interface that transforms imagined future videos into executable representations. Instead of passing predicted frames directly to the policy, MoLA leverages multiple pretrained inverse dynamics models to infer a mixture of latent actions implied by generated visual transitions. These modality-aware inverse dynamics models capture complementary semantic, depth, and flow cues, providing a structured and physically grounded action representation that bridges video imagination and policy execution. We evaluate our approach on simulated benchmarks (LIBERO, CALVIN, and LIBERO-Plus) and real-world robot manipulation tasks, achieving consistent gains in task success, temporal consistency, and generalization.

paragraphs: Video models can imagine future observations for a robot, but visually convincing predictions do not automatically provide useful control instructions. The paper identifies a mismatch between perceptual realism and the action-related causes of state changes. Passing predicted frames into a policy or directly decoding videos into actions can consequently produce indirect, unstable control.

MoLA introduces an intermediate representation focused on actions. Multiple pretrained inverse dynamics models examine transitions in the imagined video and infer the latent actions those transitions imply. These models use complementary semantic, depth, and flow cues. Their outputs form a mixture that connects the predicted visual changes to information useful for executing a policy.

This design gives imagined futures a structured interface to robot control, rather than requiring the policy to recover all relevant action information from predicted images. Evaluations on LIBERO, CALVIN, LIBERO-Plus, and real-world manipulation tasks report consistent gains in task success, temporal consistency, and generalization. The results support translating video predictions into action-oriented representations before using them for execution.
summary.tldr: MoLA converts imagined robot videos into complementary latent action representations that improve manipulation performance.

title: From Imagined Futures to Executable Actions: Mixture of Latent Actions for Robot Manipulation

abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative for text generation, distinguished by their native support for parallel decoding. In practice, block inference is crucial for avoiding order misalignment in global bidirectional decoding and improving output quality. However, the widely-used fixed, predefined block (naive) schedule is agnostic to semantic difficulty, making it a suboptimal strategy for both quality and efficiency: it can force premature commitments to uncertain positions while delaying easy positions near block boundaries. In this work, we analyze the limitations of naive block scheduling and disclose the importance of dynamically adapting the schedule to semantic difficulty for reliable and efficient inference. Motivated by this, we propose Dynamic Sliding Block (DSB), a training-free block scheduling method that uses a sliding block with a dynamic size to overcome the rigidity of the naive block. To further improve efficiency, we introduce DSB Cache, a training-free KV-cache mechanism tailored to DSB. Extensive experiments across multiple models and benchmarks demonstrate that DSB, together with DSB Cache, consistently improves both generation quality and inference efficiency for dLLMs. Code is released at https://github.com/lizhuo-luo/DSB.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models can generate multiple text positions in parallel, but deciding which positions to process together affects both speed and quality. Block-based inference helps avoid ordering problems associated with unrestricted bidirectional decoding. A fixed block schedule, however, treats semantically difficult and easy positions alike, sometimes committing uncertain text too early while making easier positions wait at block boundaries.

Dynamic Sliding Block changes this scheduling decision without retraining the model. It uses a sliding block whose size can vary, allowing the decoding schedule to adapt to semantic difficulty. The contribution concerns how inference is organized: the scheduler gains flexibility to process positions according to their difficulty instead of following a rigid partition established in advance.

The authors also introduce DSB Cache, a training-free key–value caching mechanism designed for the dynamic schedule. Experiments across multiple models and benchmarks find that DSB together with its cache consistently improves generation quality and inference efficiency. These results support scheduling as a practical source of improvement, showing that the organization of parallel decoding can matter alongside the underlying model’s capabilities.
summary.tldr: DSB adapts decoding blocks to semantic difficulty and adds compatible caching to improve diffusion language models without retraining.

title: DSB: Dynamic Sliding Block Scheduling for Diffusion LLMs

abstract: We study online inverse linear optimization, also known as contextual recommendation, where a learner sequentially infers an agent’s hidden objective vector from observed optimal actions over feasible sets that change over time. The learner aims to recommend actions that perform well under the agent’s true objective, and the performance is measured by the regret, defined as the cumulative gap between the agent’s optimal values and those achieved by the learner’s recommended actions. Prior work has established a regret bound of $O(d\log T)$, as well as a finite but exponentially large bound of $\exp(O(d\log d))$, where $d$ is the dimension of the optimization problem and $T$ is the time horizon, while a regret lower bound of $\Omega(d)$ is known (Gollapudi et al. 2021; Sakaue et al. 2025). Whether a finite regret bound polynomial in $d$ is achievable or not has remained an open question. We partially resolve this by showing that when the feasible sets are M-convex—a broad class that includes matroids—a finite regret bound of $O(d\log d)$ is possible. We achieve this by combining a structural characterization of optimal solutions on M-convex sets with a geometric volume argument. Moreover, we extend our approach to adversarially corrupted feedback in up to $C$ rounds. We obtain a regret bound of $O((C+1)d\log d)$ without prior knowledge of $C$, by monitoring directed graphs induced by the observed feedback to detect corruptions adaptively.

paragraphs: Online inverse linear optimization learns someone's hidden objective by observing their optimal choices as available options change. The learner recommends actions and accumulates regret whenever those recommendations achieve less objective value than the person's optimal action. A central question is whether total regret can remain bounded independently of the number of rounds without an exponential dependence on problem dimension.

The paper partially resolves this question for M-convex feasible sets, a structured class that includes matroids. It proves an O(d log d) total-regret bound, where d is the optimization dimension. The argument combines a characterization of optimal solutions on these sets with geometric reasoning about volume.

The authors also allow adversarially corrupted feedback in up to C rounds. By monitoring directed graphs constructed from feedback, their method detects corruptions adaptively and achieves O((C+1)d log d) regret without knowing C beforehand. The contribution is a time-independent, near-linear dimensional guarantee within the stated structured setting, together with a controlled increase in regret when observations are corrupted.
summary.tldr: For M-convex action sets, the paper proves finite O(d log d) regret and extends it to unknown amounts of corrupted feedback.

title: Finite and Corruption-Robust Regret Bounds in Online Inverse Linear Optimization under M-Convex Action Sets

abstract: Understanding complex interactions between brain regions is critical for early neurodegenerative disease classification such as Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) and Parkinson’s Disease (PD). While graph-based models are widely used to analyze brain networks, most existing approaches primarily focus on pairwise interactions between directly connected nodes, limiting their ability to capture higher-order dependencies across multiple regions. Although hypergraph-based methods have been proposed to model higher-order relations, many rely on predefined hyperedges or restrict learning to hyperedge weights, reducing flexibility and limiting their capacity to capture multi-resolution structural patterns. In this regard, we introduce an adaptive multi-scale hyperedge learning framework, i.e., MuHL, which constructs hierarchical node features and dynamically learns high-order interaction through continuous hyper-edge construction over multi-resolution graph signals. Extensive experiments on multiple brain network benchmarks demonstrate that MuHL consistently improves disease classification performance across different stages, and further identifies key regions of interest (ROIs) and their group-wise interactions from the learned hyperedges that are associated with disease progression, highlighting its potential as a powerful tool for brain network analysis with neurodegenerative disorders.

paragraphs: Brain-network analysis often models connections between pairs of regions, but disease-related patterns can involve groups of regions interacting together. Hypergraphs can represent such group relationships through hyperedges. Existing approaches, however, often fix these groups in advance or learn only their weights, limiting their ability to adapt to structures at different resolutions.

MuHL introduces adaptive learning of hyperedges across multiple scales. It constructs hierarchical node features and uses graph signals at several resolutions to learn higher-order interactions through continuous hyperedge construction. The important change is that the model learns the group structure itself, giving it greater flexibility than methods restricted to adjusting predefined connections.

Experiments across multiple brain-network benchmarks show consistent improvements in disease classification at different stages. The learned hyperedges also identify key brain regions and group interactions associated with disease progression. These findings connect predictive performance with interpretable patterns of connectivity. The reported associations support MuHL’s potential for analyzing neurodegenerative disorders, while the classification results establish its usefulness in the evaluated benchmark settings.
summary.tldr: MuHL learns groups of interacting brain regions at multiple scales, improving disease classification and revealing progression-associated connectivity patterns.

title: Learning Multi-Scale Hypergraph for High-Order Brain Connectivity Analysis

abstract: This paper explores unsupervised disentangled representation learning from a functional perspective. We define latent concepts as factors that influence observations through locally orthogonal directions, formalized as an orthogonality constraint on the Jacobian of the generative mapping. We prove that this condition yields identifiability of general nonlinear generative models, without requiring statistical independence or causal assumptions, provided the latent domain admits all combinations of factor values. Experiments with orthogonality-regularized normalizing flows empirically confirm the theory, demonstrate reliable recovery of ground-truth factors, and shed light on the success of VAEs. These findings challenge the prevailing impossibility claims for unsupervised disentanglement and provide a principled alternative foundation.

paragraphs: Unsupervised disentanglement seeks latent factors that correspond to distinct concepts without labeled examples of those factors. This paper defines concepts through how they affect observations: locally, different factors should change observations in orthogonal directions. That functional definition shifts attention toward the geometry of the generative mapping and the effects of changing each latent variable.

The authors express this requirement as an orthogonality constraint on the mapping’s Jacobian. They prove that it yields identifiability for general nonlinear generative models without requiring statistical independence or causal assumptions. The result depends on the latent domain admitting every combination of factor values, so the conclusion is tied to both the geometric condition and the domain assumption.

Experiments with orthogonality-regularized normalizing flows support the theory and show reliable recovery of ground-truth factors. The analysis also offers insight into the success of variational autoencoders. The contribution provides an alternative foundation for identifiable unsupervised representations, challenging broad impossibility claims by establishing what becomes possible under these specific structural conditions.
summary.tldr: Local orthogonality makes nonlinear latent factors identifiable when the latent domain includes all factor combinations, without independence or causal assumptions.

title: Unsupervised Disentanglement Without Compromises : How Functional Orthogonality Enforces Identifiability

abstract: We introduce ideal attribution mechanisms, a formal abstraction for reasoning about attribution decisions over strings. At the core of this abstraction lies the ledger, an append-only log of the prompt-response interaction history between a model and its user. Each mechanism produces deterministic decisions based on the ledger and an explicit selection criterion, making it well-suited to serve as a ground truth for attribution. We frame the design goal of watermarking schemes as faithful representation of ideal attribution mechanisms. This novel perspective brings conceptual clarity, replacing piecemeal probabilistic statements with a unified language for stating the guarantees of each scheme. It also enables precise reasoning about desiderata for future watermarking schemes, even when no current construction achieves them, as the ideal functionalities are specified first. In this way, the framework provides a roadmap that clarifies which guarantees are attainable in an idealized setting and worth pursuing in practice.

paragraphs: This paper develops a formal language for deciding when a string should be attributed to a language model. Its central object is a ledger: an append-only record of interactions between the model and its user. An ideal attribution mechanism combines this history with an explicit selection criterion to produce deterministic attribution decisions.

The ledger and criterion make the intended attribution rule precise enough to serve as ground truth. The authors then frame watermarking as the problem of faithfully representing that ideal mechanism. This shifts the design discussion toward a clearly specified decision rule, giving different watermarking guarantees a common language rather than treating them as separate probabilistic claims.

The framework also allows researchers to describe desired guarantees before a practical watermarking construction exists. That distinction is central: specifying an ideal functionality does not itself establish that a current implementation achieves it. The contribution is a conceptual roadmap for reasoning about attribution guarantees, clarifying what is attainable in an idealized setting and what may be worth pursuing in practical systems.
summary.tldr: The paper defines ideal attribution rules from interaction histories and frames watermarking as faithfully implementing those rules.

title: Ideal Attribution and Faithful Watermarks for Language Models

abstract: We study two recurring phenomena in Transformer language models: massive activations, in which a small number of tokens exhibit extreme outliers in a few channels, and attention sinks, in which certain tokens attract disproportionate attention mass regardless of semantic relevance. Prior work observes that these phenomena frequently co-occur and often involve the same tokens, but their functional roles and causal relationships remain unclear. Through systematic experiments, we show that the co-occurrence is largely an architectural artifact of modern Transformer design, and that the two phenomena serve related but distinct functions. Massive activations operate globally: they induce near-constant hidden representations that persist across layers, effectively functioning as implicit parameters of the model. Attention sinks operate locally: they modulate attention outputs across heads and bias individual heads toward short-range dependencies. We identify the pre-norm configuration as the key choice that enables the co-occurrence and show that ablating it causes the two phenomena to decouple.

paragraphs: Transformer language models sometimes produce unusually large internal values for a few tokens and channels. They also develop attention sinks: tokens that receive substantial attention regardless of their semantic relevance. Because the same tokens often exhibit both behaviors, it has been unclear whether the phenomena share a function or cause one another.

Through systematic experiments, this paper finds related but distinct roles. Massive activations create nearly constant hidden representations that persist across layers, effectively acting as implicit model parameters. Attention sinks have a more local effect: they influence individual attention heads' outputs and bias those heads toward nearby dependencies. The distinction separates a persistent influence on internal representations from adjustments within attention computations.

The authors attribute much of the observed overlap to architectural design, identifying the pre-norm configuration as the key enabling choice. Removing that configuration causes the two behaviors to separate in their experiments. This changes how their co-occurrence should be interpreted: appearing together does not mean they perform the same job, and their relationship depends substantially on the surrounding architecture.
summary.tldr: Massive activations and attention sinks serve distinct global and local functions, with their frequent overlap largely explained by pre-norm Transformer design.

title: Anatomy of Massive Activations and Attention Sinks

abstract: Large-scale document retrieval (search) is key in many modern industrial AI pipelines to ground models with relevant contextual information. Increasingly, Visual Document Retrieval (VDR) models, which directly embed images of document pages, are used as an alternative to text-only retrievers. While these models are historically repurposed generative VLMs fine-tuned for embedding tasks, we revisit this design choice in this paper and systematically develop strong VDR models from the ground up. Through controlled experiments, we isolate the impact of key training factors such as attention masking, multi-modal data regimes, and contrastive objectives at all phases of training. Our findings confirm current VDR performance is constrained by generative modeling, especially in multi-vector settings. Building on these insights, we train ModernVBERT, a 250M-parameter vision-language encoder that outperforms recent models up to 10 times its size when fine-tuned on document retrieval tasks. Thanks to its compact design, ModernVBERT enables efficient retrieval inference on CPU hardware, while maintaining competitive performance. Models, code and data are available at https://huggingface.co/ModernVBERT.

paragraphs: Visual document retrieval searches using representations of document-page images, supplying relevant context to downstream AI systems. Many existing retrievers begin as large generative vision-language models and are subsequently adapted to produce embeddings. This paper revisits that starting point and develops a smaller model specifically around the requirements of retrieval.

The authors run controlled experiments on attention masking, multimodal training data, and contrastive objectives across training stages. Their findings indicate that generative modeling constrains retrieval performance, particularly when a page is represented by multiple vectors. These experiments guide ModernVBERT, a vision-language encoder with 250 million parameters, rather than a retriever built by repurposing a large generative model.

When fine-tuned for document retrieval, ModernVBERT outperforms recent models up to ten times its size. Its compact architecture also supports efficient retrieval inference on CPUs while retaining competitive performance. The results connect training design to deployment practicality: choosing an architecture and objectives suited to embeddings can yield strong search quality without requiring the parameter count of the larger models compared.
summary.tldr: ModernVBERT is a 250-million-parameter visual document encoder that outperforms some retrievers up to ten times larger.

title: ModernVBERT: Towards Smaller Visual Document Retrievers

abstract: Current state-of-the-art segmentation models encode entire images before focusing on specific objects. This wastes computational resources. We introduce FLIP (Fovea-Like Input Patching), a parameter-efficient vision model that realizes object segmentation through biologically-inspired top-down attention. FLIP selectively samples multi-resolution patches centered on objects of interest from the input. As a result, it allocates high-resolution processing to object centers while maintaining coarser peripheral context. This off-grid, scale-invariant design enables FLIP to outperform META’s Segment Anything models (SAM, SAM2 and fast variants) by large margins: With more than 440 $ \times$ fewer parameters, FLIP-Tiny (0.51M parameters) reaches a mean IoU of 79.90% while SAM2-L reaches 75.87% IoU (224.45M parameters). FLIP-Large even achieves 83.26% mean IoU (96.6M parameters), still running about $2 \times$ faster than SAM2-L. We evaluate on six benchmarks in total. In five established benchmarks (Hypersim, KITTI-360, OpenImages, COCO, LVIS) FLIP consistently outperforms SAM and various variants of it. In our novel ObjaScale dataset, which stress-tests scale invariance with objects ranging from 0.0001% up to 25% of the image area, we show that FLIP segments even very small objects accurately, where existing models fail severely. FLIP opens new possibilities for real-time, object-centric vision and offers much higher energy efficiency. We believe that FLIP can act as a powerful foundation model, as it is very well-suited to track objects over time, for example, when being integrated into slot-based scene segmentation architectures.

paragraphs: Many segmentation systems process an entire image before concentrating on the object of interest. FLIP moves that focus to the input stage. It samples patches at multiple resolutions around a target object, assigning detailed processing to its center while preserving a coarser view of the surrounding scene.

This fovea-inspired design uses patches outside a fixed grid and is designed to handle changes in object scale. The authors evaluate it on five established benchmarks and introduce ObjaScale to test objects spanning an especially wide range of image areas. On that dataset, they report accurate segmentation of very small objects that existing models struggle to handle.

summary.tldr: FLIP concentrates multiresolution image processing around target objects, achieving strong segmentation accuracy with substantially smaller models.

title: Looking Locally: Object-Centric Vision Transformers as Foundation Models for Efficient Segmentation

abstract: Video anomaly detection (VAD) systems often prioritize accuracy while overlooking privacy concerns, limiting their suitability for real-world deployment. We propose the Orthogonal Projection Layer (OPL), a lightweight module that removes task-irrelevant variations to produce representations focused on anomaly-relevant cues. To address privacy risks in human-centered scenarios, we introduce Guided OPL (G-OPL), which suppresses facial attributes using weak supervision from face-presence signals while preserving non-identifying features such as pose and motion. A cosine alignment objective enforces consistent capture and removal of facial information without identity labels or adversarial training. We further present a privacy-aware evaluation framework that jointly assesses detection performance and privacy preservation, and enables analysis of how sensitive information is filtered. Experiments show that embedding privacy constraints into model design reduces sensitive information while maintaining or improving detection accuracy, supporting projection-based architectures as a principled approach for privacy-aware VAD.
originalAbstract: Video anomaly detection (VAD) systems often prioritize accuracy while overlooking privacy concerns, limiting their suitability for real-world deployment. We propose the Orthogonal Projection Layer (OPL), a lightweight module that removes task-irrelevant variations to produce representations focused on anomaly-relevant cues. To address privacy risks in human-centered scenarios, we introduce Guided OPL (G-OPL), which suppresses facial attributes using weak supervision from face-presence signals while preserving non-identifying features such as pose and motion. A cosine alignment objective enforces consistent capture and removal of facial information without identity labels or adversarial training. We further present a privacy-aware evaluation framework that jointly assesses detection performance and privacy preservation, and enables analysis of how sensitive information is filtered. Experiments show that embedding privacy constraints into model design reduces sensitive information while maintaining or improving detection accuracy, supporting projection-based architectures as a principled approach for privacy-aware VAD.

paragraphs: Video anomaly detectors need information about unusual events, but their internal representations can also retain sensitive details about people. This paper introduces an Orthogonal Projection Layer that removes task-irrelevant variation and concentrates representations on anomaly-related cues. Its goal is to make privacy considerations part of the representation design.

For scenes involving people, Guided OPL specifically suppresses facial attributes while preserving non-identifying features such as pose and motion. It uses weak supervision indicating whether a face is present, rather than identity labels. A cosine alignment objective encourages consistent identification and removal of facial information without requiring adversarial training.

The authors also propose an evaluation framework that measures detection performance alongside privacy preservation and examines how sensitive information is filtered. Experiments show reductions in sensitive information while detection accuracy is maintained or improved. These results support projection-based representations as a practical privacy-aware design for anomaly detection. The stated outcome is reduced sensitive information, rather than a guarantee that all identifying information has been eliminated.
summary.tldr: Guided orthogonal projection suppresses facial information in video representations while maintaining or improving anomaly-detection accuracy in experiments.

title: Privacy-Aware Video Anomaly Detection through Orthogonal Subspace Projection

abstract: Diffusion models have achieved state-of-the-art performance in image generation tasks. However, training powerful diffusion models remains time-consuming, which limits their practical deployment. In this paper, we revisit the learning dynamics of diffusion models through the lens of spectral bias, a phenomenon in which deep neural networks prioritize learning low-frequency modes. Through an empirical analysis of diffusion training, we observe that diffusion models exhibit a dual spectral bias. First, over training iterations, they fit low-frequency components earlier than high-frequency details. Second, along the diffusion timesteps, early denoising steps mainly reconstruct coarse low-frequency content, while high-frequency details emerge in later steps. Motivated by this observation, we propose Frequency-aware Patch Selection (FaPS), a general and fast training method for diffusion models that can be applied to both UNet and DiT backbones. Specifically, FaPS introduces a frequency-aware gating that adaptively selects image patches based on their frequency information and focuses computation only on the selected patches. Since the selection decisions are discrete and thus non-differentiable, we model the gating as a stochastic policy network and optimize it end-to-end using a policy gradient method. Our experiments demonstrate that FaPS achieves up to $\mathbf{3}\times$ faster training while maintaining comparable or superior generation quality, and improves the performance of diffusion models in limited-data settings.

paragraphs: Diffusion training spends substantial computation learning both broad image structure and fine detail. This paper observes two related learning patterns: low-frequency components are learned earlier during training, and coarse structure emerges earlier along the denoising process. Higher-frequency detail develops later in both senses. The authors use these observations to guide where training computation is spent.

Frequency-aware Patch Selection, or FaPS, introduces a gate that chooses image patches according to their frequency information. Computation focuses on the selected patches, adapting the work to the image content. Because selecting or skipping a patch is a discrete decision, the gate is modeled as a stochastic policy and trained end-to-end through policy gradients.

The method applies to both UNet and diffusion Transformer backbones. Experiments report training speedups of up to three times while preserving comparable or better generation quality, as well as improved performance when training data are limited. The contribution links an observed learning tendency to an adaptive computation mechanism, showing that selective processing can accelerate diffusion training without a corresponding quality drop in the reported evaluations.
summary.tldr: FaPS selects image patches by frequency content to achieve up to threefold faster diffusion training with comparable or better generation quality.

title: FaPS: A General and Fast Training Method for Diffusion Models

abstract: One of the most pressing challenges in artificial intelligence is to make models more transparent to their users. Recently, explainable artificial intelligence has come up with numerous methods to tackle this challenge. A promising avenue is to use concept-based explanations, that is, high-level concepts instead of plain feature importance scores. Among this class of methods, Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs, Kim et al., 2018) stand out as one of the main protagonists. One interesting aspect of CAVs is that their computation requires sampling random examples from the train set. Therefore, the actual vectors obtained may vary depending on the randomness of this sampling. In this paper, we propose a fine-grained theoretical analysis of CAV construction in order to quantify their variability. Our results, confirmed by experiments on several real-life datasets of four different modalities, point to an universal result: the variance of CAVs declines roughly as $1/N$, where $N$ is the number of random examples. Based on this, we give practical recommendations for a resource-efficient application of the method.
