paragraphs: Concept-based explanations aim to describe model behavior using meaningful concepts rather than only assigning importance to individual features. Concept Activation Vectors, or CAVs, are a prominent tool for this purpose. Their construction involves randomly sampling training examples, so repeating the procedure can produce different vectors even when the model being explained stays the same.

The paper analyzes this source of variability in detail. It studies how the number of sampled random examples affects the variance of the resulting CAVs. The theoretical analysis is supported by experiments on real-world datasets spanning four modalities, connecting the mathematical account to several kinds of data.

The results point to an approximately inverse relationship: variance decreases roughly as 1/N, where N is the number of random examples. This gives a practical way to reason about how additional samples affect stability and supports the authors’ recommendations for resource-efficient use. The finding concerns variability caused by CAV construction, making it useful for deciding how much sampling effort to invest in a more consistent explanation.
summary.tldr: Theory and experiments indicate that Concept Activation Vector variance decreases roughly inversely with the number of random examples used.

title: On the Variability of Concept Activation Vectors

abstract: Reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) has shown promise for training LLM agents to perform multi-turn decision-making based on environment feedback. However, most existing evaluations remain largely in-domain—training and testing are conducted in the same environment or even on the same tasks. In real-worlddeployment, agents may operate in unseen environments with different background knowledge, observation spaces, and action interfaces. To characterize the generalization profile of RFT under such shifts, we conduct a systematic study along three axes: (1) within-environment generalization across task difficulty, (2) cross-environment transfer to unseen environments, and (3) sequential multi-environment training to quantify transfer and forgetting. Our results show that RFT generalizes well across task difficulty within an environment, but exhibits unstable transfer to unseen environments, which correlates with shifts in both semantic priors and observation/action interfaces. In contrast, sequential training yields promising downstream gains with minimal upstream forgetting, and mixture training across environments improves the overall balance. We further provide detailed analyses and deeper insights, and hope our work helps the community develop and deploy generalizable LLM agents.

paragraphs: Reinforcement fine-tuning teaches language-model agents through feedback from an environment. Evaluating them only in the environment where they trained leaves an important question open: whether the learned behavior transfers when knowledge requirements, observations, or available actions change. This paper systematically examines that generalization question.

The study separates three kinds of transfer. It tests changes in task difficulty within one environment, movement to previously unseen environments, and sequential training across multiple environments. The sequential setting also measures whether learning later environments erodes earlier abilities. This design distinguishes handling harder tasks under familiar conditions from adapting to a different setting with a different interface.

The results show good generalization across difficulty within an environment, but unstable transfer to unseen environments. That instability correlates with changes in semantic priors and observation or action interfaces. Sequential training produces promising gains on downstream environments with little forgetting of earlier ones, while training on mixtures improves the overall balance. The findings give a qualified picture: the benefits of reinforcement fine-tuning depend on the kind of shift being tested.
summary.tldr: Reinforcement fine-tuning transfers well across task difficulty in familiar environments, but transfer to unseen environments is less reliable.

title: Does Reinforcement Fine-Tuning Improve Generalization of LLM Agents? An Empirical Study

abstract: Efficient deployment of large language models (LLMs) requires extreme quantization, forcing a critical trade-off between low-bit efficiency and performance. Residual binarization promises hardware-friendly, matmul-free inference by stacking binary ($\pm$1) layers, but is plagued by pathological feature co-adaptation. We identify a key failure mode, which we term inter-path adaptation: during Quantization-Aware Training (QAT), parallel residual binary paths learn redundant features, degrading the error-compensation structure and crippling the model’s expressive capacity. While prior work relies on heuristic workarounds (e.g., path freezing) that limit model capacity, we propose RaBiT, a novel quantization framework that resolves co-adaptation by algorithmically enforcing a residual hierarchy. Its core mechanism sequentially derives each binary path from a single shared full-precision weight, ensuring each path corrects its predecessor’s error. This process is stabilized by a robust initialization that prioritizes functional preservation over mere weight approximation. RaBiT redefines the 2-bit accuracy-efficiency frontier: it achieves state-of-the-art performance, rivals even hardware-intensive Vector Quantization (VQ) methods, and delivers a 4.49$\times$ inference speed-up over full-precision models on an RTX 4090.

paragraphs: Residual binarization represents model weights through stacked binary paths, offering hardware-friendly inference without matrix multiplication. Its intended advantage depends on successive paths compensating for approximation errors. This paper identifies a training failure called inter-path adaptation: parallel paths learn redundant features, weakening that compensation structure and reducing expressive capacity.

RaBiT enforces a residual hierarchy algorithmically. Each binary path is derived sequentially from a single shared full-precision weight so that it corrects the error left by its predecessor. An initialization procedure prioritizes preserving the model's function, helping stabilize this process. The approach addresses redundancy while avoiding the capacity restrictions associated with heuristic strategies such as freezing paths.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance at two bits, competitive accuracy with hardware-intensive vector quantization methods, and a 4.49-fold inference speedup over full-precision models on an RTX 4090. These results connect the training mechanism to a practical accuracy-efficiency benefit. They support residual-aware construction as a way to make multiple binary paths contribute complementary information in highly compressed language models.
summary.tldr: RaBiT makes binary weight paths correct successive residual errors, improving two-bit language-model accuracy and delivering a reported 4.49-fold inference speedup.

title: RaBiT: Residual Aware Binarization Training for Accurate and Efficient LLMs

abstract: Memory is increasingly central to Large Language Model (LLM) agents operating beyond a single context window, yet most existing systems rely on offline, query-agnostic memory construction that can be inefficient and may discard query-critical information. Although runtime memory utilization is a natural alternative, prior work often incurs substantial overhead and offers limited explicit control over the performance-cost trade-off. In this work, we present BudgetMem, a runtime agent memory framework for explicit, query-aware performance–cost control. BudgetMem structures memory processing as a set of memory modules, each offered in three budget tiers (i.e., Low/Mid/High). A lightweight router performs budget-tier routing across modules to balance task performance and memory construction cost, which is implemented as a compact neural policy trained with reinforcement learning. Using BudgetMem as a unified testbed, we study three complementary strategies for realizing budget tiers: implementation (method complexity), reasoning (inference behavior), and capacity (module model size). Across LoCoMo, LongMemEval, and HotpotQA, BudgetMem surpasses strong baselines when performance is prioritized (i.e., high-budget setting), and delivers better accuracy–cost frontiers under tighter budgets. Moreover, our analysis disentangles the strengths and weaknesses of different tiering strategies, clarifying when each axis delivers the most favorable trade-offs under varying budget regimes. Code is available at https://github.com/ViktorAxelsen/BudgetMem

paragraphs: An agent’s stored experience may contain information that matters only for a particular question. Constructing memory offline without knowing that question can waste resources or discard useful details. BudgetMem processes memory at runtime and makes the cost of that processing an explicit decision, allowing the system to adapt its effort to the current query.

The framework organizes memory work into modules, each with Low, Mid, and High budget tiers. A compact neural routing policy, trained with reinforcement learning, chooses tiers across modules. The authors examine three ways to implement these choices: changing method complexity, changing inference behavior, or changing the size of the model used by a module.

On LoCoMo, LongMemEval, and HotpotQA, BudgetMem exceeds strong baselines when a high budget prioritizes performance. Under tighter budgets, it provides better accuracy–cost frontiers. The analysis also distinguishes where different tiering strategies work best. These findings indicate that runtime memory processing benefits from query-specific allocation and that the preferred way to spend extra computation depends on the budget regime.
summary.tldr: BudgetMem learns how much computation to spend on each memory module for a given query and budget.

abstract: Online learning algorithms have recently risen to prominence due to their strong theoretical guarantees and an increasing number of practical applications for large-scale data analysis problems. In this paper, we analyze a class of online learning algorithms based on fixed potentials and non-linearized losses, which yields algorithms with implicit update rules. We show how to efficiently compute these updates, and we prove regret bounds for the algorithms. We apply our formulation to several special cases where our approach has benefits over existing online learning methods. In particular, we provide improved algorithms and bounds for the online metric learning problem, and show improved robustness for online linear prediction problems. Results over a variety of data sets demonstrate the advantages of our framework.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes online learning algorithms that update a model as observations arrive. Its formulation uses fixed potentials together with losses that are kept in their nonlinear form. This choice produces implicit update rules, making the computation of each update a central part of the method.

The authors show how to compute these updates efficiently and prove regret bounds. Regret provides a way to assess the accumulated consequences of the learner's decisions across the sequence. The framework therefore addresses both whether the updates can be carried out practically and how their cumulative performance can be controlled theoretically.

The authors apply the formulation to several specific problems. For online metric learning, they provide improved algorithms and bounds; for online linear prediction, they demonstrate improved robustness. Results across a variety of datasets support the advantages of the framework. The contribution is a general treatment of implicit learning updates together with concrete cases where retaining the nonlinear loss offers stated benefits.
summary.tldr: Efficient implicit online updates come with regret bounds and offer improvements in metric learning and robustness for linear prediction.

title: Implicit Online Learning

abstract: In this paper, we consider online prediction from expert advice in a situation where each expert observes its own loss at each time while the loss cannot be disclosed to others for reasons of privacy or confidentiality preservation. Our secure exponential weighting scheme enables exploitation of such private loss values by making use of cryptographic tools. We proved that the regret bound of the secure exponential weighting is the same or almost the same with the well-known exponential weighting scheme in the full information model. In addition, we prove theoretically that the secure exponential weighting is privacy-preserving in the sense of secure function evaluation.

paragraphs: This paper studies online prediction using advice from multiple experts when their performance information is private. Each expert observes its own loss at each step, but confidentiality prevents sharing that loss with others. The challenge is to use those private values to guide prediction without requiring their disclosure.

The authors develop a secure version of exponential weighting using cryptographic tools. Exponential weighting uses expert losses to determine how their advice contributes to prediction; the secure scheme enables those losses to be used under the privacy restriction. This preserves the role of performance feedback even though participants cannot openly exchange it.

The paper proves that the secure scheme has the same, or almost the same, regret bound as conventional exponential weighting in the full-information setting. It separately proves privacy in the formal sense of secure function evaluation. These are complementary guarantees: one concerns prediction performance over time, while the other concerns confidentiality during computation. The result connects a private information setting to familiar online-learning performance bounds.
summary.tldr: Cryptographic exponential weighting uses experts’ private losses while retaining the same or nearly the same regret bounds and providing secure-function-evaluation privacy.

title: Online Prediction with Privacy

abstract: Online learning typically aims to perform nearly as well as the best hypothesis in hindsight. For some hypothesis classes, though, even finding the best hypothesis offline is challenging. In such offline cases, local search techniques are often employed and only local optimality guaranteed. For online decision-making with such hypothesis classes, we introduce local regret, a generalization of regret that aims to perform nearly as well as only nearby hypotheses. We then present a general algorithm that can minimize local regret for arbitrary locality graphs. We also show that certain forms of structure in the graph can be exploited to drastically simplify learning. These algorithms are then demonstrated on a diverse set of online problems (some previously unexplored): online disjunct learning, online Max-SAT, and online decision tree learning.

paragraphs: Online learning usually compares a learner's performance with the best hypothesis chosen after seeing all the data. For some hypothesis classes, however, even finding that best hypothesis offline is difficult. This paper proposes local regret as a benchmark aligned with settings where local search and local optimality are more practical.

Local regret compares performance with nearby hypotheses rather than requiring comparison with the global best. A locality graph defines which hypotheses count as neighbors. The authors present a general algorithm that can minimize local regret for arbitrary such graphs. They also show that particular graph structures can make the learning procedure substantially simpler.

The algorithms are demonstrated on online disjunct learning, online Max-SAT, and online decision tree learning, including some previously unexplored online problems. The contribution changes what successful online learning asks for when global optimization is challenging. Its guarantee concerns the chosen neighborhood structure, making the definition of locality an essential part of both the learning objective and the opportunities for computational simplification.
summary.tldr: Local regret benchmarks online learning against nearby hypotheses, with algorithms for arbitrary locality graphs and simplifications for structured graphs.

title: On Local Regret
